entries.title: 2CO 2:12–16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -17ie preaching of the gospel,. "Furthermore, when !came to 'l'roas," etc. The subject of these verses is the preaching of the gospel. Notice- • I. THE DIFFICULTIES CONNECTED WI'l'H IT. "Furthenn6re, when I came to T~oas·to preach Christ's gospel, and a door was opened unto me of the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia." Just at 'the time when the apostle was about opening his mission at Troas, and the prospect of usefulness seemed most suitable, he encountered a serious difficulty, and that difficulty was the absence of Titus, whom he fully expected. The disappointment cost him such great anxiety that he resigned his purpose, retired from the scene, and wended his way in another direction. Strange that an inspirecl man should have met with such a disappointment, and stranger still that a disappointment should have so disheartened him that he relinquishes for a time the grand message with which Heaven had especially entrusted him. .Antecedently we might have supposed that a man going forth in a true spirit to preach the gospel would encounter no difficulties, that Heaven would sweep away all obstructions from his path; but not so. Perhaps no class of men encounter more difficulties in their mission than ministers. Many become so baffled, confounded, and depressed that, like Jeremiah, they exclaim, "I will speak no more in thy Name." II. THE TRIUMPHS ACHIEVED BY IT. "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place.'' The grandest of all victories is the victory over sin. He' who conquers the moral foes of one soul achieves a far grander triumph than he who lays a whole army dead upon the battle-plain. There is no grandeur, but infamy, in the latter conquest. It is here taught that these victories were achieved whenever they preached. "Always causeth us -to triumph." Wherever they preached, "in every place," and always through God, "thanks be to God." He is the Author of their victory; _he constructed the weapon, he instrncted the soldiers; he inspired and gave effect to the strokes. • III. THE INFLUENCES BEBULTING FROM IT. '' For·we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved; and in them that perish." Observe:. 1. The. 1nan.wa:d aspect of gospel preaching. (1) It quickens some. "To the other tho savour of hfo unto life." (2) It destroys others. "To the one we are the savour of death unto death." These effects occur wherever the gospel is preached. 2. The Godward aspect of gospel preaching. "We are unto God a sweet savour of Christ.~• Whatever the results of preaching, baneful or beneficial, it is acceptable to God if rightly ~ischarged. Af, the preaching of the gospel is the cause of immense good and tlie occasion of great evi_l. Like the waters of the sea, the li"ht of the·firmament, the breeze of the atmosphere, 1t is the Divine cause of good; but ~an, through the perversity of his nature, may make it the occasion of his ruin. • IV. THE SOLEMNITY CONNECTED WITH IT. Po.11I felt its solemnity and exclaims, "Who is sufficient for these things?" Who, of himself, is "sufficient'' _to expound the meaning of the gospel, to exemplify the spirit of the gospel, to inwork into h~mo.n souls the eternal principles of the goeptl ? Paul adds in another place, I' Our sufficiency is of God."

-The way in which the gospel sliooldt be yreaclted. "For we aro n?t as many, which corrupt the Word of God: but as of sincerity, but as o~ God, in the sight of God Epeak we in Christ." 'l'he words suggests the way in wlncb the gospel should be preo.che<l. • oa. n.1-17.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 43

L WITH OONBOIOU8 HONESTY. "As of sincerity.n ".rhis Is a state of mind in direct · antagonism to all duplicity. No man who is not true to hjs convictions and to himself can preach the gospel. He must be a trne man who would preach truth, a loving man who would inculcate love. To have conscious honesty he must preach his own personal 'convictions of the gospel, not the opinions of others. II. WITH 00Nsc10us DIVINITY. "As of God, in the sight of God." 1. He must be conscious that God sent him. From God, not from schools, sects, Churches, or ecclesi- astics, but direct from God himself. 2. He must be conscious that God sees him. "In "the sight of God." 'l'his consciousness will make him humble, ean:i.est, fearless, caring ·nothing for -the frowns or smiles of his audience. III. WITH c0Ns01ous CHRIBTLINESS. "Speak we in Christ." To be" in Christ" is to be in his character, in his Spirit. "The love of Christ constraineth me," etc. He who is conscious of the Spirit of Christ within him will be free from all self-seeking, all eordid motives, all cravings for popularity and fame.

entries.title: 2CO 2:1–11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Further explanations ancl clireceions touching mattei·s just a;.scussed. The most copious writer in the New Testament is the man whose inward constitution and life are most fully brought into view. If the fact itself is noteworthy, the art of -its management is even more significant. Didactic treatises would have excluded this method of blending the abstract and the concrete, and therefore the epistolary form which St. Paul adopted. What do we mean by this form? Much more, indeed, than e, facile and graceful way of communicating facts and truths. In the Epistle we have the personality of the writer interblended with doctrine, duty, experience; so that in St. Paul's case we have not merely the gospel as a body of facts and truths, but the gospel in the consciousness of a leading exponent, and, in some respects, the most prominent representative of certain phases of thnt gospel. Gentile Christianity, as distinguished from the earlier Judaic Christianity, could never have been understood except for this intermingling of Christianity as a system and Christianity as a life in the -history of our apostle. Both the conditions met in him as they met in no other apostle. The two things must not be confounded. Many in our day foll into this error and speak of Christianity as if it were only "a life." It is a life, but it is something else besides and something antecedent to life. Now, the epistolary style, and still more its method of thought, allow full play to the wholeness of Uhristianity. Its dogmas are preserved. Its experimental nnd practical forces are maintained. Its individuation is provided for. And thus, while seeing the system, we see also its life in the soul. If the psalmist, King Dnvid, is the signal representative of formal and spiritual Judaism in the Old Testament, St. Paul is the corresponding figure in the N cw Testnment. At this point we are able to estimate the very great and specific value of the Second Epistlo to tho CorinthianA. Beyond any of his writings, this un[olds the author, and does it with such masterly skill and on so comprehensive a scale as to give a twofold insight into his system nnd life. What an extension of the "Acts" I No St. Luko could have done this. It was the " Acts '' in their secret head-springs in the man, and tho man only could record whnt they were. 'fhe account of his personnl feelings is resumed in this chapter. Not only for their sakes, but for his own, the visit had been post- poned, since he was unwilling to come in sorrow. The" rod" wo11ld have been painful to him ; they wero to oxercise discipline under the directions of his letter nod thus forestall an occasion of grief to him. If he had made them sorry, who hut they coukl give him joy? '!'his was tho reason for his writing, the reason too of deferring his visit; and thus the two things hnd been designed to co-operate in one result. A controversy is like n disease; the mode of treatment must be varied to suit its stages. No doubt personal presence, conversations, direct appeals, arc best at some times for adjusting difficulties; at other times, letters nre preferable. '!'he discernment of the apostle prompted him to write and then to aw!\i~ the effect; and it was nil in the interest of pence nnd for his and their consolation. Inspired by this conficlencc, he harl written them 11, severe rebuke. It was a most paiufol duty; it was a duty, however, of love; an<l. because ot this coincidence, conscia 1cu and alicction being nt work in his soul, 44- THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cH. u. 1-17.

he had suffered most keenly, " Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears." The great soul was not af1aid of words nor of the critics of words. He had a rare kind of courage. It was the bolJness to say how much he thought and how much he felt, and to send forth his words laden with the meanings they bad for him, that they might convey exactly those meanings to others. The love ,vas not overstated, for it was a father's love towards the children of his heart: " More abundantly unto you." Evidently his paramount aim is to assure the Corinthians of his warm affection for them. Other feelings are held in abeyance; no mention now ot suspicions, jealousies, backbitings, and other wrongs, by which he had been tortured• only the love, the impassioned love, he cherished for those whose sorrow and joy wer~ his sorrow and_joy. H~w naturall_y the way is prepared for what follows! "If any have caused grief [referrmg to the mcestuous person], he bath not grieved me, but in part, that I may not overcharge you all." The Revised Verson, " If any hath caused sorrow, he hath caused sorrow, not to me, but in part (that I press not too heavily) to you all." Conybeare and Howson, "A.s concerns him who has caused the pain it is not me that he has pained, but some of you (some, I say), that I may not pre;s too harshly upon alL" Many commentators read it thus: "If any have caused grief, he J,ath grieved not me, but more or less (that I be not too heavy on him) all of you." What is the point of interest is the light in which St. Paul now regarded the offender and the punishment inflicted upon him. Punishment had been punishment; it had expressed righteous indignat.ion, npheld official order, vindicated the holy authority of law. It had been effectual in bringing the flagrant sinner to repentance and had proved a warning to others. But were the effects to stop here ? A great work had beeu done and yet other results were possible-were most desirable. Precisely here the farsighted wisdom of St. Paul attracts our admiration. Discipline of a mechanical or of a military kind is cheap enough. True reformatory and saving discipline is a costly t'iing, requiring forethought and afterthought, the looking" before and after," which has won its place among the aphorisms of statesmanship. Much fruit falls and rots just ae the ripening season approaches. Special care was needed, so the apostle argued, lest Satan should spoil the wholesome act in the sequel. "Sufficient to such a man is this puniBhment, which was inflicted of many." " Sufficient " leads the sentence. And the "many" has its weight, since in nothing is the power of the many so much felt as in condemnation. " There iB no oreature loves me, .And if I die, no soul shall pity me." This is Gloster perfected in King Richard. St. P11ul urges the forgiveness of this gross offender. On the contrary," Ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow." Make evident your love to him; so he beseeches them. If he is restored to their affection, this would prove that the Church was "obedient in all things." All through ho keeps the diITTlity and authority of the Church in commanding view, and, as ho had laid a most solemn duty on its conscience, so now he recognizes its high relationship in the matter of reconciliation. Would the brethren forgive him? So would he, and that too in the most impressive manner-" in the sight of Christ." The reaso11ing of tbe apostle at this point ought to make a most profound and lasting impression on Christian think_ers. Sincere motives and upright intentions do not always preserve good men from temble blunders in administering Church discipline. All unawares, the imagination e~aggerates, right foeling becomes jealous of itself, motives are looked at askance, a spunous consistency sets t1p its tyrannical claims, and, in no long time, law parts company with authority, and equity i6 crushed by justice. No attitude in which St. Paul appears before us is so finely characteristic of high manhood as when he pleads for extreme tLou"htfuluess and tender consideration in the use of legitimate power. Who ever ~ull"e~ed from the numberless forms of injllStice as he did? Who died daily as he did? 'l'he " beasts " at Ephesu8 were not merely Buch as do physical violence, but in their utter want of all moral sensibility to truth and right. Yet this was not the worst. A.sk a man who bas ha<l a large experience in public life what has occasioned him the greatest amount of vexation, and he will tell you that it was the misrepresentation and carping criticism and wilful littleneBS of spirit pursurng him continuolly which had most cu. II. 1-17.) THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

embittered his career. St. Paul was subjected to these annoyances tbrou!(h all the middle period of bis apostolic life. And what did he learn from them? To he <listrnstful of his own heart, to keep _an open and vigilant eye on his in6rmities, to he specially guBrded as to the amb1t1ous uses of power, and to foreclose every avenue to his soul through which an entrance might be effected of a fanatical temper in rebuke, in the management of Church troubles, and in the relation sustained to the other apostles. In the_case of the C~rint~ian offender we see his lofty bearing. ~eady to forgive, glad to forgive, yet he waits till he can say to the Church, "If ye forgive anythin" I forgive also." And hear his reason," Lest Satan shonld get an advantage of us: for°;_eare not ignorant of his devices." Never could he have been St. Paul, apostle of the Gentiles, without this intense conception intensely realized of Sa.tan as an infernal a."'ent of prodigious power and unceasing activity. In his theology, in his way of looking 7't men and things, in his calculation of the forces to he met in the great conflict, it would have been inexplicably strange had he ignored or depreciated this gigantic spirit of evil. Elsewhere we have his allusions to Satan in other aspects of his character. Here he is the schemer, the wily plotter, the adroit strategist, observant of every movement, and on the alert for every opportunity. St. Paul was not afraid to acknowledge that in this matter at Corinth Satan might even yet turn things to his advanta::;e. Recall the words (1 Cor. v. 5), ." 'l'o deliver such a one unto Satan, for the destruction of the flesh;" and yet they were to labour a.nd intercede "that the spirit may be saver\ in the day of the Lord Jesus." And now, this repentant and forgiven man, shoul,l they not save him from the snares of Satan ?-save themselves, too, from being over- reached by the arch-enemy of Christ and all goodness ?-L.

entries.title: 2CO 2:12–17
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0oming to Troas; disquietude; defence of his apostleship. Quite abruptly St. Paul mentions that he came to Troas. Why he left Ephesus he does not say, but we infer it was because of his anxiety to see Titus, and hear from him how his letter to the Corinthians had been received. There was a fine opening at Troas to preach the gospel, and yet he was greatly disquieted as 'l'itus did not meet him. "Taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia." Here he met Titus, though, in the excitement of joy, he fails to state it. The sudden outburst of gmtitude, "Thanks be unto God," expresses his exultation over the good tidings Titus hail brought from Corinth, so that here, as is frequently the ea.so, wo got the outward history of events from the biography of the apostle's heart. All he had expected, and even more, had been realized, and he breaks forth in thanksgiviog. .. Ye that in waters glide, and ye thu.t walk The earth, and sto.tely trend or lowly creep, Witness if I be silent, morn or ev'n, To hill or valley, fountnin or fresh sho.do, Mu.de vocal by my song, and tnught his praise." St. Paul was not a silent man in his happiness. No depth of emotion safolied him unless it could be imparted to others. On this occasion his soul found uttcrnuco in thanking God, "which always causeth us to triumph in Christ." A militnry triumph rises before him; the victorious general is returning to the capital; the long procession moves before his eye; and, in the train, the captives brought home are conspicuous. Such a captive is the apostle following the ch1uiot of his Lord. "Yet (at the same time, by a characteristic change of metaphor) a.n inconsc-boa.ror, scattering incense (which was always done on these occasions), as the procession moves on" (Conybeare and Howson). Christ is the fragrance; " we are unto God a sweet i;avour of Christ." Whether men are saved or lost, Christ is Christ, and the fragrance cannot perish. ThE1re will be a " savour of death unto death " nnu a " savour of life unto life;" but, in eit.her issne, the glory of God's government is maintained. For, so far as we can see into the relations of Christ to man and of man to Christ, tho fundnmental fact in each aspect of the subject is human freedom. Of his own freewill Christ took upon himself our flesh and blood, sutrorod, and died; and of our owu free-will made such by him and acted on as such by the Holy Spirit, we 1Lccept hi:1 atoneme~t. If we reject the offered mercy, the act of our rt!joction testifies to tho infinitude of the mercy, and the" savour of Chrlat" is none tho less" aweo~" in itsdf, 46 THE SECOND EPISTLE_ TO THE CORI,NTHIA~S. [oH. u. 1-17,

"And who is sufficient for these things?" Here is no one-sided gospel, that accommo. dates conscience to taste, and allows a compromise between duty and inclination. Here is a gospel that is the "savour of death unto death" and of "lifo unto life." Who is competent to maintain its stem truthfulness by preaching both these.doctrines? The test of a faithful minister lies in the wise and earnest use of each class ot facts. Is anything so difficult? Take the natural intellect; take the natural a.Jl"ections. take language as the ,·chicle of expression; and by what p·,wer of culture can a pr~cher be foUDd who can set forth the gospel in its twofoldness of "death unto death" and "life unto life"? St. Paul, in the seventeenth verse, answers the question as to sufficiency. Now, as always, it is not simply the gospel which is the power and wisdom of God, but his way of preaching it. He declares that "many corrupt the Word of God;" not of this number is he. And where does the danger of corruption exist? Jn not holding with a balanced mind the "death" ,and the "life," so as to shun .over.: statements and under-statements in each instance. 'l'o preach after St. Paul's manneD· one must have sincerity-the truth unmixed with human speculations; he must pree.ch what God has revealed as to his Law and its righteousness, no more, no less• &nd he must preach it in Christ, himself in Christ, his gospel in Christ, and so pre;ch as to spirit and temper and manner that the fragrance shall breathe in a.lJ, his words.-L. Vcrs. 3, 4.-Sympathy in gi·ief and joy. How far from a formal or mechanical ministry was that of the apostle! He entered into the circumstances and the feelings of those for whom he had laboured. Nothiug which affected their interests was indif- ferent to him. Some in his position would have said," We have,done our duty; it is no affair of ours how they act; why should we trouble ourselves regarding them?" Not so St. Paul. When the Corinthians acted unworthily, ·his -sensitive heart was distressed; when they repented, that heart boUDded with joy. This was not altogether. the effect of natural temperament ; it was the fruit of true fellowship of spirit with his Lord. I. THE SPIRIT OF SYMPATHY IS THE SPIRIT OF CHRIST AND OF CHRISTIANITY. In the earthly life of our Saviour we behold evidences ot this spirit. He rejuiced in men's joys; he wept by the grave of his friend; he sighed and groaned when he met with instances of unspirituality and unbelief. It was pity which brought him first to earth and then to the cross of Calvary. Similarly, with the precepts of the New Testament. The lesson is often virtually repeated, "Rejoice with those who do rejoice, and weep with those who weep." II. THE SPIBIT OF SYMPATHY IS 6OllETmES THE OCCASION OF SORROW. 1. The spectacle of a professing Christian falling into sin awakens commiseration and distress in the mind of every true follower of Christ. 2. The spectacle of a Christian conniving at sin, or regarding it with comparative unconcern, is painful in tho extreme to one solicitous for Christian purity, _3. Sorrow, from whatever cause, awakens sorrow in a mind sensitive as was that of Paul. IIL THE SPIRIT OF SYMPATHY IS SOMETllrlEB THE OOOABION OF JOY. Even amidst personal difficulties and opposition encountered_ in his ministry Paul was not indifferent to the joys of his converts. And when those whose conduct had pained him camo to a better mind and afforded him satisfaction, he rejoiced with them in their happiness. If there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth, surely he most resembles the Father of spirits and his immediate attendants whose heart fa lifted up with exhilaration and delight by anything that manifests the growth and victory of the Divine kingdom upon earth.-'l'.

entries.title: 2CO 2:11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The devicea of Satan. The course of St. Paul with regard to the Christian Church at Corinth was one of great difficulty. A flagrant case of immorality demanded his decided interference. Yet he wished to deal, both with the offender and with thosewho made too light of his offence, in such a way as not to endanger his personnl influeuce over the Corinthian Christians generally. If he were too. lax or too severe, in either case he would give his enemies an opportunity to maHgn him. And lie knew that there were Juda.izing teachers who were ready to attribute the immorality to Paul's doctrines of grace. So that the apostle trod a very difficult path, which Satan had set with snares on either band. He needed to be on his guard against the infidioufl oH; n. 1-17.J THE SECOND El'IS'l'LE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 47

machina.tions of the enemy, a.nd ,he ga.ve the Corinthians to understand that such was his .attitude, • I. SATAN'S DEVIOES ABE MANY AND VARU,!!D •. The resources af an earthly foe ouo-ht not, to be under-estimated by a general who would gain the victory; and if the tactics vary with circumstances; vigilance an~ self-possession, coura.ge and care, are all needed. Satan besets Christians with many temptations,; if he cannot tempt them into consciou,i sin, he will· endeavour to entrap them into some error of judgment and conduct which may give him an advantage over them. IL SATAN'S DEVICES ARE SKILFUL AND CBA.FTY. In the temptation of our Lord this was abundantly manifest, and, the Saviour gave his disciples to ~nderstand that they would be called upon to endure the assaults of the same unsleepmg foe. Against his ever-varying tactics, against his all but inexhaustible resources, it becomes, therefore, every Christia.n soldier to be upon his guard. ill, SATAN'S DEVICES ARE THE MEANS OF SNARING MANY OF THE UNWARY, Some who once ran well have been hindered. Some who have resisted one enemy have fallen beneath the attack of another. 'fhe annals of every Church, however pure, tell of those against whom the adversary has directed his blows only too successfully, "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." IV, SATAN'S DEVICES NEED TO BE WITHSTOOD WITH WATCHFULNESS AND l'RAYEK, It is something not to be ignorant of them. The unwary a.nd unthinking are entrapped through very ignorance. Yet knowledge is no sufficient protection. A distrust of our own ability and a reliance upon superior power and wisdom are indispensably necessary in order to safety and deliverance. Well may the inspired counsel be received with gratitude and acted upon with diligence, " Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.''-T.

entries.title: 2CO 2:12
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -.An open door, Men a.re prone to think what doors are open to them to enter, through which they may pass to their own profit, or advancement, or pleasure. Paul's was an unselfish and benevolent nature. He was a true follower of Christ, who came, not to do his own will, and not to be ministered unto, but to minister. Again and again, in the course of his life, his hea.rt was gladdened by the spectacle of a door of holy service set open before him by God's providence, inviting him to enter in and in the name of the Lord to take possession, I. 'l'HE OPEN DOOR LE.ADS TO OPPORTUNITIES OF WORK FOB CHRlBT, To the truo Christian this is more desirable than aught beside, Paul went nowhere but some door opened before him. A synagogue was open ; he entered it, and reasoned out of the Law or the propheui. A market-place thronged with citizens a.fforded him opportunity for preaching the true God and the eternal life. Even a prison door, when it closed upon him, did not shut him off from human souls. It is well thnt Christians should think, not so much of their own interests, as of the service of their Master, II. THE OPEN DOOR .lB BET OPEN BY DIVINE PROVIDENCE, " Opened of the Lord" is the apostle's expression, We mn.y not see the hand, but we should not ignore it. Whon God himself makes " way, his doing so is " command to his people to adopt and to follow it. \Vhen he opens, " no man can shut." III. THE OPEN DOOR IS A DOOR OF rn0MlBE TO THOSE WHO WILL ENTER IN, Why is the door set open? Is there no purpose in this? Surely it is a want of faith to hold back when the Lord himself so mnnifestly encourages his servants; to "go in and possess the land." • IV, THE OPEN DOOR Wll.L BE, SHUT AGAINST THOSE WHOSE NEGLIGENCE OR DIS• OBEDIENCE HINDERS THEM FROM ENTERING IT. As the door of salvation will be closed against those who fail to enter in, so the door of service will be 8hut to exclude those who turn aside when the hand of God ha.a opened_it and has beckoned them to enter, but has beckoned them in vain.-T.

entries.title: 2CO 2:14–16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-77ie solemnity of Che ministry. A Roman triumph, to which the apostle refers in this passage, was the most magnificent of earthly pageants. The con,queror, in whose honour it was given, was an iUWJtrious commander, who bad defeated an enemy or gained a province. The 1'0uto traversed by the triumphal procession la.;y through Rome to the Capitol itself. 'l.'he spectators who fea~tcd their eyes 48 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIIE oORIN'l'HIANS. [en. u. 1-17.

, upon the sight were the vast population of the city. Before, the victor passed onwarJs the captives taken in the campaign, and the spoil which had been wrested from the foe. Behind, followed the army, flushed with victory and rejoicing in the insolence and i pride oi' military m1.gbt. 'l'he conqueror himself, mounted aloft upon bis car was tbe centre of observation and attraction. Every mrLrk ()f honour was paid to him. Sacrificcij were offered by the priests to the gods to whose favour victory w11s. ascribed. Incense- bearers marched in the procession, and fragrant clouds ascended, floatina in the air and mintli~g with.the shouts and wi~h the strains of ma!tial music. Anl'in the temples sacnfic1al offermgs were accompamed by the presentation of the odorous incense. • I. 'l'HE TRIUMPHS oF THE GOSPEL. The warfare of the Word is against the sins of the rebels who have defied the authority of the Most High. In apostolic times the proaress of the gospel, though often opposed and often checked, appeared to the view of Pa~l as a triumphal progress. God, who had triumphed over the enemies whom he converted into his friends and comp1mions, made them, as his representatives, triumph in their 'turn and admitted them to share his triumph over the enemies of truth and righteousness. ' 11 THE INCENSE-BEARERS IN TlIE TRIUMPHAL TRAIN. There is a prodigality of wealth in the imagery here employed. Paul and hie fellow-ministers were themselves both captives and also incense-bearers-" unto God a sweet savour of Christ." As the Son of the Eternal is infinitely acceptable to his Father, so those who share his mission and pnrpose, and faithfully pnblish his gospel, are well-pleasing to him, as the odour of the fragrant incense to the nostril. III. THE ACCOMPAl-"IMEXTS AND RESULTS OF TlIE GOSPEL TRIUMPH. These are twofold and opposed. 1. To the peri,;bing the ministry is a sentence of death. Some captives were taken aside and put to death in cold blood as the procession approached the Capito line hill. The incense to such was deadly-an odour premonitory of a violent and miserable death. Thus the proclamation of the gospel, in itself an unspealmble blessing, is actually the occasion of the condemnation of unbelievers, who reject and despise it. 2. To those in course of salvation the ministry is a message of life; Welcome and pleasant alike to God and man, the glad tidings of redemption tell of life to those whose desert is death. A welcome and delightful fragrance to the saved, it promises participa- tion in the glorious victory and the eternal reign of the Divine Redeemer.-T.

entries.title: 2CO 2:14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The triumph. The emotional and susceptible nature of the Apostle Paul was quick to recognize either opposition or success. And when it occurred to him, in the providence of God, to meet with instances in which his message was gratefully welcomed and he himself was cordially appreciated, his heart was fille<l with joy, and be was eager to utter forth gratitnde and praise. When elated with prosperity in his evangelistic work, he felt that God was always making him to triumph. His spiritual successes were to him more glorious than the triumph which the victorious general enjoyed upon his return to Rome, when he ascended the Capitoline hill, with his fellow-warriors in the procession and his captives in hie train. What an ins[Jimtion do these words c,f the apostle afford to those who are engaged in the service of tho Saviour, and are expr.riencing the vicissitudes of earthly ministry I I. IF THERE 18 WARFARE, THERE WILL DE VICTORY. The Christian lire is a. warfarr, involvino-0 effort, dao~er, and resistance. Much more manifestly does thiR figure apply to those who preach the goi;pel, especially as evangelists among the heathen, tho degraded, the unbelievi~g. Such stand in n~ed _both of. spiritual courage and ol spiritual weapons. And m the stress of the confl1ct, m the n01se and tumnlt of warfare, it is well for them to remember that the issue is not uncertain, that conquest is close at hand. JI. IF THERE ARE ENEMIES, THEY WIJ.L BECOME EITHER CAPTIVES OR, DETTF.R STILL, Al,LIES AND FELLOW-SOLDIERS. When spiritual opponents are many and daring, and when their onset is sore and perhaps alarmin)(, the heart of the soldier of Christ may sometimes sink within him. But he is required to estimate the fortunes of the war, not by human lJrobabilities, but by Divine predictions. Of those who oppose themselves none shall prevaiL Some shall be vanquished and put to shame. Others shall confess the justice and the grace of Christ, shall lay down the arms of rebellion, shall enlist in the apiritual host, shall take to them the armour of God. III. JI THBRE 18 DISAPPOINTMl'!NT, THERE WILL BE REOOMPENSE. Paul knew often OB. u. 1- 17.J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 49

enough what it is to be cast down. The higher the hope, the bitterer the sorrow when that hope is frustrated. It sometimes happens that, where the Christian warrior spends all his strength, and attacks the enemy with courage and perseverance, -there he experiences the most humiliating rebuff. Then let him be assured that different experience is in store for him. Foes shall yield, whose stubbornness, it seemed to him, no power could subdue. Victory shall be to the faithful and to the brave. IV. lF THERE BE A SHARING OF CHRIST'S CROSS, THERE SHALL BE ALSO A SHARING OF ms THRONE. Our Lord, the Captain of our salvation, knew by experience the power of the enemy. And can it be expected that with us all will be prosperou~? Shall we not be followers of him, and know the likeness of his death? Thus shall it be given to him that overcomcth to sit down with him upon his throne.-T.

entries.title: 2CO 2:16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" Who is suffir:ienH" Those to whom the ministry of the gospel of Christ is merely a profession, who regard the offices of religion as a routine, who consider chietl.y such emoluments and advantages 11s may be connected with it, read these words with astonishment and without sympathy. But those who think as Paul thonght of the ministry, with a wondering amazement at the grace of God and at the provision made in Christ for the passage of that grace to man, those who realize the preciousness of the soul and the solemnity alike of life and of eternity, cannot but cherish a conviction that, for a service so high and holy as the ministry of God's Word, no human qualification can suffice. I. THE INSUFFICIENCY OF HUMAN POWER. To understand this we must regard: 1. The deficiencies of the human agent. No minister has an 11dequatc view of the Saviour he preaches ; none has a sufficiently keen sympathy with the souls of his fellowmen; none has a power of persuasion commensurate with the necessities of the case; none has the burning zeal for God which was perfectly displayed by Christ alone. 2. The peculiar difficulties of the work to be accomplished. 'l'he ignorance, the levity, the prejudices, the wilfulness, the gross sinfulness of men,-all must be taken into account if we would have a just conception of the magnitude of the great task which is entrusted to the Christian minister. IL THE SUFFICIENCY OF DIVINE GRACE. 1. This is revealed to those, o.nd to those alone, who are sincerely conscious of their own powerlessness and the inadequacy of all human aid. 2. God's own commission is an assurance that he will not withhold the assistance needed. The work is his; his is the call and his the authority. 3. God, by his Spirit, assists all lowly and faithful agents in his service, strengtheni!!g the feeble, so that by their means, however seemingly inadequate, great results are accomplished. 4. By the same invisible but marvellous agency God overcomes the obstacles encountered in the sinner's heart, and makes the word of man effectual becauso the vohicle of the power and grace of Hcaven.-T.

Vor. 4.-The pains of rebukin,q. I. THESE ARE VERY REAL TO GRACIOUS NATURES. Somo delight to castigate; but they are not gracious or noble-they aro rather fittod to foel the rod than to wield it. An affectionate parent often suffers moro than his chastened child; a faithful pastor than the rebuked Church member. Pan! said that if he came to Corinth he would not spare; before he came, he did not spare himself. '!'here was grief at Corinth, but as much or more in Macedonia. Joy in causing suffering is a mnrk of degradation. We condemn pleasure obtained from cruel sports; pleasure obtained from wounding minds is even more barbaric and revolting. We may feel compelled to rebuke, and that sharply. Wo can never be justified in extrncting joy from the suffering occasioned. I!, WHEN REBUKE IS PAINFUL TO THE REBUKER IT IS MORE LIKELY TO PROVE EFFICACIOUS TO THE REBUKED. 1. There is evidence of qualification to rebulce. 'l'ho rebuke docs not spring from personal feeling. 2. Undue harshness will be avoided. 3. A gracious tenderness is likely to permeate the severest rebulce. 4. If lcnown to tha rebulced, a salutary influen~e will be exercised. Nothing is moro irritating or hardening than to be rebuked by one who evidently enjoys his office. But if the one who points out our fault is evidently deeply pained himself, we must be very obdurate if we are insensible to snch an appeal. The wayward child is conquered, not by tho rod in his mother's hand, but by the tears in her eye~. TI, COlllN'l'flIAN8 1 11 50 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE COJ;UNTHIANS. [oH. n. 17 17,.,

III, 'l'HE OBJECT OF RIGHT REDUKING IS NOT THE PAIN OF ,THE REDUKED. This sl1ould ever _be kept in mind. We are not ju~ges to pass sentences of mere punishme,nt. We may grieve our fellows, but only for their good. We may cause pain, but only as a means to something else. Castigation is a beginning, not an end. We have effected nothing except failure if we have merely caused sorrow. It is a thankless task indeed merely to make men sad. It is a noble one to make them sad that we may make them holier. ~v. RIG~ REBUKL'-G IS EVIDENCE OF MUCH LOVE. N?t to suffer sin upon our ne1gh~ur is a great duty ! b~t the best natures are apt to shrmk from reproving. Great love will compel them, as it did Paul. We often cannot show our love more conclusively. It may not at once be apparent to men, but it will to God-and to mea. by-and-by. The strongest evidence of Paul's love for the Coria.thian Church was exhibited in the rod which he held over it. So of God himself: those whom he loves he chastens. (Heb, xii. 6).-H. •

entries.title: 2CO 2:5–11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Restoring the backslider. L CHURCH DISCIPLINE SHOULD BE ADMINIS- TERlm BY THE CHURCH. "This punishment which was inflicted by the many" (ver. 6). Not by an individual, be he the pope himself, nor by priests or clei·"y, but by the whole body of the individual Church or a majority of its memb~rs. A Christian bas a right to be judged by bis peers. II. CHURCH DISCIPLINE SHOULD EVER HA VE IN VIEW RESTORATION, Its object is not to punish the offender so much as to do him good, ~nd at the same. time to preserve the Church's purity. Church discipline should not be regarded as a final act towards the backslider, but with it should ever be associated prayers and, hope that the severance may be brief. The Church rejects that she may accept ; she casts out that she may receive back again. So Church discipline should never be of a character to hinder repentance or to render restoration impossible. III. CHURCH DISCIPLINE SHOULD BE ADMINIBTERED WITH GREAT DISCRETION. 1. On the one hand, it may be too slight and not produce suitable effects, 2. On the other, it may be so excessive as to drive the offender to despair. 3. In either case Satan will gain aa. advantage (ver. 11), which he is ever seeking and has often found when the Church or its lea<lers have attempted the delicate task of discipline. 'l'he Church's discipline of persecution and intolerance has served .the devil's purposes admirably iu many a dark century. And the Church's discipline of indifference and false charity has done similar service in many a century boasting of its light and breadth of thought and liberty. IV. P&.'ITENCE ON THE PART OF AN OFFElfDER IS A STRONG ARGUMENT FOR PROMP'l RESTORATION TO FELLOWSHIP. The duty of restQration is not so fully recognized as it might be. Often it is the predilection of the powers tha.t be, rather than the condition of the offender, which determines whether· he shall be restored or not. But when the honour of the Church has been vindicated, and the offender ,is undoubtedly contrite, the way of duty is clear. A Church which will not restore then, deserves to be excommunicated itself. , V. RESTORATION IS NOT TO BE TO TOLERATION, DOT TO LOVE. The love is to exist whilst the discipline is being inflicted. It ie to manifest itself unreservedly when discipline is removed. Many are restored to. suspicion, ~oldness, cout_eml?t-a r~st?ra• tion which paves the way for a more fatal fall. If God forgives some profossmg Christiane as they forgive others (and this is their frequent prayer), their share of the Divine forgi\·eness is likely to be a very slea.der one.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 2:14–17
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The constant triumph of the faitliful minister. I. HE TRIU.MP,HS DECAUSE WHEREVER HE GOES BE MAKES KNOWN GoD AND CHRIST. 'l'bis is a true triucµph. Jf be succeeds in doing this he has a great success-the success of performance of duty and of fulfilment of the Divine will. Moreover, the kingdom of God is nlmost certain to be extended. Apparent failure, when more closely examined and tried by the test of_ time, will often be found to be success. II. l:hs 'fllIUMPH IB NOT DEPENDENT VPON THE RECEPTION OF ms MESSAGE, 1. To some hi,B word is a savour from death unto death. 'fhe Christ proclaimed is to them a dead Christ, and his gospel lifeless and powerless, leading them only to douser s11iritual. oH. u. 1-17.J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 51

death. This is very dishe\irtening when viewed under one aspect. But Christ is preached, the work is acccptal1lo to God, the Divine mercy is vindicated, and the responsibility of the disastrous issue re.sts solely on the rejecters. The excellence of the truth is aemonstrated by its rejection on the part of the vile and sin-loving. 2. To others hi5 word .i·s a savour from life unto life. .Here the triumph is unquestioned by all. A livW,g IJhrist is recognized, and one who has life-giving power. _Ill. HE TRIUMPHS ONLY. AB HE IS FAITHFUL, For only so does he honour God and set forth the truth as it is in Jesus. The faithful minister: 1. Does not corrupt the Word of God (ver. 17). Many do (1) by false interpretation, (2) bias, (3) insinuation, {4) omission, (5) addition. Prompted by (1) gain, (2) applause, (3) carnal preferences. 2. But (1) distrusts. hfuiself, crying," Who is sufficient for these things?" (2) uses utmost. sincerity; (3) gets his message from God-" of God" (ver.17); (4) speaks as in the sight of God; (5) speaks in Christ, in communion with him as the Head. IV. H:rs .TRIUMPH IS. O:F Gon. He is le.d in triumph by God (ver. 14). God h!lll triumph~d over him, and now God triumphs through him. His sufficiency is of God. ( eh. iii. 5). He has no power when he only has his own; he has all power when he bas God's.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 2:1–4
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
..:...The sorrow of faithful love. The apostle has still in mind the unfaithful member who had brought so sad a. disgrace upon the whole Church. His conduct in the matter, especially in changing his mind when he was fully expected at Corinth, had been misrepresented, and made the occasion of accusations against him as a fickle-minded, self-willed man. He therefore here explains why he did not visit Corinth while it remained uncertain bow the offending member would be· treated. He bad no thought but for the truest well-being of the Corinthian Church. He could not leave them to go on in sin. He could not bear to think that those whom he had instructed in Christ were indifferent to sin. Love,. feeling sorrow for the sinning member and for tho dishonoured Church, cannot be satisfied without eame&i; wa.rnings about the sin ll.Ild efforts to remove it. . Such efforts carry and express both the sorrow and the love. illustrate by the patient, gracious pleadings of God with sinning and backsliding lsrael, as given in the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Hosea. I. SucH SORROWING LOVE CAN PERSONALLY SUFFER. Here it led the apostle to act in a way which brought to him the bitterest form of suffering, even the suspicion o.nd mistrust of his very friends. Even that he would bear, if but his desire for the spiritual welfare of the Corinthion Church could be realized. "Men might think thot it had cost him little to write sharp words like those which he has in his mind. Ho remembers well what he felt as he dictated them-tho intensity. of his feelings, pain th11t such words should be needed, anxiety ns to their issue, the very tears which then, os at other times, were the outflow of strong einotion. Those who were indignant 11t his stern worcls should remember, or at least learn to believe this, and so to see in them the strongest proof of bis abounding love for them." The heart of St. Paul was in this matter 11s the heart of him who su.id, "As many as I love I rebuke and chasten," Illustmto whot a pressure on personal feeling it is. for the parent or teacher to chasten. '!'hey often suffer much more than do those whom they feel called to smite. Even the misunderstanding, and even the ten1porary hatred, of those whom we would benefit, mu,,t be borne, in our earnest endeavours to deliver them from the dominion nml defilement of their sins. II. Suen SORROWING LOVE CAN DEAL SEVERELY WITH TUE SINNEII. It is never love to pass by sin. It is no true love that touches the sin too lightly and give~ inefficient and unworthy apprehensions of it. St. Paul seemed to be too severe. Ho could not be. The case coiled for nn extreme of severity. It was not merely tbot tho offence was an open and scandalouo one, but, whnt was oven worso, the Church soemcd to bo pervaded by a false tlentiruent concerning it, and manifc~tcd no distress in having tho guilty member among them. In somo wny, St. Paul folt, ho must urouso thom tu a sense of their shame. Strong l:mguuge, refusal to givo them a personal visit, 1u,ythin~ that woul<l wakE:n o. sense of ain, were necesso.ry. It ha<l been tho time for sterncct rebuke, 4.nd still love needs to use severity. For somo forms of sin tho gontlor pdr- sua.sions are ine!Ticicnt; ruen must be roughly shaken out of their self-confidences, at,ll their pride must bo humbk<l an<l broken. The Church of mo<lorn days ea gnwcly fail~ 52 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [ea. u. 1-17,

of her witness and her duty because she has no "discipline," no severe dea\incrs for har grave offenders. She bas no love to burn against transgressors. " III. Suen SORROWING LOVE CAN SHOW FINE CONSIDERATION FOR THE FEELINGS OP OTHERS. Paul did not wish to make his second visit to Corinth in grief, and if he had carried out his first plan that would have been the almost inevitable result. He would wait, delaying bis visit, so that he might have the chance of seeing them with a smile on hi_s fa.ce, after receiving the tidings of their heeding hi~ warning :1nd putting a.way the sm. "The second reason St. Paul alleges for not commg to Corinth is apparently a selfish one-to spare himself pa.in. .And he distinctly says he had written to pain them, in order that he might have joy. Very selfish, as at :first it sounds• but if we look closely into it it only sheds a brighter and fresher light upon the exquisite unselfishness and delicacy of St. Paul's character. He desired to save himself pa.in because it gave them pa.in. He desired joy for himself because his joy was theirs. He will not separate himself from them for a. moment ; he will not be the master and they the school; it is not I and you, but we; 'my joy is your joy, as your grief was my grief.'" Do we love enough to rebuke and punish those whom we love?-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 2:5–11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The Church's dealings with unworthy members. "The main defence of the apostle against the charge of :fickleness in the non-fulfilment of his promise was that be had abstained from going to Corinth in order to spare them the sharp rebuke ne must have administered had he gone thither. A great crime had been committed; the Church bad been compromised, more especially as some of the Corinthians had defended the iniquity on the ground of liberty, and St. Paul had stayed a.way after giving his advice, that not he, but they themselves, might do the work of punishment. He gave sentence that the wicked person should be put away, but he wished them to execute the sentence. For it was a matter of greater importance to St. Paul that the Corinthians should feel rightly the necessity of punishment, than merely that the offender should be punished." We notice- I. THE SINNER WITHL'i THE CmraCH GRIEVES THE WHOLE CmraCH. If one member suffer, all the members suffer with him; and if one member sin, the whole Church ought to feel grieved and distressed by the sin. St. Paul argues that, if a Church fails to clear itself of complicity with the wrong of its members, the guilt of such wrong attaches to it as well as to him. No man within Christ's Church can be alone in his sin, for we are "members one of another." The judgment of the Church may be the means of winning the penitence of the erring member. I!. THE SINNER WHEN PENITENT SHOULD FIND THE LOVE AND FOilGIVENESB OF THE WHOLE CITTIBcH. In relation to him there should be harmonious and united Church action. Yet, in actual fact, the wrong-doing of individuals too often creates party feeling. Some take the side of the wrong-doer and prevent the full exercise of Church discipline. lll. SUCH FORGIVENESS OF THE CHURCH MAY EXPilEBB Goo's FORGIVENESS. It is only becoming, and only efficient, as following upon God's forgiveness. And it has its special use in being the earthly assurance of the Divine forgiveness and acceptance. The Church can give no absolution ; it can only find expression for the absolution which God has already granted to the penitent, and add its forgiveness of the wrong so far as it disturbed Church relations. In the proper expression of Church feeling towards moral offenders, the Apostle Paul, as a recognized Church leader, herein sets an efficient example. He is as jealous for the Church's honour And mercifulness as be ie for tho restoration of the penitent offender.-R. T. • Ver. 1L-8atanic devices within the Church. Tho reference hero made to Satan must be regarded as figurative. It should not be used as an argument for tho oxistence of a supreme evil spirit, however the existence of such a spirit may bo assumed, St. Paul ha.a elsewhere used the figure of" delivering unto Satan" (1 Tim. i. 20). By thiY we are to understand a solemn excommunication or oxpulsioh from the Church, possibly with the infliction also of some bodily disease. The offender was to bo left to feel all the physical and social consequences of his wrong-doing, in the hope that, through suffering, be might be brought to a sense of his sin. Satan is thought of as the power which leads men into vice and then torments them when they have followed the leadings. The apostle conceives of God as ovorrullng tbo very sin, and consequent ea. n. 1-17.J 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE To 1'HE CORINTHIANS. 53

suffering, for good, through them bringing the Rinner to a hopeful penitence and humility of heart. There was, however, this danger to be recognized anJ. guarded against. Satan might, as it were, outwit the Church, in its dealing with erring members, and make the suffering following on sin produce remorse rather than repentance. "Penitence works life, remorse works death. The latter ~s more destructive even than self-righteousness, for it crushes, paralyzes, and kills the soul." There must consequently be a judicious limitation of the punishment, and a watchfulness for the first opportunity of showing mercy and granting restoration. "Not to release the offender from the bondage when he was truly penitent would be to afford the enemy of souls an opportunity of which he would not be slow to avail himself. Nothing is so likely to plunge a man into every kind of crime as despair." For St. Paul's experience of Satanic schemes, devices, and strategy, comp. eh. xii. 7 ; 1 Thess. ii. 18 ; Eph. vi. 12. We may treat the subject in its wider and more general applications if we illustrate the following and other ways in which Satan may be said to get advantage within a Church:- 1. BY OVERMASTERING INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS. Failure does not come to the Church as a whole, but to individuals in it. All are exposed to temptation and evil. We must be in the world, and Christian men may yield themselves to the power of the "lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life." Some of the gravest of our Church anxieties arise from the moral failure of individual members. Illustrate cases occurring in youth-time ; but especially cases in men's middle life, when the passions for wealth, sensuality, or drink often:gain an overmastering energy. Show also the force that may be gained by the suddenness of the temptation, and by the condition of spiritual unwatchfulness in which the man may be found. The forms of failure which we usually find are dishonesty, immorality, or self-indulgence in meat or drink. But, by the law that those in the Church are members one of another, the failure of one is the shame, and should be the distress and grief, of all. Satan disturbs and injures a whole Church if he can gain influence over one member; and to do this is ever" one of his devices." II. BY SECURING THE HARSH AND UNLOVING TREATMENT OF THOSE WHO FAIL. But he was watchful for signs of gracious influence effected by the punishment, and ready at once to restore and forgive the penitent.. He never " breaks the bruised reed or quenches the smoking flax." Man's punishments are always in danger of running to excess. Ill. BY MAKING A CHURCH INDIFFERENT TO THE MORALITY OJ' ITS MEMBERS. Lo.xity, cnrelessness about purity of life, uprightness of relations, o.nd consistency of conduct, often <lo creep into Churches, and they are among the most grievous of "Satt\Il's de- vices." Illustrate from the evil work done by Carnal Security, in the town of Mnnsoul, as described in John liunyan's 'Holy ,var.' Illustrate by the lesson that wo.s taught in the failure of Isrncl at the siege of Ai, when the "accursed thing" was in their camp. IV. BY PERSUADING A CHURCH TO MAKE ITS FORGIVENESS A. FORMALITY, NOT A FULL RESTORATION. 'l'oo often this grave mistake is made: the offender is formally restored io membership, but he is not really tnken back into the love and trust of tho brethren, and he receives no Higns of restored confidence and no help back to goodness. Ho is a blighted man, and it seems to him that his slip or foll can never really be forgotten, never reo.lly be wiped out, and therefore he must hang down his head among the brcth rcn to his dying ,lay. 'l'he Church's forgiveness ancl rcstoratio11 must bo liko God'~, n help to the erring one towards realizing the glorioWl cou-.1,leteneas of Gocl'e forgi vings, for- 54. THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [en. n. 1-17.

gettings, and restorings. For he casts our sins behind his back, and into the depths of the sea. "As the punishment of man is representative of the punishment and wrath ?f God, so_ the absolution of man is representative of the forgiveness of God." T. • Vers. 1~, 13.-:--P,·ovidential doors .. Introduce by describing the leading instances of prov1dent1al deliverance, care, and gmdance in the life of the Apostle Paul. Especially dwell_ on the cases in which his life ,vas preserved from peril and from the plots of his en_e~1es. ri:he refe1:ence made _in_our text is rather to the gracious way in which his m1ss1onary Journeymgs and m1ss10nary spheres had been opened before him; and the illustration may be taken from the singular way in which doors were opened and shut, when the Divine will was for the apostle to preach the gospel in Europe (see Acts xvi; fi-9). For the figure of a "door" for an "opportunity," see 1 Cor. xvi. 9; Rev. iii. 8. The truth of the Divine providence ordering our iives is• not one that is so familiar to us as it was to our fathers. Possibly our warmer·thought of God's fatherly care has taken the place of the colder conception of an impersonal providence. Still, it may be well to revive the older notion and make it glow·with Christian sentiment and feeling. I. THE ORDERING OF PROVIDENCE FOil EVERYBODY. Irrespective of religious state arid relations. Illustrations of this are found in all times of· danger, disease, or calamity. Some are taken and some are left. We constantly rea~ of remarkable providential escapes. II. THE SPECIALITY OF PROVIDENCE FOR CHRISTIANS. It nia.y in part be that Chris~ tians more readily recognize the hand of God in their rescuings and guidances, but we may also believe that God gives a special protection to his own. Such a belief may be a great comfort to us, but it must be kept from becoming exaggerated and extravagant. The Christian cannot always be preserved, because his suffering may be for the' good of the whole. III. THE ATTITUDE IN WHICH CHRISTIANS SHOULD STAND TOWARDS THE EVER-ACTIVE PROVIDENCE. It may be shown to include (1) 'earnest watchings; (2) patient waitings; (3) prompt actings; (4) full and unhesitating obediences; and (5) thankful rejoicings. -R.T.

Heroes, in tlie older days of the apostle, were usually great generals, leaders of mighty armies, conquerors of other nations-men whose "glory" came from desolated cities, down-trodden races, wasted harvests, and crushed and bleeding hearts. And such heroes were permit~ed to have a "triumph," as it was called. A triumphal procession was arranged_ in th~1~ honour, an_d to this event the Roman generals looked as to the very goal of their amb1t10n. Magni• ficent and thrilling scenes they must have been. The general '!as received, at the g~tes of the imperial city, by all that was noble and grave and venerable among the ollic~al~, and he was led from the gate through the crowded and shouting streets t~ the Capitol. First marched the ancient men, the grave· senators of the Roman council, headed by a body of magistrates. Then came the trumpeters, making the air ring again with their prolonged and joyous blasts. Then followed a long train of carriages a"nd fr~'?es l11den with the spoils brought from battle-fields or plundered from conquer~d c1t1es, the articles which were most remarkable for their value, or rarity, or beauty bemg fully exposed to view. There might be seen models of the forts or cities whi_ch had been captured ; gold and silver statues, pictures, handsome vases, and embro1dere~ stuffs. Then came a band of players on the flute, and then white bulls and ox?n d?stmed ,f?r sacrifice; and incense-bearers, waving to and fro their censers, and· sendmg forth their sweet savour. '!'hen were seen caged lions nnd tigers, or monstrous elephants, or other 8trange creatures, brought as specimens from the captive lands. And then the procession filled with pathos, for there followed the lenders of the conquered foe, and tl~e lnng train of inferior captives, all bound and fettered, and altogether ~ sad and humiliating sight. At last came the great conqueror, standing in a. spleD;d1d chariot, drawn Ly four milk-white horses, magnificently adorned, the conqueror ~canng n roynl _sceptre, aud having his brow encircleJ with a laurel crown. officers, the horse-soldiers, and the vast army of foot-soldiers, each one holding aloft a spear adorned ~ith laurel boughs. And so the procession moved on through the crowded, shouting· streets until it reached the Capitoline hill. There they halted, dragged some of tl;iose poor captives aside to be killed, and then offered their sacrifices and began their triumphal feast. St. Paul's mind was evidently full of such a scene as this, and he took his figures from it. He says that God permits us, as apostles and ministers, always to triumph with Christ. We are, through grace, always conquering generals. But St. Paul fixed his thoughts chiefly on those miserable, naked, fettered captives, who were going on to death. He could not help thinking-What was the sound of the clanging trumpet and the piping flute to them-poor hopeless oues? What was the savour of sweet incense .in the air to them-poor agitated ones? Some among them may indeed have had the promise of life, and to them the savour of the incense would be sweet; it would be" life u'nto life." But so many of them knew what their fate must be; they dreaded the worst; they trembled as they came nearer to the ascent of the hill; and as the wind wafted the savour of the incense to them they could but sadly feel that it was a savour of "death unto death'." And the apostle thought of his life-work of preaching the gospel. It was even thus with the savour of the gospel-triumph. To some it was death, to others it was life. Not, indeed, at 'the arbitrary will of some proud general, but as the necessary issue of the relations in which men stand to a preached gospel; for "he that bath the Son bath life, and he that bath not the Son of God hath not life, but the wrath of God abideth on him." I. THE PROPER RESULT OF A PREACHED GOSPEL IS LIFE. It was God's gracious purpose that men, "dead in trespasses and sins," should have life, and havo it more abundantly. In his Son Jesus Christ life and immortality are brought to light. In the early days God set before men life and death, and, with all holy persuasions, urged them to choose life and good. This was the one absorbing purpose and endeavour of the Lord Jesus. Whilo he was here he was ever doing one thing-quickening life, restoring life, renewing life: the life of health to those affiicted, of reason to those possessed with devils, of knowledge to ignorant disciples, and even of the body to those smitten and dead. .And the apostles carried his gospel forth into nil the world as the light and life of men. Dwell upon the significance and interest of the word "life,'' and explain the new life in Christ Jesus, which the Christian enjoys. II. THE MOURNFUL RESULT OF A PREACHED GOSPEL OFTEN 1B DEATII. Our Lord used forcible but painfnl figures to express the death of the impenitent and unbelieving: "outer darkness;" " wailing and gnashing of teeth; " "worm that never dies;" "firo that none may quench." ,ve must feel the force of these things, for no man cau worthily explain the!]l. This "death" wai:l the moumful issue of II preached gospol when the Son of man was himself the Preacher. Foolish (fadnrenes besought hiw to depart out of their coasts, and leave them to their night and death. Hardened Capernaum, exalted even to heaven in privilege, must bo thrust down to hell. St. Paul must turn from bigoted and prejudiced Jews, and go to tho Gentiles, leaving the very children of the covenant in a darkness that might bo felt. Ho who camo to give life is practically found to be a Stone ot' stumbling and a Rock of offence. Five foolish virgins put their hands about their flickering lamps as they cry against the closed door; and this is the simple, awful ending of their story, "The darkness took them." Wo do see men hardened under a preached gospel now. Illustrate by tho dropping well at KnBres- borough. Water ought to soften and melt, but these waters, falling upon things, encrust thorn with stone, :me! even tum them into stone. Such may have been the droppings of the " water of life" upon us. 1'here aro only these two issues. Tho gospol must either take us by the band and lead us up into the sunlight or it must bid us away down into the dark. Only two issues, but what issues they are I Lifo I As we think of that word, all joy, light, and heaven come into our view. Death I As wo sp~ak that word, all darkness, woe, and hell oome into our thoughts. " Who indeed is sufficient for these things? "-even for the preaching of a gospel which must prove to be o. "savour of life unto life or of death unto doath."-R. '1'.

entries.title: 2CO 2:17
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Conscious simpU~ity and integrity. "The ~ord for• corrupt,' formed from a word which signifies • huckster,' or • tavern-keeper,' implies an ndultemtion like that which such people commonly practised. We, says St. Paul, l)!ay no such tricks of trn<lo THE SECOND ,EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cB. III. 1-le.

with what we preach; we do not meet the taste~ of our hearers by prophesying deceits. The ,ery fact that we know the tremendous issues of our work would hinder that." God's gospel word, the message of eternal life in Christ Jesus, may be adulterated or corrupt~d in three ways. 1. By mixing up with it foreign, inharmonious, merely human, teachings. 2. Or by making the gospel revelation into a stiffened, formal creed, over the precise terms of which we may wrangle and dispute. 3. Or by dis- Jilacing the true motive in preaching it, and giving place to low aims, and purposes of merely selfish ambition, and longing for the praise of men. The appeal of the text has its special force when we remember of what things the Judaizing party accused thu apostle. St. Paul's enemies forced this appeal from him. Usually it is enough that the sincer~ and true man sh?uld keep on bis _faitbfnl ~ay, little heeding the opinions or accusations of others, trustmg the care of his reputation to God. But occasions do arise when something like public vindication becomes necessary, and a man is called to assert bis conscious integrity. Of this we have two ,ery striking instances recorded 1n Scripture. Samuel, when set aside by the mistaken longing for a. visible king, felt deeply hurt, though more for the insult thus offered to Jehovah, the ever-present but invisible King, than for his own sake. He pleaded thus with the people: "I have walked before you from my childhood unto this day. Behold, here I am : witness against me before the Lord, and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith? and I will restore it you " (1 Sam. xii. 2, 3). And David, misunderstood and slandered, turns to speak to God in the bearing of the people, and says, " Judge me . . . according to my righteous- ness, and according to mine integrity that is in me" (Ps. vii. 8). Consider- L THE GREAT GOSPEL TRUST. 1. On the one side, the trust of Divine revelation and message. Illustrate by the direct communications of the Divine will made to the ancient prophets. These they were expected to deliver with all simplicity and com- pleteness, and without making any additions of their own to them. 2. Oa the other side, the trust of men's souls. The world was given to the apostles as the sphere in which their 11:ospel message was to be deli vored. Such a trust demanded seriousness, sincerity, and holy zeaL It should ever call out the best that is in a maa. II. THE PERIL OF ITS INJURY THROUGH THE GUILE OF THE SELF-SEEKER. Men will surely take their impressions of it from the character of the men who preach it. If we get a soiled idea of the gospel preacher, as an insincere, self-seeking maa, it is only too likely that we shall have a soiled and stained image of the gospel that he preaches in ' our minds. Men can make golden glowings or deep shadows rest on the gospel that they declare, the message which they have in trust. !II. 'l'HE FORCE OF IT AS PilESERVED WHEN THE AGENT IS GUILELESS AND SINCERE, The stream gets no foulness as it flows through him. Illustrate how men of transrarent character and beautiful piety put honour on religion. 'fhe commendation of Christ's gospel to men is (1) the pure and stainless Christ himself, and then (2) the graciousness and charm of his servants who are like him. The force behind gospel preaching is tho , life of the men who preach. The simple-minded, sincere, uncorrupted man may posi- ' tively make additions to the pra.::tical power of the gospel upon men.. Distinguish, however, between simplicity and moral weakness, and also between gwlclossncss o.n<l ignorance. The simplicity required is" unity" as opposed to" double-mindedness;" it is being wholly for God. - R. 'l.'.

entries.title: 2CO 3:1–5
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Sou'l-Zitemture. "Do we begin a.gain to commend ourselves?" etc. l1! the early Church it was customary for the member who was travelling into another locality to take with him a letter of commendation from the Church to· which he or she belonged. The apostle says he did not require such a document . from the Corinthian Church, as some others did, for they themselves were letters written on hts own heart ; and his ministry was a letter written on their hearts also. They were tht- • living "epistles of Christ, . . . written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the livinn God ; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy ~bles of the heart." Our subject is so~ literature, or Christianity written on the heart ; and I offer five remarks. ' . l. Christianity written 011 the soul is CHRISTIANlTY IN TH!!; MOST LEGIDLE -F0BM. There are some whose caligraphy is difficult to decipher and whose thoughts are difficult to understand; their ideas are misty and their sty lo involved; but what is written on the soul is written so clearly that a child can make it out. II. Christianity written on the soul is CHRISTIANITY IN THE MOST 00NVINOING FORM. Books have been written on the evidences of Christianity; not a few by the ablest· men of their times, such as Paley, Lardner, Butler. But one life permeated and fashioned by the Christian spirit is a far i:pore convincing power than any or all of their most magnificent productions. He who has been transformed by Christianity from the selfish, the sensual, and corrupt, into the spiritual, the benevolent, and the holy, furnishes an argument that baffles all controversy and penetrates the heart. III. Christianity written on the soul is CHRISTIANITY IN THE HOST PERSUASIVE FOBH. There are many books "persuasive to piety," and many of then;i very powerful; but the most powerful of them a.re weak indeed compared to the mighty force of a Christly life. There is a magnetism in gospel truth embodied, which you seelt for in vain in any written work. When the "Word is made flesh" it becomes "mighty through God." • IV. Christianity written on the soul is CHRISTIANITY IN THE· ;MOST ENDURING FOBM. The tablet is imperishable. You may put truth on paper, but the pa.per will moulder; put it into institutions, but the institutions will dissolve as a cloud; put it on marble or brass, but the_se are corruptible. , • . V. Christianity written on the soul is CHRISTIANITY IN THE DIVINEST F0BM. The human hand can inscribe it on parchment or engrave it on stone, but God only can write it on the heart. "The Spirit of the living God." Paul was but the amanuensis, God is the Author.
