entries.title: 2CO 3:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The new covenant. I. A COVEN.A.NT OF. THE SPIRIT. The old covenant, the Law which came by Moses, we.s the" letter "-precepts laid down to be literally obeyed, fixed and rigid, external and ritual. The new covenant, the gospel, is the coveuant of love, of spiritual obedience. The Jew, under the old covenant, could not be exempted by any piety of spirit from the letter of the legal ordinance ; but under the new covenant the spirit of the observance is chief. 'l'be old covenant did riot supply the inward power producing obedience-it was. something outside of man, imposed upon him. But the new covenant has for an essential feature the power of God operating in the heart, leading to newness of life. The old covenant approached man from without, the new covenant works from within. One is " letter "--external; the other is "spirit "-internal. II. A covEIUNT OF LIFE. In the old covenant there was the holy Law nnd the command to fully obey it: "The Law is not of faith; but, The man that doeth them shall live in them" (Gal. iii. 12). The old covenant demanded perfect obedience: "Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the Law to do them" (Gal. iii. 10). Thus the old covennnt tended to condemnation and death, because fallen human nature failed to keep the perfect Law of God. 'l'he "letter" of unswerving righteousness convicted man of sin, and then "killed" him. Not that the Law was evil, but that it showed the evil in man. "The wages of sin is death." The Law, by discovering sin, showed that the wages were due. The old covennnt thus left man condemned, and, if man was to be justified and restored, there was urgent need of a new covenant. We find, thus, that the old covenant is ever pointing to the new, and that the design of the former was to lead to the latter: "The Le.w was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ" (Gal. iii. 24). Moreover, the Jew possessed the new covenant as well as the old, though not so fully unfolded as we have it. Men condemned by the old covenant lived the life of faith upon the Son of God who WI\S to come, and thus participated in the life-giving principle of the new covenant. This new covenant is a covenant of life: 1. Because Christ has perfectly fulfilled the Lnw of God on man's behalf, and to man this perfect obedience is imputed. Uondemnntion is tlnrn avoided. Life is secured for mnn by man's Substitute. 2. Mnn's personal transgressions nre atoned for by the sacrifice of Christ. 3. The Holy Ghost is given to kinJlo spiritual life in man, to sanctify his nature, to bring him at le.st ioto full accord with the perfect Law of God. Ill. A COVENANT NOT TRANSITORY. The old covcnnnt bo.s passed away. The new coverwut puts men in a position with rcl11.tio11 to God which is an everlasting one, Death and the next world will not c11ll for the abrogation of this covennnt, nor any cu. m. 1-18.) THE SECOND EPISTLE TI) THE CORINTHIANS. 77

changes occurring during the residence of the human family in the world. 1'hs old covenant was imperfect; it demanded ;;omething beyond itself; it was desi"'ned to do this. There is no such element in the nelV. lt is complete; it calls r:i. nothin"' outside of its own provisions. , "' IV. A COVENANT OF SURPASSING GLORY. 1'his arises largely from points already noticed. 1. Its spiritual character. 2. Its issues in bringing life, not death, to fallen men. 3. Its enduring character. 4. Its direct initiation and administration by the Son of God. "'!'he Law was given by Moses, hut grace and truth came by Jesus Christ" (John i. 17). 'l'hc inauguration of the old covenant saw the face of Moses illumined. The new covenant came with the transfiguration of Christ. 5. Its marvellous revelation of Divine love. The old covenant laid the emphasis upon Divine righteousness; the new, whilst displaying with untarnished lustre this attribute of Deity, exhibits pre-eminently the love of God.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 3:15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The veil on the hea1-t. The veil which Moses put on his face (F:xod. xxxiv. 33) obscured its brightness. The apostle seizes upon the event, so familiar to readers of Jewish history, to illustrate moral blindness, and especially the moral blindness of Je1Vs in his own day. As moral blindness is subjective, he dpeaks of the veil not upon those things which are obscured, as in the case of the face of Moses, but a; upon the heart. l:ipon the heart, because in spiritual matters the inability docs not spring from the bead, but from the heart. This veil upon the heart- I. OBSCUBES THE GLORY OF THE OLD DISPENSATION. It did so to Jews in Paul's dA.y; it does so to Jews now. The true glory of the old eovem,nt lay in its foreshadowing of the new. It was a covenant ·of types aud shadows. Underlying its legality was a deep spirituality. The Law condemned, and only condemned, but the "Law" was not the whole of the old covenant. Associated with the Law was the embryo of the gospel. And unveiled hearts looked through condemnation and shadow and type to the delivering Messiah, by whom men could be justified by faith aud not by works. But the veil upon the heart caused the Jew to regard the old covenant WI complete in itself, and to disregard the deeper spiritual meanings of its provisions. From him its true glory was thus bidden. A rigid system became much more rigid. The win<>s of a dispensation rising to eomething higher were clipped. A hard, narrow cr;d was substituted for an expansive and noble theology. II. HmEs CHRIST. It did so when Christ came. When tbo Messinh appeared, veiled hearts failed to recognize him. The Jews would have wolcomcd a Messiah who ea.me to continue Judaism as Judaism was understood by them. But the dovelopment of Judaism into Christianity, the fruition of the old covenant in tho now, had no charms for them; on the contrary, it was obnoxious to them in the highest degree, as spirituality ia ever to a carnal nature. In the Christ they could not see tho Christ. He was not their Christ, and by facile logic was thus demonstrated to bo no Christ at all. "Their minds were blinded" (ver. 14). From many to-day Christ is thus hidden. To them "a root out of a dry ground" is as beautiful as he. They think the fault is in him, but it is in themselv68. Falso conceptions of the objects, duties, and plensurcs of lifo possess them, and are the coloured media through which Christ is looked at. 'l'hey see a darkened, shorn, maimed Christ; the trt1,11 Christ is hidden from thorn. Ill. CAUSES MEN TO BEST IN SELF-RIGHTEOUSNESS. '!'his was the only way of justifi- cation which was apparent to the Jew upon whose heart the veil rested. '!'he veil shut out all, except legalism. So with many now. It is their righteousness, not tho righteousness of Christ, to which they look. They seek to eave themselves, not to be saved by another. Each is a Messiah to himself. But poor rest is secured. The voices of old sins make themselves heard, and to their clamour no satisfactory response is forthcoming. Present power to do right is found lacking. 'fhis is not to be won- dered at, seeing that the Source of all true spiritual power has been abandoned. Piety becomes either a vague dream of the future or & dismal formality of the present. IV. KEEPS MEN tJNDER CONDEMNATION, The Law of God condemns, and if only the bare Law is seen there is no deliverance. Self-righteousness, if attained to in perfection, would not cancel past sentences on sin. But self-righteousness practically is ever self-un- riahteousness and, instead of atoning for sin, continuously increases it. The most moral ru';..n has but the cheerless vision of a broken Law imperiously demanding its penalties. 78 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORIN'l'HIANS. [ce. m. 1-18,

V. THE VEIL IS REMOVED AS WE TURN TO THE LoRD. (Ver.-16.) When the Jew, led by the Spirit, believed on Christ, the veil, which had obscured his vision of the old covenant, and which had thus ~rvert;ed his being and life, was removed. He saw then the true significance of the old economy, and perceived ihat Christ in his own person and work, constituted the very fulfilment of the Law. Old thincrs 'passed away, all things beca.me new. The veil is destroyed for ever as we come to Christ. The apostle has, no doubt, in his mind the action of Moses: "When Moses went in before the Lord to speak with him, he took the veil off" (Exod. xxxiv. 34). Our turning to the Lord is a sign that the veil is rent in twain like the veil of the temple, and as we reach the Lord and are taught by the Divine Spirit, the veil vanishes, obscurity gives place to brightness, and we marvel that we ever could have been as we once were. ,vhen Moses ea.me out from the presence of the Lord he again assumed the. veil, but he is not here an example to us; for we a.re not to come out a.gain, but to abide with Christ, to be "for ever with the Lord."-H. ' ' •

entries.title: 2CO 3:18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-fle great change. I. Wr,.AT THIS CHANGE 1s. Into the Divine likeness. Thii:, which was lost through the Fall, is recovered in the gospel. Believers become like Christ, who is the Brightness of the Father's glory, and the express Imacre of his person (Heb. i. 3). The change is not merely of opinion, or feeling, or even "conduct, but a change of being. It is not something connected with ourselves, but our very selves which are changed, and changed so as to be like Christ. 1. A marvellous change. For before men believe, they are singularly unlike Christ. By nature like Satan ; by grace like Christ. 2. An all-desirable change. For ennoblement, peace, joy, 1U1efulness. ll THE MANNER OF THE CHANGE. It follows upon turning to the Lord (ver. 16). As Moses, standing before God, was singularly changed in countenance, so that his face reflected the Divine glory, so we are changed as we are _turned towards Christ, as we turn towards him in penitence and faith and in desire to be his. The figure of a mirror is employed. 1. We may read "reflecting as a mirror," and theu the idea conveyed will be that, as Christ shines upon us, .as he acts upon us, we become changed. Or: 2. If we read "beholding as in a mirror," the thought will be that, as we gaze upon Christ as be is reflected in the mirror of the gospel, we become like him. Both thoughts are correct, though it is by the Divine actiou we are changed, our looking upon Christ being only the means by which the Divine aqtion rea.ches us. IIL A SPECUL FEATURE OF THE ORANGE,. Progressive-" from glory to glory." The change is often gradual. There is a great. fundamental change at convarsion. A condition of "glory" is reached, but there i, a glory beyond thjs. We "grow in grace." .At first we are "babes in Christ," but we develop into the stature of perfect men in him (Eph. iv. 13). Conversion is but the first stage. Many seem to think that it is the final one. Justification is enough for. them ; sanctification is not in their thoughts. But this is not the salvation of Christ. We are saved for holiness~ for usefulness, for the service of God, and as continuously we p:aze upon Christ iu faith, and as his power falls upon us, we p&Bs into a further "glory.'' IV. .A CONDITION OF THE CBANGE, Our face unveiled. And here face stands for heart. The veil occasioned by the old enmity, by prejudice, by misconception, by i~norance, must be removed. This will be so with all who in sincerity turn to the Lord. "When it shall turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away" (ver. 16). 'l'ho more completely our face is unveiled the more rapidly shall we pass from" glory w glory." We should strive to r~move all that is likely to hinder our de_velop_ment in~o the likeness of Chriet. Anythmg that comes between ourselves and him will do this. H.,art-veils are of very various patterns. V. THE STRIKING USEFULNESS OF THE OH ANGE, Adopting the reading "reflecting as a mirror," we see that: 1. Those who tum to the Lord reflect the glory of the Lord. 'l'hey show forth Christ. Men take knowledge of them that they have been with. Jesus. They reflect the redemptive glory of Christ.. They exemplify the power of his salvation. 'l'hey are monuments upon which is inscribed "Christ, and him crucified." They reflect the love of Christ in Christian activity. Having been saved themselves, they desire the salvation of all around them. What a thought, that we may reflect Christ ! 2. As they seek to reflect Christ the change progresses. It is when we are diligent in the llfas:er's busine.<;&, when we consor.rate ourselves to him, when we strive oa. m. 1-18.J 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORIN'£HIANS. i9

to set him forth in daily life, that we become .ehanged into• his image, As we strenuously endeavour to be like him we become like him. Our -endeavour to reflect him is responb-d to by the change in us which enables us to reflect him. Reflecting his glory 11,e a mirror, we are changed into the same image. VI. THE WoRKER OF THE CHANGE. The Holy Ghost, "the Lord the Spirit." Christ working by his Spirit, who takes of the things of Christ and reveals them unto us. "The Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my Name" (John xiv. 26). 'l'ho work is Divine; it calls for Divine power. We cannot work this change, yet we can " turn to the Lord," that it may be worked.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 3:2
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-A living letter. Apollos had carried to Corinth written credentials (seo Acts xviii. 27; xix. 1). Why had Paul not done eo too? He claims that he needed them not. The converts in that city were themselves his credentials. His appeal to the Corinthians on this point proceeds on a principle easily understood and often applied. 'l'he best testimonial a teacher can produce is the proficiency of his pupils. The most satisfactory evidences of the skill of a physician are the patients who have recovered health under his care. The convincing proofs of the comp~tcncy of a gardener are tho prosperity of the plants and the abundance of flowers and fruits which he produces from the ground. So was the Church at Corinth itself the best diploma or commendation of the apostle who had founded it and watched over it (see 1 Cor. iv. 14-16). A good teacher needs no letter of commendation to his own pupils, or a father to his own children. Seizing the idea of a letter, and showing that the Corinthian saints themselves formed the only letter he needed to produce, St. Paul used this as an illustration in two forms. 1. The Christians at Corinth were written on his heart, for they were dear to him (eh. vii 3; Phil. i. 7). And this was no secret. The tie of affection between St. Paul and the Corinthian brethren wes "known and read of all." 2. Christ had written upon their hearts what served as a powerful letter of commendation for his servant Paul. Let us pursue the second use of the metaphor. A Church is an epistle of Christ, open for all men to read. I. THE AUTHOR OF TBE LETTER. This is Christ. Whatever Divine thoughts aro given to human minds, or spiritual impressions are stamped on humo.n henrts, µrocoed from Christ. And it is true of Churches in all ages. As Christ is tho livin~. One, he ie ever writing new epistles-in harmony with those which were written at the beginning-and yet new and fresh and suited to the current time. II. 'l'BE AJUNUENBIS. At Corinth this was Paul. In modern Churchos it is tho faithful ministry of the Word. The epistle is not invented or dictated by us, but "ministered by us." The mind of Christ is thereby conveyed to and impressed on tho company of believers. Ill. 'l'BE TABLETS. 'l'hey are not of stone, but of the heart. The ministrntion of death was written and engraven on stone in the form of ten commandments. 'l'ho more glorious ministration of the spirit and of righteousness is inscribed on the convic- tions and affections of living men. 'l'he law of Christ is put into the inward parts and written on the heart. For this end, too, the Lord knows how to eof,01t tho tablets, to make the heart tender and warm, and so susceptible of the instruction and impression of the Word. Oh to have a still heart, not restless, that the writing may be plain, and to have a lowly heart, not hard, that the engraving may be deep I IV. Tal!l JUNNER OF WRITING. "Not with ink." St. P1.u1'11 letters were so written, ae were those of other apostles (2 John 12); and by ink of the scribo and the printer have they been preserved and propagated. But for writing on the heart porishl\blo material is unsuited. Jehovah wrote the Law on tho tablots of stone with hiij own hand; and on the tablets of the human heart Jesus Christ writes, using ministry 118 ho pleases in the process with the linger or power of God-" tbe Spirit of the living God." And so, in all times and all Churches of the saints, the application of tho truth is by tho living Spirit. V. TBE THING WRITTEN. It is the mind of Christ. Ye "have learned Christ, and the truth as it is in Jesus.• There is no higher truth to learn, no better messe.go to carry. VI. THE PUBLICATION OP THE LETTER. It is "manifestly declared," and may be known and read of all men. Thie is said of the Church collective, for such is the temple of 80 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [cH. m.1-18.

God and such is the epistJe of Christ-an argument surely for Christian consistency and for brotherly concord, that the sacred epistle may not be rendered unintelligible. ~f each memberofa_ Church abide in _his place, a1;1d all ~ogetber dwell in peace and walk m the truth, there lS produced an epistle of Chnst which puts the gainsayer to silence. Thank God that even a faulty Church or blotted epistle has somethina of a Divine element, some impression and expression of Christ! The obligation whi~h lies on the Church may )>a p~~ ~n ~eh member thereof. Would that Christ were more apparent and more leg1ble in Christians! Let your character be a consistent representation or epistle of rour Lord, and let it be an ori~inal, not a copy of some other man's religion but a genm~e P:oductic,n of Jesus Christ_ by" the Spirit of the living God." If you g~ to t~e Lord J~t1fymg y_ourself and accnsrng others, he will only write on the ground ; but 1f you with a penitent heart accuse yourself, he will write on you his grace and truth. Hereafter, when you have overcome, he will write on you his new Name.-F. Ver. 6,-ne letter and the spirit. The contrast between letter and spirit is in Scripture peculiar to the pages of St. Paul (see Rom. ii. 29; vii. 6). The subject specially occupied him, as the champion of Christian liberty and a profound thinker on tbe relations of the Old and New Testaments. J. THE 00:!ITRASTED TERMS-LETTER AND BPIBIT. A more frequent opposition is between flesh and spirit (see John iii. 6; vi. 63; Rom. viii. 1-13; Gal. v. 16-25). 'l'be distinction is obvious between a fleshly and a spiritual disposition, and the alterna- tive is shown to be one of life or death. "To be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace." But, by letter and spirit must be intended things of which it is possible for men to be ministers. St. Paul was a minister, not of the letter, but of the spirit; and the context shows that by letter he meant the old covenant, and by spirit the new. Not that there was nothing but letter in the one and Ilothing but spirit in t.be other. The contrast is between predominant characteristics; and characteristically, though not exclusively, the old covenant was letter and the new covenant was spirit. Therefore the latter excelled in glory. 'l'be old economy, or testa- ment, is not spoken of with disrespect. It was adapted in the wisdom of God to the training of the Hebrew people as his chosen nation. It was not a mere dead writing, but had a meaning in it which was Divine. The very term "letter" implies some import or significance. And there was enough in the Old Testament to educate tho minds of men in religious ideas, and bring home sacred obligations and hopes to their hearts. But it is called "the letter" because that which bulked largely in it was a code of law and a handwriting of ordinances. In its prescription of law it was to sinful men a ministration of death; and in its ritual of worship it was inferior to that holy liberty which we now enjoy in everywhere worshipping the Father in spirit and in truth. 'fhe old covenant had shadows, the new has substance; the old had rudiments and elements, the new has perfection; the old had pntterns of heavenly things, tho new ha.a heavenly things themselves; the old was a dispensation of dimness as of light seen through a veil, the new is one of unveiled faces and God's marvellous light. The new economy, or testament, while characteristically one of" spirit," is not altogether without letter. As every soul must have a body, and every essence a form, in order to be known among men, so has the spirit of the New 'l'estarnent embodiment and exact expression. Bnt here lies the contrast. Pre-Christian religion contained a small proportion of spirit and life in a large bulk of letter and ordinance. Christianity has n large proportion of spirit and life in a bulk of law and form as small and light ne poss1Lle. 'l'be teachings of Christianity are facts and principles, not propositions and restrictions; its institutions are simple outlines, not precise ceremonies; and its laws are moral sentiments, not minute mechanical directions. II. 'l'BE EFFECTS WHICH FLESH AND SPIRIT SEVERALLY PRODUCE. The letter, void of spirit, kills. The epirit, in whatever form or letter conveyed, gives life. We must stilf be on our guard against making that absolute which is intended only as a Atrong comparative. We must not say or suppose that under the M058:iC _economy there ~as uotbing but condemnation, bondage, and death. Beneath and w1thm the letter which had such promiilence, there nas spirit; and men who knew how to penetrate the letter got the spirit, and with it goi life. But the more that men made of mere traditional letter and form, the less they knew of the spirit ol li~rty and the power of godliness. CE. III. 1-18.J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 81

Most apparent was the killing power of the Jett.er in that generation of Hebrews to which Pan! himself belonged. They gloried in circumcision, but had it in the flesh only, and not in the heart. They sought life by the law of works, and fell under its condemnation. The more devoted they were to religious peculiarities and ceremonial restrictions, the more did a shadow of death cover them. 'l'hey clung to the types and would not recognize the Antitype. They trusted to a covenant which had exhausted its use and was passing away. So this letter-worship destroyed spiritual life. Israel after the flesh fell under a ministration of death. On the other hand, in that new dispensation, of which St. Paul was such an earnest minister, and in which spirit predominates, there is abundance of the grace of life. 'l.'rue that, under this dispensation also, a formalist or one who is self-righteous may turn the life into death. Externalism and traditionalism are as powerless as ever to make alive. But, when the letter which in some manner is indispensable to mortal worshippers is kept in due subordination, the spirit gives life, and the ministration of righteousness is exceeding glorious. The converts in that city were themselves his credentials. His appeal to the Corinthians on this point proceeds on a principle easily understood and often applied. 'l'he best testimonial a teacher can produce is the proficiency of his pupils. The most satisfactory evidences of the skill of a physician are the patients who have recovered health under his care. The convincing proofs of the comp~tcncy of a gardener are tho prosperity of the plants and the abundance of flowers and fruits which he produces from the ground. So was the Church at Corinth itself the best diploma or commendation of the apostle who had founded it and watched over it (see 1 Cor. iv. 14-16). A good teacher needs no letter of commendation to his own pupils, or a father to his own children. Seizing the idea of a letter, and showing that the Corinthian saints themselves formed the only letter he needed to produce, St. Paul used this as an illustration in two forms. 1. The Christians at Corinth were written on his heart, for they were dear to him (eh. vii 3; Phil. i. 7). And this was no secret. The tie of affection between St. Paul and the Corinthian brethren wes "known and read of all." 2. The contrast between letter and spirit is in Scripture peculiar to the pages of St. Paul (see Rom. ii. 29; vii. 6). A more frequent opposition is between flesh and spirit (see John iii. 6; vi. 63; Rom. viii. 1-13; Gal. v. 16-25). entries.title: 2CO 3:18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The Christian transfiguration. When Moses, the minister of tho Lnw, communed with God, his countenance became irradintcd, nnd, on his roturn to tho people of Israel in the camp, he was obliged to put o. veil over his fuco. But that radiance did not lnst long. It fnded from the prophet's countenance ; and thi~ i~ tl\kon to illustrate the passing away of the glory of all that legal ministration. 'l'he Jows who rejected that gospel which St. Paul preached were still occupied with the Law. Moses stood before them still ; and, when Moses was road, they failed to see that tho lustre had faded from his face. Yet it was so. ~ot that the Law W88 at fault or obscure; not that Moses misled or clouded their minO..'- 'l'he veil was no more on his face, but on their hearts; and so they persisted, and th& bulk of that nation still persist, in trusting to Moses and rejecting the more glorio118 ministration by Jesus Christ. 'l'ho anti- Christian Jews are dimly reading the words c,t their lawgiver instead of rejoicing in tho light of the Lord. But" we all," whether Jews or Gentiles in tho flesh, who havo believed the gospel, enjoy a ministration of righteousness and glory. L THE GLORY OP THE Lonn. Moses saia to Jehovah, "1 bciiecch thco, show me thy U. OOBINTWANS, 0 82 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COIUNTHIANS. [cu. m.1-18,

glory." Aod he had some vision of the Almighty, and heard Jehovah God proclaim hi11 Name as he pa.ssro by; but the God of Israel said, "Thou canst not see my face.'' Now t_his, which was imi:,ossiblo under tbe old covenan~ and ~hich was thought of by the faithful a.s the ble.ssmg of a future state (Ps. xvu. 16), 1s not only possible but actual under the new covenant. Christ is the Image of the invisible God. We see the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. He who of old surrounded himself with clouds or dwelt "in the thick darkness" :uow reveals himself brightly in his Beloved. 'l'he New Testament is, more fully than the Old, a revelation. God is revealed in a. manner surpassing all the partial disclosures among the Jews, and correctina all the O vain imaginations among the heathen. The holy Child was Immanuel, God with us. The Man who lived so purely, spcke ~o w!sely,_ and suffered so patiently, revealed the unseen G?<1; and God wa.s. glorified m him. So the apostle regarded Christianity as the breaking forth of new hght on the human race, and that the very radiance of God in Jesus Christ his Son. So let us regard it. Truly the light is good-the inner light of the New Testament-the glory of the Lord. IL Co~--n:MPLATION OF THAT GLORY. We behold it as one looks upon a mirror on which an object out of his reach is reflected. Our Lord has ascended to the Father and we do not see him face to face in the present life, but we look on the Divine testim'ony and, as we look, we gain "the excellency of the knowledge of Christ." In order to this: two things are necessary. 1. We must have our faces unveiled. The veil is preju- dice or unbelief. The ignorance of God, long spread over the earth, is described by a. prophet as " the covering cast over all people, and the veil that is spread over all nations." The removal of that covering or veil results in the turniog of nations to the Lord. Alas ! readers of the New Testament may be· as blind to its true meaoina and beauty as any Jews were in reading the Law. A vague light, perhaps, comes tb;ough the veil, but there is no clear discernment of that glory of the Lord which gives to the New Testament its surpassing power and value. St. Paul knew this well, and felt him- self unable to make all men see what he saw. From some who heard him his gospel was hid. It was and is the preacher's duty to manifest aod proclaim the truth; but blinded minds and veiled hearts could, and still can, defeat the testimony. St. Paul himself had once been very blind. When light shone in the face of the martyr Stephen as he stood before the council, " as it had been the face of an angel," Saul of 'farsus was only bewildered and irritated, and hi:i consented to Stephen's death. Soon after, on his way to Damascus, a strong light from heaven shone round about him, and the voice of the Lord reached his ear. Some holy light through the veil fell on his countcno.oce, but the veil was not yet removed, and the Pharisee was not yet a Christian. Illumination came to him when, at the word of the disciple Ananias, the eyes of his body, which hnd been blinded by the sudden effulgence on the way, were opened, and at the same timo the eyes of the inner man were freed from the scales of unbelief, and God shone into his heart. 2. We must form a habit of beholding that glory. We do not presume to say what amount of ble~sing may bo gained through even a rapid or occasional glance cast on the Lc-rd Jesus; but what 1he apostle intends is an habitual and daily contemplation of that "brightness of the Fat,hel"'s glory." No study of books, acquaintance with doctrines, or observance of rites can do for us what is done by the habit of "lookiog to Je~us." IIL 'l'HE TRANSFORMING POWER OF SUOH CON1'EMPLATION. "Changed ioto the same image." A moral metamorphosis is wrought, not magically as by a spell or chnrm, but in the manner proper to a moral nature, by the moulding influence of a now ha.bit ot thought and affectioo. This proceeds on the well-koown principle that, whatever we look upon with frequency and with coo genial feeling, stamps itself on our minds and characters. He who looks upon evil becomes evil. He who occupies himself with trifles grows trivial. He who associates with the wise growR wise. Ho who admires the good himself becomes ,::ood. So likewise ho who beholds the pure and gracious image of God in the face of Jesus Christ is changed insensibly into that image, learns to think the thoughts of God aod to exhibit the mind of Christ, 'l'wo important features of this great change arc ioclicated in the text. 1. It is a progressive one. "From glory to glory." No doubt, if we could abide continually under the radiance of Christ, his glory would transform us more rapidly and c1mpletely than is the experience of average Christians. And we lllllst nut dwell on lhc i(l,,a of gradualness so ns to· excuse a low level of Christian on. ru. 1-18.J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE OORINTHIANS. 83

attainment. But the truth lies here, that, as we receive out of Christ's fulness grace for grace, so are we transformed into his likeness from glory to glory, the licrht of the Lorcl gaining upon us and dispelling all the darkness until we are "light''in the Lord.'· 3. While this change follows a law of moral influence, it is produced by the 11ctivo operation of a Divine power-" as by the Lord the Spirit." The reference is to the Lord Jesus as "a quickening Spirit," who is here brought into contmst with Moses, the minister of the killing "letter." At the same time, wo know from other Scriptures th11t the Lord pervades his Church on earth and renews men in his own im11ge by the gracious presence and work of the Holy Ghost. Without this doctrine of spiritual operation, both direct and indirect, we fail to apprehend the transformin~ power of a pure Christi1111ity. Note iu conclusion: 1. The connection between faith and character. Some raise II cry that faith leads to mysticism 11nd genders dispute, while nothing is wanted, nothing is to be valued, but an exemplary character and a good life. But what if such character anrl. life are best attained by the habit of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ? It might as well be said that it is of little consequence whether a man can see or is blind, so long ns he walks and works well. He cannot walk or work well unless he can see. No more can one walk or act like Christ unless he looks to him in faith. Others raise a different cry. 'l'hey are all for faith, and yet show no conformity to Christ. All such boasting is vain. The effect of beholding the glory of the Lord is to be changed into the samo image. If there is no such change the faith is only in ima~ination, not in henrt. 2. The far reach of the principle of assimilation to what we habitually and willingly behold. In this way are Christians conformed to Christ in this present time. Dut the principle carries much further. It is thus that the saints will be glori fled with Christ at his appenring. "We know that, when he shall appear, we shnll bo like him ; for we shall see him as he is.'' 3. The evil ca,e of those who see in Christ " no beauty that he shcnJd be desired." They miss both the way of peace o.nd the way of holiness. Alas I when the gospel is set before them, the veil lies upon their hearts. They can see something to be admired in the wisdom of snges and tbo courngc of heroes, a.nd yet see nothing in the Son of God. They may look on nature with admiring eye, and see•• the glory in the grass and splendour in the flower;" but Jesus Christ is to them "as a root out of a dry ground." Lord, remove the veil I Shine into tbcso hearts with power !-F.

-The best commendation. It was an early custom in the Christian Church for teachers to carry with them "letters of commendation" when they pnssed from town to town. Of this custom wo have an indication in Acts xviii. 27, "When Apollos wns disposed to pass into Achaia rCorinth], the brorhren rof Ephesus] wrote, exhorting tho disciples to receive him." It seems to hnvo bean made a chnrge ngainst the apostle that he never presented nny credentials, but ossunied an authority for which he had no warrant. The apostle is here replying to such o. chnrge, and hie pico is that, having so manifestly received the greotor commcmlation of God's witness with his work, he in no senso can need man's good word. His converts woro the beat possible commendation. His letters wore those written by God ns truth on human hearts. From tho Christian standpoint the only satisfactory 11roof of coll to ministry is tbo Divine seal sot on the work of the ministry. It was tho pion of St. Peter, when accounting for hie admitting tho Gentiles into tho privilogcs of tho Christian Church, that the" Holy Ghost had fallen upon them, ovon as upon us o.t tho bcginnin;;." And that was folt to be an all-sufficient attestation of tho work which St. Peter hml done. In the same way St. Paul pleads that spiritual results had followod his ministry among the Corinthians. Ood 1,ad sot bis seal upon it, and that was his wholly so.tisfactory commendation, and tho basis or any authority ho claimed. Spcnking in a figure he says, "The Uorinthin.ns aro an epistle." He regards Christ ns the Author, nn<l himself as the amanuensis. ·rho characters of this opistlo wero preserved by no visible or perishable metium, but by the invisible operation of the Spirit. Wo consider- I. TBE USEFULNESS OF HUMAN COMMENDATIONS. Such are found to bo necessary in the intercourse of nations. 'fhe ambassador is dulr. furnished with his credentials; nn,l the representative of the buHiness fir01 carries with him his authority to net in the THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORlN'l'HIANS. [cH. m. 1-18.

name of t.~e ~rm. So it is _found of practical value that ~lergymen and ministers going to other d1stncts or countries should have such attestation as will win for them the confidence of those to whom they may happen-to minister, Several questions of interest arise in connection with this subject. 1. From what central bodies, or from what indi- viduals, should such letters of commendation come? 2. What should they properly concern? And can they ever wisely go beyond the attestation of personal character and ministerial efficiency? Men must be judged by their works rather than by the opinion which others may have formed concerning them, Still, in every age Churches have needed to be guarded against plausible but unworthy men, who force themselves into positions of influence unawares. And this has been the special trouble of all smaller Churches, and those existing apart from Christian organizations. Every ordinary man should depend for his acceptance upon his letters of recommenrlatiou. II. TEE LIMITATION OF THE DEMAND FOR SUCH LETTERS. Sometimes they are merely vexations. The demand for them is a mere piece of officialism. Some men so stand before the world that no letters about them can be necessary. And the letters may only concern (1) character, (2) efficiency. They should not deal with disputable opinions. A full and fair estimate of character is sufficient to give confidence that a man's work will be honest and faithful, Commendations of so-called "orthorloxy" or "heterodoxy" can never be anything but mischievous. We may commend the man • we had better take care not to co=end hie opinions. Of these let those to whom h; ministers be the judges. 111. GoD's WAYS OF MAKING BUCH LETTERS WHOLLY UNNECIESBARY. From the case or St. Paul we learn that God may so manifestly show his acceptance of e. man and a man's work that no other credential can possibly be necessary. A man's labours and successes may sufficiently declare that he is a man of God, e. messenger of God. Illustrate by such case.s as Luther, Whitefield, Brainerd, etc. We must well arprehend that, because a thing is unusual, it is not therefore untrue. And in Cl'ery age men have been raised up whose strongly marked individuality leads them to take fresh lines of thought and of work. Men may hesitate to give such men. their c1·edenlials; it is enough if God manifestly accepts them.-R. T.

He works at the wi1Z of another, holding himself ever in attitudes of dependent and submissive obedi• ence, saying continually, "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" 3. He works in the strength of another, leaning upon the "everlasting arms." Taking these as characteristic features of the Christian ministry, it will be readily shown in what a marked way they contrast with the spirit of the self-depending and self-seeking worldly roan. III. IN CHRISTIANITY THE MAN IS .ACTUALLY ENDUED WITH DIVI:SE POWEB. "Oar sufficiency is of God." It is this truth that needs such distinct assertion for the sake of the Christian worker himself, as well as for the sake of those to whom his work is a witness. The Christian is a man quickened with a new life; it is that "new life" which finds expression in his working. '1.'be Christian is a man st1aled by the Holy Ghost, who dwells in him, and that Holy Ghost is his secret strength and inspiration. Two figures may be contrasted. The water flowing in pipes, and the sap flowing in the branch. The latter is the only figure that efficiently represents the relation of power and agency in the Christian worker, and it is the figure used by our Lord himself. The union and relation are such that, while the full manhood is retained, and even nourished into vigour, the vitality, the real force behind the manhood, ani! the direction of all details of action, are God's. The Christian conceives of himself as not even able to think anything as of himself, much less to do anything. He is "strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might."-R. T.

-The letter and the spirit. It does not appear that St. Paul had in mind the different senses in which Scripture can now be read. '1.'he older revelation consisted of exact directions for the guidance of life and conduct, The new revelation consists of principles and examples by the help and application of which a man may guide his own conduct, But, while this distinction is carefully noted, it should be observed Lhat, in the older revelntion, there was both letter and spirit, and devout souls recognized and lived in the light of the inner principles, the spiritual truth which precise injunctions did but illuslrute. F. W. Robertson says, "It was the business of Moses to teach maxims, o.nd not priuciples; rules for ceremonial, and not a spirit of lifo. entries.content: -The oW, covenant and the new. In some sense it may be said tliat teachings respecting the relations between the older revelation in Judaism and the newer revelation in Christianity were special to. the Apostle Paul. On this point he had direct revelations from Christ, and the liberal form which bisteachiags took exposed him to the peril of being misunderstood and misrepresented, and brought persecutions around him. No man could be found more truly loyal to the older revelation than the apostle of the Gentiles, but while he honoured it he saw clearly that it bad its day and its mission. That day had now passed; that mission had been fulfilled. 'l'he older covenant had made open and plain the way for the new, and it was loyalty to the old for Paul to accept fully the new, in which it found its fulfilment, its completion, its glory; for the ministration of Jesus and the Spirit is but Judaism glorified, the gospel of the letter passed into the gospel of the spirit, Three contrasts are here dwelt u1ion. The old coveuant and the new are conceived as- L A :MINISTRATION OF DEATH AND A IIIINISTBATION OF LIFE. St. Paul bad said (ver. 6) that the "letter killetb." He meant that it crushed hope und effort, since no man could reach a perfect obedience. 'l'he old covenant condemned all who failed even in the leost thing. It provided no life, no strength in which obedience could become possible. On the other hand, the new covenant provided a new life for the will and a new grace unto obedience. 'l'he old crushed down henrt and hope, and made a man cry out, "I cannot." 'rhe new cheered him, lifted him up, and made him say, "I can, through him who strengtheneth me." II. The new is abiding, for there can be nothing higher than or beyond that s1iiritual righteousness which is its sublime aim to accomplish.-ll. T.

entries.content:
-The character and work of a true minister of Oln-ist. entries.title: 2CO 4:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The condition of wnregenerated men. "But if our gospel be hid," etc. These words give an appalling view of ungodly men, I. They are BLIND TO THE GOSPEL. " If our gospel be hid [or,' veiled']." Men have different organs of vision. There is the bodily eye: the gospel is not "hid" from that -they can see the volume that contains it, they can see the print, and perhape read its chapters. There is the intellectual eye to discover its sense and discern its meaning. There is the spiritual eye, the conscience which discerns the moral significance of thiug~; this is the eye which alone can see the gospel, it.s real essence. And this is the veiled eye, the eye of conscience is closed, so that the gospel is no more discerned than the bright heavens are observed by the man who is born blind. II. They are PERISHING IN BIN. "It is hid to them that are lost," or veiled from them that are perishing. Soul-ruin is a gradual process. Souls are neither ruined nor saved at once. The wicked are "going into everlo.sting punishment;" they are Dot hurled there at once; step by step they proceed. With every sin their sensibility of conscience is perishing, their power of will is perishing, all the better tendencies ~f their nature are perishing. It matters not how strong in body, how prosperous lll wealth, how elevated in society, they are perishing. Startlingly solemn this I III. They are VICTIMIZED DY SATAN, "In whom the god of this world bath blinded the minds of them which believe not." Observe: 1. Satan is uot a princiµle, but a personality. 2. Satan has immense dominions. "The god of this world.". Sat~n is '1: personality that has accese to human souls. He enters men, acts on their sprmgs ~t thought and fountains of feeling. 3. Satan is a personality whose action on the sou! J8 essentially r,ernicious. "The god of this world bath blinded the minds of them which believe not. ' He closes the moral eye of the soul, "lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the Image of God, should shine unto them." Yer. 5.-Prw.ching. "For we preach not ourselves," etc. Here is-- I. A BAD POSSIBILITY in preaching. What is that? To "preach ourselves." 'fo preach ourselves is to propound our own notions, to exhibit our own ta_lcnts, gcmus, and learning, to parade our own productions. It is to put self, not Christ, 1u t41: frout. In these days the egotism of the pulpit has become all but intolerable. II. A GLORIOUS THEME for preaching. "Christ Jesus the Lord." l. l'n:acll him <llL rv. 1-18.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 93

as the Mediator between God and man. He whose grand mission it is t.o reconcile man to his Maker. 2. Preach him as the great Example foi: man's imitation. fie who embodies the ideal of human perfection and blessedness. III. The RIGHT SERVICE in preaching. "Ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake." The true preacher is : 1. •Tho servant of souls. 2, 1'he servant of souls inspired by love for Christ. " Servants for Jesus' sake."

entries.title: 2CO 4:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -True soul-light. "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." There are two lights in the soul. There is tho light of nature. This light consists of those moral intuitions which Heaven implanted within us at first. These intuitions are good enough for angels, did for Adam before he fell; but now, through sin, they are so blunt and dim that the soul is in moral darkness : "The light that is in thee is darkness." The other light is that of the light of the gospel. This comes because the light of nature is all hut gone out, and comes as essential to our spiritual well-being. This i~ the light to which the passage refers, the new soul-light. The words call attention to three facts concerning it. I. IT EMANATES FBOM TRE RIGREST SOURCE. "God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, bath shined in our hearts." The reference is here to the creation (Gen. i. 3). It reminds us: 1. Of antecedent darkness. The state of the soul before this light enters it is analogous to the state of the earth before God kindled the lights of the firmament. It was cold, chaotic, dead. In what a sad condition is the unregenerate soul! 2. Of almighty sovereignty. "Let there be light"-" Let light be, and light was." The luminaries of the firmament were kindled by the free, uncontrolled, almighty power of God. So it is with real spiritual light. It comes because God wills it. Everywhere he " worketh according to the counsel of his own will" II. IT REVEALS THE GRANDEST SUBJECT. Light is a revealer. All the hues and forms, beauties and sublimities of the earth would be hid from ns without the light. What does this soul-light reve.111? "1'he light of the knowledge of the glory of God.'' Gospel light entering the soul makes God visible as the eternal Henlity, the Fountain of being, and the Source of all blessedness. Where this gospel light is not, the soul either ignores or donies him; or, at most, speculates about him, and at bost hns now and then flitting visions. But under the radiance of the gospel, God is tho Reality of all realities, the Fountain of all existences, the Root of a.II the sciences. In thi8 light they see God, and through him they see and interpret his universe. IIL IT STBEAllS TRBOUGH TRE St'BLIMEST MEDIUM. "In tho face of Josus Christ." There is undoubted allusion here to what is Mid of Moses (eh. iii. 13) when tho Divine glory was reflected on his face, and produced such a splendour and mnguificenco that the children of Ismel could not steadf11Stly look upon it. 1'he sense hero is thnt, in the fa.co or the person of Jesus ChriHt, the glory of God shone clearly, a.nu the Divinity appeared without n veil. This light coming through Christ, "who is the im11go of the invisible God," is : 1. True light.. He is the Truth. 2. Softened light. '!'ho soul could not et.and the light coming directly from the infinito Sourco; it is too dnzzliu~. Through the medium of Christ it comes so softened as to suit our weokness. a. Quickening light. It fall■ on the soul like the sunbeam on the seed quickening into life.

entries.title: 2CO 4:7
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The t~ gospel miniatry. "But we have this treasure," etc. 'Ihe words lead us to consider the true gospel ministry in various aspects. I. As CONTAINING AN INESTIMABLE TBBASUilE. 'l'he gospel is a systum of incal- culable worth. The most valuable things in nature a.re employed to represent it- wa.ter, light, life, etc. There are four criteria that detem1ine lho worth of a thing- rarity, utility, duration, ~he appreciatwn of the higl•est authorities. All these applied to the gospel demonstrate its surpassing value. II. As TRE SEBVIOE o:r FRAGILE MEN. "In e:irthcn vessels.'' To whom have tho inestimable truths of the gospel been entrusted for exposition, enforcement, nnd distri- bution? Not to angels, but to frail and dying men. 1. '!'hey havo frail bodies. They ure subject to infirmity e:x.haustion, decay, otc. 2. 'l'hey have frail minds. 'l'he moHt 94 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, (011. Iv. 1--18,

yi&orous in intellect is wea.k, the most lofty in. genius is feeble, the moat enlightened' 1s ignorant. III. As DEVELOPING A DIVINE PORl'OSE, '' That the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." 'l'he grand reason why frail men are employed to preach the gospel is that the glorious renovating and soul-saving effects may evidently appear as the work of God, and not of man. When sermons prove effective in convertiu" souls it is n?t becaus,e of the origi~ality of thei~· thought, the force of their logic, the splendoU: of their rhetoric, or the maiesty of their eloquence, but because of the Divine power that accompanie.s them, "Not by might, nor by power," etc.,

entries.title: 2CO 4:8–12
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Tl'ials in the cause of Ghrist. "We are troubled on every side 11 etc. 'l'hree remarks are suggested. ' I. That TRE TRIALS E:-.COllNTERED IN TRE CAUSE OF CHRIBT ARE SOMETIMES VERY GREAT. Hear what Paul says about his trials:" We are troubled on every side." He speaks of him~elf as hemmed in by enemies, pursued by enemies, stricken down by enemies, and dragging about with him, as it were, a living corpse. It may be laid down as a principle, that the man who is earnestly engaged in any righteous cause in this world will have to encounter trials. The old prophets had their trial~, somo of them were insulted, so~e incarcerated, some martyred. So with John the Baptist, and so with the apostles, so with the confessors, reformers, and genuine revivalists. II. That, HOWEVER GREAT THE TRIALS ENCOUNTERED, TREY ARE NOT BEYOND BEAR• ING. The apostle says that although "troubled on every side, yet not distressed," or straitened; though "perplexed," or bewildered, yet not benighted; though "persecuted," or pursued, yet not "forsaken," or abandoned; though " cast down," or stricken down with a. blow, yet not perishing. The idea. is that he had support under bis trials; they did not entirely crush him. The true labourer in tbe cause of Christ, however great his trials, is always supported: 1. By the approbation of his own conscience. 2. By the encouraging results of his own labom·s, 3. By the sustaining strength of God. "As thy days, so thy strength shall be." Ill. 'fhat THE BIGHT BEADING OF THESE TRIALS BUJISERVES THE GOOD OF SOULS, 1, In the right bearing of these sufferings the sufferer reveals the life of Christ to others. "Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus." Rightly endurcll sufferings bring the sufferer so near to the sufferings of Christ that he is in a. sense a sharer of those sufferings, and hence in them the life of Jesus is made manifest. Who that has witnessed the true Christian languishing on the bed of suffering and dcnth has not seen the spirit of the life of Christ revealed? 2. In tbe right bearing of theso sufferin"s the sufferer promotes in himself and olhcrs the Christian lifo. " For wo which live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus miaht be made manifest in our mortal flesh. So then death worketh in us, but life i11 yo~." " God," says Dean Alford, "exhibits death in the living, that he may llleo exhibit life in the dying."

entries.title: 2CO 4:13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The speech of truefaieh, "We having the same spirit of fnith," etc. The world is full of speech. Human words load the atmosphere. All the speeches may be divided into three classes. 1. Speech without faith. Vapid and voln.tile talk. 2. 8peech with wron.~ faith. Wrong faith is of _two. de~cription~. (1) Fnith in wr~mg subjects. Men believe errors. (2) Improper faith m right subiccts. Weak wavcnng, etc. 3. Speech with true faith. Take the true faith as faith in Christ, In him, not in propositions concerning him, propositions either including doctrines or facts. I offer three remarks concerning the speech of this faith. I. IT IB INEVITABLE. '!'he man who truly believes in Christ feels that" necessity is laid upon him," that he 0 can~ot but speak the thi~gs seen_ and heard.". Such _is the influence of faith on man'11 social sympathies that his emot1011s beoome 1rrepress1ble. II. entries.title: 2CO 4:1–6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Glory qf the apostolw ministry; how its duties we1·e discharqed. It is still "this ministry." 'l'he question, "Who is sufficient for these things?" has been answered in part by a state~ent of his "sincerity " and " plainness of speech," and ~e now_ proceeds to speak ?f hIS courage and steady zeal. " We faint not," allowing no difficulties or dangers t:<> dishearten us. But what was the nature or spirit of this resolute energy? Energetic men, brave men, who are bent on their purpose, are not always choice or chary of the means employed to gain their ends. "Hidden thincrs of dishonesty," plots, schemes concocted in secret, were renounced, nor did he in any w;;y adulterate the gospel. Not only did he preach the Word, hut he delivered it as received from the Lord Jesus. The mirror was kept clean and bright, so as to reflect the image. Of course, he contrasted himself with his opponents, who used intrigues to acquire influence. If certain men handled the Word of God deceitfully, he was not one of that number, for his single aim was; "by manifestation of the truth," to commend himself "to every man's conscience in the sight of God." Divine truth, such as the gospel c::mtained, was a manifestation, a showi11.g of ita real and intrinsic character, to the only faculty competent to receive it as a 11elf-evidencing system; and that faculty was the conscience. Reason lies back of all our reasoning, and is greater and truer than our formal logic. Instinct antedates experience, and is the condition precedent to experience. And these instincts with their intuitions constitute their own evidence and form the basis of all knowledge. St. Paul argued that the spi.titual doctrines of the gospel, if faithfully presented to the conscience, would be recognized and accepted by conscience as the truth of God. History is history; testimony is testimony; judgment is judgment; coOBCience is conscience; a!ld he will not disparage any one of these to exalt another, but will keep each in its place according to the constitution of our nature. Yet the human mind, made in God's image, must be master of its impressions, sovereign over its motives, lord of itself when most obedient to God; and, accordingly, it must have a conscience to witness "magisterially," as Bishop Butler puts it, for the authority of God. It was not to worldly taste and selfish intellect St. Paul appealed in preaching the gospel, nor to low and mercenary feelings of any kind, but to the conscience as the supreme sense of right in man. And was this all? Nay; they commended themselves, their persons, their private and public lives, their experience and conduct, to the consciences of others. Witness what we are, what we do, how we live, as well as what we preach, was St. Paul's argument. No man enjoyed true appreciation and love more than he; but, most of all, he sought the testimony of their conscience that he was their servant for Chri:it's sake, and was in no respect crafty and dishonest in his relations to the brethren. Private character and public charaoter are, alas I too often disjoined, and not seldom arc opposites; but St. Paul thought that gifts and graces should go together. What he professed as an apostle he would practise as a man, and in each respect he would commend himself to conscience. On no account would he have tho confidence and regard of the Church except so far as he impreHsed this purest and Hafest kind of human judgment. And he did this most solemnly, "in the sight of God." Observe, then, it was not to their consciousness but conscience, to which his ministry, character, Ami life appealed. Nor was this limited to the Church. It was exhibited before all, believers and unbe- lievers, a 11avour of !if,,, a 8avonr of dc-alh. The manilestation of t.he truth would commend itself to every u1an'11 o )nscicnce; aud yet the general verdict- of conecicnc11 OH, 1v, 1-18,] 'l'.l:IE SECOND EPISTLE '1'0 THE CORIN'l'HIANS. 07

would be accepted and acted on by some, while it would be opposed and disobeyed by many. But who were the rejecters? "If our gospel be.hid, it is hid to them that are lost" (who are no_w perishingJ, not finally lost, but at pr':58nt unsaved, their day of grace not over, salvation yet possible. The state spoken of 1s one of mental blindness which includes the want of spiritual perceptions and the darkness of the understandincr'. Conscience is instructed, but the intellect overpowers conscience. Conscience is o~ the side of truth ; intellect on the side of the senses. Conscience entreats warns, condemns, in the name of God ; intellect is sophistical and imperious in behalf of the carnal man. And the intellect is thus alienated from its rational subordination to a ruling conscience by a usurper who is Satan, "the god of this world." Men have allowed him to assert 80vereignty over them, have made him "a god," and have yielded to his wicked agency what belongs to the one God. They havo robbed God to give him power over their bodies and souls, \Vithout this clear and vivid recognition of the personality, the activity, the prodigious energy of Satan, the theology of St. Paul would have no consiste!lcy, no logical coheronce, uo adaptiveness to the convicting and renewing work with which be associates it. With him, human depravity is not an abstract thing, an isolated thing, but part and parcel of a vast system of evil, an immense empire of untruth, deception, fraud, cruelty, of which Satan is head and front. Is unbelief powerful? Satan is behind it. Are the lusts and appetites of the flesh tyrannic? Satan is the tyrant. Are men blinded to their interest and well-being? By him, "god of this world," are they blinded. One who estimates human depravity solely by what it is in itself will have a very different view of its actual character in experience and outworking from one who looks at it as an instrumentality in such hands as Satan's. In the former case it is the man iudulging in depravity for his own gratification-he personally and individually and directly is its motive, impulse, and end; in the latter there is a kingdom and a despotic ruler, whose objects are furthered by widening his dominion and enhancing his sway. St. Paul is explicit. Satan is the blinder, and he is the blinder as "the god of this world." And he blinds the minds of men, "lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the Image of God, should shine unto them." Tnrn to the close of the previous chapter and read of the "open face," of the reflected" glory of the Lord," of the assimilating power of the "image,'' of its transforming wonder in changing "from glory to glory." And now take this awful contrast-a fo.llen angel, a dethroned principality and power, the "god" among his hierarchies, the "god'' of a world whoro men are on probation for an immortality of good or evil, and this "god" of darkness busy everywhere to hide the only light that reveals Christ o.s tht1 Image of God. Hero is tllis light in t.he history of Christ'd lifo, death, resurrection, exaltation. It is glorious. It is preached as a "glorious gospel;" it is preached by men who h11vo "renounced the hidden things of dishonesty," and who themselves, by tboir candour, intogrity, purity, commend thoruselves to every man's conscience under the oye of God. But So.tan oxert.s all his skill o.ud influence, controls myriad agencies, works continually and works so succes11fully that the minds of many 11re blinded by uubolicf. Destroy boliof and you destroy the soul. And this is the Satanic might of ovil, the climo.x of all his influence, that the blindnllSS with which he shrouds the soul is the blindness of uuboliof. Can he think of" the glorious gospel of Christ" and not be humbled? " We pronch not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Je,ms' s1\ko." And now the idea which has occupied so much of bis atteution-tho veiled foco ot Moses, the open viHion of Christ, tho irua;;e of the ~'ather in him, the glory that oxcelloth, the ministry as a manifestation of glory, Christian growth o.s an expansion from one degree of resplendency to another till it reaches" the perf~ct_ day," and the_ contras~cd blindness of unbelievers who are under Satan's power,-th1e idea., so suggestive, attains its final expression in the sixth ven;e. God had once said, "Let there ho light, and there we.a light." It was the opening grandeur of creation; but was this all? This was to be the permanent symbol of God, the source and centre of more associations and suggestions than any other object in the material uni verse, a creative force to the imagination of metaphor, image, and illustration that cannot be mea:iured. -'\nd, as such, St. Paul uses it when he says that "God, who comma.nd_ed tho hght to shmo out of darkness hath shine<l in our hearts." What fuller embod1m~nt could the thought take than ,: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ"'/ II, COBINTBIANB, B 98 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cn.1v. l-l8.

"Light," "knowledge," "glory of God,"" face of Jes\18 Christ,"-what n collocation ot sublime ideas !-L. V11s. 7-18.-Ministers in their weakneu and strength; present affliction and future issues. There is the ever-recurring contrast. It is now the ministry as a "treasure" and this treasure is " in earthen vessels." We understand the apostle to refer to the body ~~en spcakini;; ?f t~e "~lay_ vessel," the co~trasted elemen~s being the glory of the mm1stry as a Divine illummat1on and the fragile human form m which it was con- tained. It was thus that "the excellency of the power" was seen to be "of God and not of l~s." N~t only ,~as it ~he I!?wer of God, bt~t of ''. exceeding greatness" (Kiing), and while tbe ' surpa.ssIDg might demonstrated itself m the gracious and widespread effects of the ministry, it was also obvious in the physical support given in the midst of such unprecedented labours and trials. To illustrate this "surpassing might" (Cony- beare and Howson), St. Paul adduces his own experience. As it respects the "earthen vessel:" 1. Troubled on every side. 2. Perplexed. 3. Persecuted. 4. Cast down. 5. Always iiying; bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesns. As it respects the" excellency of the power:" 1. Not distressed. 2. Not in despair. 3. Not forsaken. 4. Not destroyed. 5. Life of Jesus made manifest in our mortal body. These ideas of su!Tcring are taken from the body. 1. Pressed or hemmed in on every side. 2. Benighted ou our path. 3. Pursued in a conflict. 4. Thrown down and expecting to be killed. 5. The dying of the Lord Jesus never absent as a. bodily impression. '!'his is the second of those vivid pictures St. Paul has given of his personal life, the :first being found in 1 Cor. iv. 9-13. There is a marked difference between the two representations, tho former referring to the contrast between himself and the self-sufficient Corinthians, while the latter sets forth the contrast between "the glorious gospel" and the weakness of its ministration by means of men. Here the prominence is given to the similarity of his own life to that of Christ, "that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh." Had he spoken in tbe previous Epistle of self-denials and voluntary sufferings over and above "other apostles," going on a warfare "at his own charges," planting a vineyard and eating not "of the fruit thet·eof," a shepherd who "eateth not of the milk of the flock"? No such allusions (except in the reference made in the twelfth verse) are found in this chapter. Before him, in full view, is the career of Jesus of Nazareth, his resignation of the comforts of earth, the homelessness and other privations he endured, and he, the apostle of the Gentiles, is conformed in outward or physical a.,pects to the sufferings of Christ. Still more, the life of Christ's resurrection and exalted glory appears in him, and this life, so manifested in " our mortal flesh" ancl the more signally exhibited because of infirmities and afflictions, is for their benefit. "Death worketh in us, but life in you." But is death a shadow, a discouragement, a pnralyzing terror? Nay; tlie life imparted to the Corinthians through him returned from them to his own soul. He believed and spoke ; they heard and believed. Furthermore, he had another consolation, the hope of a resurrection, when he and they should be_ presented by Christ to the Father for final acceptance. Yes; the fellowship would be immortal as well as glorious. "All things are for your sakes," whatever had befallen him, and this "abundant grace," extended to P.n ever-enlarging number, would swell the volume of thanksgiving to God. In his min? "the glory of God" is never associate~ ~ith nurrow bounds, never with a few, always with the" many"-" through the thanksg1vmg of many redound to the glory of God." 'l'his is his manhood; lnrgeness in everything ; breadth of thought and sentiment for this world and the futm:e I II manhood ~bat ~ould ~reathe in nothing smaller than a universe. ~ow much he 1s w~rth to us ~n t~1~ p11rt1cularl On this account" we faint not." Notbmg had power to dishearten his spmt or depress his efforts. The burden rallied the strength ; the heavier the weight the more energetic the resistance. Another contrast-outward men, inward man: man in each. St. Paul, who is the theologian of the 13ible on the subject of the_ bod:y: no less t~nn of tho soul, is here in one of his favourite moods, and, as usual, his philosophy (1f we choose so to'rcgard his discernment) is as profound as his piety. '"fhough our outward man periHb." It cannot but perish. "Dust thou. ar~, and unto dust shalt t~ou return." 'l'he body exists for no independent purpose, it 1B for the soul, and the 1deo.l of the soul determines the ideal of the body's history, It eats, eleeps, works, for the soul, It decays for the sake of the soul. Now, this decay which the apostle is consider..

ing, we may look at in the light of mod.em physiology, St. Paul is no teacher of physiology or of science in any form., but he mentions facts, which we can interpret by aid_ o~ recent scien".8. What, then, do_ we ~now of d~y as _a bodily law? We know it lS a law co-existent and co-operative with our physical life. It sets in early, goes on continuously, and ends only when the body diei,. It is a successicm of decays. Viewed in this light, decay is a function of activity or a sequel to activity, and accordingly, a conditi()'TI, of renewal. Exercise the arm like a blacksmith, and it rapidly wastes matter. Exercise the brain as a student, and certain constituents are constantly thrown off and expelled from the system. Yet, in all this, there is reproduction and even growth. The decay has an order ; it proceeds from the less serviceable to the more useful functions. Early in life, animal sensations are in excess. The outer world floods the young senses, and no image is painted on the brain that is not a copy of something external But this abates. It lessens by providential law. The spirits decline in boisterousness; perceptions are not so vivid; reflectiveness increases; and the pulse is more of a pulse of thought, will, emotion. What we can spare best is the first to decay. Long before eye and ear show signs of failing other organs begin to advertise their decline. And henee the decay proceeds e.s to time and method in such a form. as to anawer the ends of the body in its relation to the soul. Seldom are there violent changes. No great revolutions oecur. Little by little the alterations go on, so that the mind is insensibly accommodated to them. Agreeably to this law, decay contributes till late in life to the development of the mind. Not until decay bas accomplished higher ends does it tend towards dissolution. Gently, indeed, the hand of tho Father touches the frail tenement, here a nerve and there a muscle, so as to make it less a body for the earth and more a body for the soul. Physiologically, therefore, there is a basis for St. Paul's theology of the body. Now, physiolo~sts may say, as some of them have said, that their science has nothing to do with religion, and, forsooth, this in one sense may be true. But it is certain that Christianity has a good deal to do with their science. Nor, indeed, have we to look further than the text for proof of the fact that, while St. Paul was doing nothing more than unfolding the glory of the gt>spel, one or mor., of the rays of that splendour shone on facts which science is only just now beginning to understand. But the inner man, what of him? "Renewed day by day." We have seen that Providenee uses decay for restoration and even enhancement of power, and moreover, not until physical development has attained its ma.a;imum in respect to mind, does it happen that decay operates towards dissolution. Outward and inward-both tho man, as we have said-and yet the differencing adjectives are very expressive, Look o.t the outside of a tree, the rough bark adapted to the bard usages of wind and weather, ancl fitted to enclose and protect the fibre and circulating sap. So of the body. It is o. sheath to the soul, preserving its freedom from beiog overpowered by the outwo.rd worlJ. and gue.rnnteeing self-direction to its activity. More than this, body is a developing instrumentality of mind, and, in this respect, fulfils the special purpose of Providence. Nevertheless, the soul he.a its own prerogatives. It is God's image, and, WI such, witnesses to its own nature as infinitely different from matter. Wo e11ll it soul becnuso it is perfectly unlike body. We call it spirit because "God is a Spirit." Such words WI body, soul, spirit, stand alone and contain the truth of all truths. Now, the apostle urges this contrast; body decays and dies, spirit under the influonee of the Holy Ghost is renewed daily. Spirit has a capacity for interminable growth. Day by day, o. clearer knowledge of itself, a keener penetmtion of consciousness, a decpor sense of sinfulness in its nature, and, Anomalonsly enough, while gaining a victory more and more ovor pa,·- ticular sins, having 110 acuter conviction of inbred sin. Day by day, tho worlcl fnllinp; away from its senses, and yet, amid the decay of sensuousness, n continual nsccnsion o( delight and gladness as the spirit loses its hold on merely resthetic beauty and enter" more fully into moral beauty, so that, while the body becomes more and more tho "temple of the Holy Ghost," the earth grows into a sanctuary of God, whoro tbo hours fail not to observe their ritual of worship and the air is nover so hushed as not to breatho praise to God. Day by day 1 Ah I are there not idle days, apparently useless days, even days when prayer and holy service seem a burden? Doubtless; but wo must not conclude that these se11SOns are altogether unprofHable. If we ore learning nothi_ng else, we are leoming bow weak and impotent we are, and how unreliahlo ore our constlt~tlon r.n<l habits except we have daily renewing grace. God leavee us to ourselves eomctunes, that 100 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. Iv, 1-18.

we may find out what company we keep when he is absent. Day by day, the most precious of all is a growing nearness to the Lord Jesus Christ. We can recall the time when he was mainly to our young souls a traditional Christ. We knew him by the hearing of the ear and by the sight of the eye. Voices there were that spoke of him and commanded our listening. Faces there were that shone with unearthly light and touched our eyes to a reverent gaze. They are gone now. Sorrow has done its work, and, if that be done, all other work is made effective for spiritual progress. How real he becomes when we suffer as Christians! In the loneliness that comes with all profound grief, what a personal Christ is he to our hearts! Hearts, we say, for the revelations of sorrow, the fullest and grandest ever made to the soul, are all revelations of the blessed Jesus to the affections. Once we could not have thought a possible, but, in later years, the secret of the Lord is with us, and we commune with him as friend with friend. The wonder now is, how we could ever live an hour without this sense of sonship possessing the soul. "Out of the depths" we have learned to say, "Abba, Father," and then we can r~joice with "joy unspeakable and full of glory." The outward man perishing, the inward man renewed day by day, how would such a man as St. Paul look upon trial and adversity? We know more of the nature, variety, and depth of his sufferings than of any one among the saints of the New Testament, and yet be calls his ajftiction light. It is also "but for a. moment." Why he spoke in this way is made clear at once, for the light and momentary affliction is working for bis benefit, fulfilling a purpose, executing a design, and this is a " far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." These words are best left to private meditation. "Glory" in contrast with "affliction," "weight" with "light," "eternal" with" moment," and then the "exceeding," the "more exceeding,'' the "far more exceeding;" we honour the sublimity most by thoughtful silence. And this working, which is now going on by means of Christ's presence in affliction and derives no merit from him, is so far realized by the apostle that he cannot look upon the things about him other than as transient. It is not the mere decay of the outward man nor the evanescence of the world's glory that produces in him this exalted state of mind. The point of view is altogether different. From the height of spiritual life as essentially eternal life, he glances at the panorama of the world as it passes by, but his look-the fixed eye, the earnest gaze-is on the things which are eternal. For him this eternity has already begun ; and while every new grief and every repetition of an old sorrow "worketh" a deeper feeling of the spiritual and eternal life within, he is equally well assured that ea.eh one adds something to the accumulated glory of the heaven awaiting him as an apostle of the Lord Jesus.-L.

All truth is precious and powerful. But the truth, as it is in Jesus, is supreme in moral, spiritual power. The truth of God's righteousness and love, as they are united and harmonious in the gospel of Christ, is the greatest morn! force which has entered and wrought in our humanity. It has power to convince the judgment, to convert the heart, to control the will, to constrain the life. 2. 'l'his truth exercises its power by simple manifestation. It does not need our apologies or defence, our ornaments or recommendations. It does its work best when it is simply allowed to 6hine h_y its own light, to take its own course. II. Some religious teachers appeal to men's interests, others to their fears, some to their superstition, others to their vanity. But the true appeal is to the conscience. " Why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right?" "I speak as , unto wise men, judge ye what I say." Other principles of action address themselves to inferior parts of human nature, and produce proportionate results. But Christian truth aims high, calls forth into action the noblest faculties of t.he soul. Literally translated, the phrase is, "to every conscience of men," which seems to suggest that, whether the conscience be enlightened or crude, sluggish or active, it is evermore, when aroused, a witness to God's Word. entries.title: 2CO 4:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The gospel veiled. Those things which are int.ended for man's welfare are often so perverted by sin that they become the occasion of the greatest evils. So that it is proverbial that the best things, when abused, prove to be the worst. The 0"Ospel of Jesus Christ, when it is received aright, is a power to enlighten, bless, and save. But to those who reject and despise it the gospel becomes the occasion of condemnation and de.qtruction. l. 'l'HE INVlBmLE Abi"D SPIBITUAL POWEB TEAT VEILS THE GOSPEL FROM THE EYES OF l'dEN. 'l'he expression used by the apostle is very strong; he attributes this miscbievoue act to" the god of this world," apparently a personal principle of evil working in human society and in human hearts. Elsewhere we are reminded of the might of the evil one, who is designated" the ruler of this world," "the prince of the power of the air." II. THE MEANS BY WHICH THE EYES OF HEN ABE VEILED. These are runny, and are craftily adapted to the varying characters and habits of men. 1. Sc11Suality often incapacitates for spiritual vision; for the more it makes a mnn sensitive to the attmctions of carnal pleasure the more it hinders his spiritual apprehensions and dulls hie spiritual vision. 2. Worldliness fills the whole horizon of vision with tho things o( earth and time, and thus shuts out the shining of the true light which is from he:wen. 3. The pride of human reason, which fancies it.~e\f to be independent and all-powcrfnl, obscures in the case of many the rays of Divine truth which often reach tho lowliest and the least esteemed among men. III. 'l'HE EFFECTS WHIOB THIS BLINDNESS PRODUCES IN THE 'MINDS OF MEN. 1. The glad tidings are regarded with indifference. 2. Christ himself, the very "lma~e of Go<l," is contempbted with aversion and repugnance. There is no spiritual sympnthy to draw the soul to the holy and the gracious One; his very features are rogarded through a distorted medinm. 3. All spiritual e.i:cellences lose their charm, fail to awaken to admiration and emulation. 4. The true condition in which they lie is aHogother ignored and denied by the spiritually blind. 6. For lack of light they perish; tho spiritually and wilfully blind doom themselves to death.-T.
