entries.content:
-The IMme of preaching. Christianity was first diffused by the proclcmintion of the living voice, and the same mothod hne always hold the most prominont position in the history of the Church and especially of its missions. Yet t.hc success of this motbod has been in proportion to the prominence which preachers give to thoir themo in comparison with their own individuality. I. THE THEME TIIE APOSTLE DISCLAIMS. "We preach not ourselves." 1. I.e. not about ourselves, as is the way with many. Not our own speculations, our own theories, our own fancies. Not even our own experiences in the religious life. 2, For it wns felt by the modost and the wiso that such preaching could only bo to offer, in many cases, weakness, folly, and ignoranco; in all cases human imperfection, and infirmity, to mon who know quite enough of all this, and who stand in need of what is superhuman and Di vino. ll. 'l'BE TIIE!dE IN WEICH THE APOSTLE OLORIICB. 1. Christ as an historical Person. It was and still is necessary, in the first pla.ce, to inform the hearers of tho gospel of tho nctual facts of our Lord's earthly manifestation-his incarnation, his ministry, his humiliation and obedience, his sufferings and death, his resurrection and exaltation. All good, sound doctriuo is based upon fact. 2. Christ as a Divine Person; i.e. the Lord, He is to be preached as being what he ueclareu himself to bo-ono with tho l<'athcr, the King of angels aud of men. It is such an all-sulliciont Friend and llelper that man neetl& • If l11ou wert leae thnn One Divine, My soul would be dismayed ; But through thy human lips God aaya, • 'Tia I ; be not arraid I'" 102 Tm; SECOND EPIS'l'LE TO 'l'llE CORINTHIANS. 3. Christ as a Mediator,complete in all the qualifications needed to discharge the duties of all the offices he sustains. 4. entries.title: 2CO 4:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The light of spirit'IJ,Q,1, knowkdge. Nature is a parable by means of which the Creator and Lord of all is ever teaching us concerning himself and his will. All the vast forces and sublime objects of nature have their spiritual analogues. So is it as appeaI'!I from this passage, with light, which typifies the truth, the gospel of God. We learn- !. WHENCE THE LIGHT com:s. Physical light comes from the sun, and the sun was kindled by the Creator. He said, " Let there be light, and there was light." So all intellectual and moral light is from the Father of lights. He is light, and in him is no darkness. "He clotheth himself with light as with a garment." Our souls :find their full enlightt,nment and satisfaction in the revelation of bis mind, which is as the rising of the sun upon our benighted nature. II. WHAT THE LIGHT IB. In the apostle's view this is "the knowledge of the glory of God." If this be so, God is not the Unknown, the Unknowable. The glory of the Eternal is not so much in his power and wisdom as in his moral attributes, his holiness, and love. The revelation of the Divine character is as light to his intelligent creation. It is welcome, cheering, illuminating, reviving. ill. WHERE THE LIGHT smNEs. "In the face of Jesus Christ." In our Lord's resurrection this light shone visibly from his face, as it had done on the occasion of .his transfiguration. But really and spiritually it is always streaming forth; for Christ is himself the "Emanation of his Father's glory." Behold his face when teaching: the light of Divine knowledge is upon it. When pitying and healing the sufferer, the light of Divine compassion and love is there. When patiently enduring insult, upon it rests the lustre of majestic sweetness. When dying on the cross, the light of sacrificial victory is kindled on the features. When uttering his royal commands from heaven's throne, "his countenance is as the sun shineth in his strength." IV. WHITHER THE LIGHT PENETRATES. "Into your hearts," says the apostle. As the sunbeams only awaken the sensation of light when they fall upon a receptive and sensitive eye, so the revelation of God's character implies a receptive and responsivP heart. Though light ever shines from Christ, multitudes have no benefit or enjoyment from it. When the heart turns like the sunflower to the light, then the day dawns within, and the whole spiritual nature comes to bask in the light of God. V. WHY THE LIGHT SHINES. In answer to this may be summed up the whole spiritual purpose and significance of the Christian revelation, 1. That we may perceive it. It is, alas! possible to hide from the light at noonday. But those who welcome the heavenly light rejoice in it, are guided by it, and know its power to inspire hope eternal. 2. That we may wall~ in it. "Walk ye in the light of the Lord;" "Walk in the light while ye have the light." For God's truth is profitable to all men, having the faculty of directing those who will be led by it into paths of wisdom, peace, and life. 3. That we may reflect it. The light of God is not absorbed by the soul that receives it. It is shed upon those who are around. Christians are" tho light of the world "-11re "light--bearers,'' through whose agency the earth is to be filled with the nu..liance of spiritual and immortal noon.-T.

It iii the truth which Paul declared, the Oll, 1v. 1-18.J THE SECOND EPIS'l'LE TO 'l'HE CORlN'l'BlANS. 103

gosp~l which he preached, the mys~ry which he unfolded, The promise of free pardon for sm, ~fa new l_a"! an~ pow~r for hfe, was what the apostles were privileged to convey to manktnd, This IS still, as 1t was then, the true wealth of the world which enriches the mind and heart of man. 2. Upon whose authority this "treasure,,' is so described. This is the highest authority, that of the Divine Christ, who desicrnates his gospel the "true riches," "the treasure hid in the field," "the pearl of great p~ice •" who reminds us of" treasure in heaven;" who tells us that "where our treasure is th:re will our heart be also;" who counsels to buy of him "gold tried in the furnace."' 3. What Diakes this treasure so valuable? It is unvaryingly satisfying: it is inexhaustible• it is enduring, and not like the " riches that ta.ke to themselves wings;" it is accessibl; to all, so that the poor in this world, having it. are "rich in faith." IL EARTBli:N VESSELS. 1. Explain the figure. As Eastern kinl!S stored their gold, silver, and jewels in earthen jars, so a plain casket may hold a costly jewel, n miry soil may yield a.n abundant crop, a battered ship may carry a precious freight, a lamp of clay may give a brilliant light, a mean book as to appearance may contain noble thoughts. So it is no objection against the gospel that those who preach it are in many respects unwort.hy of a.n office so dignified. 2. Exhibit its application. Christ was apparently a peasant, a carpenter's son; yet he was tho Son of God most high. The apostles were fishermen, toll-takers, tent-makers; yet they were the hernlds of salvation to mankind. The upper rooms where the early disciples met were not comparable to heathen temples, but they were scenes of Divine communion. Among those who frequented the a~scmblies where Christian ordinnuces were observed were not many noble or great, but there were inheritors of the kingdom of God. The npostlo Wl\.i deeply conscious of defects and weakness, was often distressed by humiliations nnd persecutions and contempt. His frail body, his fallible jndgment, his imperfect character, bis lowly and harassed condition, all contrasted with the prcoionsness of the gospel which was deposited in his heart and ministered by hie labours. If it wns so in the case of St. Paul, how much more manifestly was it so in tho case of those far less gHtcd and far more bnrdened with infirmity I Ill. DIVINE GREATNESS. To what purpose was this armn~ement which the npostle here describes? He himself gives the true reBSon. 1. 'l'hnt all Christian labourers nit\)' fool their littleness and their woakness. 2. That they mny recognize the exceeding greatness of the spiritual power of God. 3. That they may give Heavcu the glory, alike for what they receive and for what they impart.-'!',

entries.title: 2CO 4:1–6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Eow men should preach. I. WITH FAITH. Many preach with despair and prepare the way for failure. We should reflect that the pl'eaching of the gospel is the divinely appointed way for saving men. We are likely to have success if we lay hold of God when we seek to lay bold of men. Our own salvation furnishes abundant evidence of the Divine power to save. "God shined in our hearts" (ver. 6); "We obtained mercy" (ver. I). What God bas done for us be can do for others. And we have the Divine promise that the Word shall not return unto God void. "Light shall shine out of darkness" (ver. 6). We must seek a. faith which will pl'event us from fainting even when the outlook is darkest (ver. 1). If we have not faith, how can we expect our hearers to have it? II. WITII COURAGE. We must not faint because of foes. Many an assault upon strongholds has failed because of half-heartedness and cowardice. Preachers should be very bold and very brave. We have nothing to be ashamed ot in our message. Shall the devil's work be done more bravely than Christ's ? Shall the highest service on earth be marked by vacillation and timidity? "But that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life or by death n (Phil. i. 20). The Church would be more aggressive if she were more courageous. Preachers should have stout hearts as well as tender ones. III. WITH PERSEVERANCE. We must not faint because of difficulties. Discouragements arc many, but persistcncy will bnry them all. The preacher's motto must be, "On! on I on!" He must spend and be spent in the service. After the manner ascribed to British soldiers, Christ'11 soldiers must never know when they are worsted. "Line npon line, precept upon precept." Many tLings come to the pr.__ncher who can wait and work. IV. WITH GREAT IIONESTY AND SINCERITY. '' Not walking in craftiness" (vt,r. 2). The preacher who wants bis hearers to walk in holy ways must not walk in devious ways himself. He must not be e. trickster. Some seem willing to do anything to please; but the object of the ministry is not to please. Meat cut with a dirty knife is likely to become unsavoury, and the gospel administered with knavish arts will lose its beauty and power. V. WITH PURE DOCTRINE. ., Not handling the Word of God deceitfully" (ver. 2). "Manifestation of the truth" (ver. 2). Christ gives us pur0 doctrine to preach, aml woe unto us if we adulterate it I We must not season it to the tastes of the carnal, or keep back portions likely to offend influential sinners. 1. We preach in the sight of God. How, then, dare we tamper with his truth I 2. We are to commend ourselves to every man's conscience. Nothing but preaching the truth will do this. We may commend ourselves to men's fancies by preaching our own, and to their predilections _by trimming doctrines according to their demands; but on,y by preaching uure doctrine shall we reach the consciences of men. Theological juggling may please men no~ a little; gospel doctrine will convict them. To our own Master we stand or fall. 'T1s a poor thing to please men if we displease him. Let Luther's caustic saying," Counterfeits of money are burned, but falsifiers of God's Word are canonized," bo never so true, the preacher must adhere to the doctrine delivered to him, though he lose nil earthly things by doing so. In a heterodox world nothing is so likely to be so popular as heterodoxy. VI. WITu PURITY OP LIFE. "Wo have renounced the hidden things of shame" ( \'er. 2). If we preach we should p1 actise. Christianity is often weak brcause Chris• OH, 1v, 1-18 J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 10!"

tians are inconsistent. Men want to ,ee the gospel as well as hear it. A preacher must live as well as talk. A man cannot preach withoot himself. There is always more in the pulpit than the sermon-there is the man. We inevitably wonder what the gospel has done for the gospel preacher when he so earnestly recommends it to us. And life has a strange power of revealing itself in preaching. It peeps out. I£ the preacher has e. Judas-life it will betray him sooner or later. But when the man speaks e.s well e.s his sermon, e. mighty influence is exerted. The light mwt shine in our own hearts and lives (ver. 6). VII. WITB DISCERNHENT AS TO CAUSES OF NON-SUCCESS. The apostle teaches that those who reject the gospel when faithfully proclaimed are those whose minds are blinded by the god of this world (ver. 4). They have yielded themselves so utterly to evil influences that the gracious message of God through Christ fails to interest or arouse them. They are "perishing." Their rejection of the gospel says nought against the gospel or against the manner of its promulgation. 'l.'he fault is not in it or in the preacher, but in themselves. It is well for a preacher to realize the possibility of such cases, so that undue discouragement may be avoided when they are met with. VIII. WITB HUMILITY AND SELF-SUBORDINATION. 1. Preachers are not to preach themselves (ver. 5). A man may very easily preach himself even when he takes his text out of the Bible. There is not a little temptation sometimes to ministers to preach themselves. "Let him that thinkcth he standeth take heed lest he fall." 2. Preachers are to be servants for Jesus' sake (ver. 5); servants of those to whom they preach. Nut only servants of Christ, bnt servants of men-" your servants "-for Christ's sake. The preacher who would win souls must sacrifice self. For acoustics it is well for tl1e pulpit to be above the people, but not otherwise. Be who would catch fish must not be seen. IX. W!Tll LOYALTY TO CHRIST. (Ver. 6.) Preachers must be tme in all things to hiJU from whom they have received their commission. They must believe in him, love him, follow him, preach him, live him, obey him, and in all things seek to glorify him.-H.

V. THE OBJE<n' OF THE DIVTh'E CHOICE. 1. The ttninf.errupted woricing of the Divine power, An "earthen vessel" can do nothing but receive and pour forth, What egregious folly for a minister of Christ to seek to enter into partnership with his Lord for the production of a theology! 'l'he earthen vessel cannot do anything, and should not attempt to, 2. The glory of the Divine Being, No glory can attach to the mere earthen vessel. God is "all in all," Tbis should be the desire of every servant of God. Many, it is to be feared, are robbers of God in this matter. entries.title: 2CO 4:16–18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Heavy a.fftiction made light. Paul's troubles were exceedin"lY heavy. So the troubles of many believers have been and are. The sufferings of sai~ts often seem severer than those of sinners. For them the furnace is made seven times hotter. But Paul with his heavy sorrows speaks of them as light, and speaks of them as they really seemed to him to be under the conditions to which he refers. No affliction could well be heavier than his, and yet it was light. So is the believer's- I. WHEN HE CONSIDERS DURING HOW SMALL A PORTION OF HIS LlFE IT HAB TO BE noR1''E. It is but "for a moment." Not so long as a second contrasted with a thousand years. Eternity makes time short. Our troubles are like Pharaoh's horsemen-they cannot pass the Red Sea of death. In this flash of our existence we may weep, but iu the ever-continuing life of heaven we shall rejoice. "There shall I bathe my weary soul In sens of heavenly rest, And not a wave of trouble roll Across my peaceful breast." Our cross is borne but for a moment, our crown for over. 11. \VHEN HE CONTRASTS THE PRESENT BRIEF Tll0UDLE WITH THE ETEllNAL WEIGHT OF GLORY. True thoughts of heaven prevent exaggerated views of earthly sorrows. When the future is shut out we can easily sit down and lament, but when faith sees the "inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, and that fadeth not away" (1 P~t. i. 4), o~r present griefs dwindle into insi"nificance. "For I reckon that. the suffonngs of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed" (Rom. viii. 18). Why should we be disquieted so much by these things when those are so near? Shadows hang heavily over us until the sunshine of the coming glory breaks through the clouds, and then the shadows flee away. Wby should we concentrate thought upon the short present when the long future is so fair'l If wo think much or the home, the journey homewards will seem short, and the troubles of the way ?f little accotlllt. Every hour of sorrow brings us an hour nearer the land that 18 11orrowless. And what shall we possess thero? 'l'he apostle strives in vain to find lan"'llll."'e tiufficienily strong to describe even what he on earth could perceive of heaven _,;'m~re and moro exceedingly an eternal weight of glory" (vcr. 17). Ill. \'vllEN THE MEANING OF PRESENT Tll0UIILE IS !mALIZED, 'ro the true child of God : l. It may mean the destruction of the outward man, but it assuredly means the renewal and development of the inward. It is not even present injury-it is present good. It is medicine, not poison. 2. It prepa~cs us for the comi~g glor_y. '!'he fire consumes the dross, the knife cuts away the diseased pa1t, the _chisel strikes off that which would impair the beauty of the statue. '!'he apprenticeship of sorrow fits us for ea. 1v. 1-18.] '£HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 107

the long service of glory. Through much tribulation we unter the kinudom and are prepared for its duties. The joys of heaven are dependent on the sorr~ws of earth; without the latter we should not be ready for the former. "Tribulation worketh patience,n eto. (Rom. v. 3). 3. Whilst suffering cannot in any way merit salvation affliction rightly endured shall not be without reward. If we fight the fiaht of faith: and endure hardness as good soldiers of Jesus Christ, we shall receive" a crown of righteo11Suess which fadeth not away. Be nu, much concernea a.bout the things of this life. (Ver. 18.) These are perishing. The imperishable are our better portion. Look not at the things which are seen; they are not worth looking at. "Set your affection on things above" (Col. iii. 2.) 3. Look at things umeen by the carnal seme, but clear to faith's vision. (Ver. 18.) entries.title: 2CO 4:5
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Not M!lj, but the Lord. Two imputations had been cast on St. Paul du1ing his absence from Corinth, and to each of these this verse contains a reply. It hnd been said that he sought commendation; and he answered that he set forth, not himself, but bis Lord. It had been said that be tried to domineer over the Churches ; and ho answered that he was a servant of the Church for Jesus' sake. I. THE PROMINENCE GIVEN TO THE LORD. "We preach not ourselves." By this disclaimer is not meant that the apostle excluded all reference to bis own faith or experience, and maintained an altogether impersonal tone while delivering Christian testimony and instruction to the Churches. Extant specimons of his preaching and writing indicate the contrary. St. Paul freely spoke of his own experience of tbo mercy of God and sustaining grace of Christ, of his faith and hopo, his sorrow nnd joy. So have all wise and successful ministers of the Word of lifo shown thoir own hearts to tho people as holding the gospel precious. 'l'hey have so.id, " What we preo.ch to yon we ourselves know and believe; what we commend to your accoptnnco wo have ourselves accepted and proved; so we come before you, not mcroly as messengers by whom tidings are sent, but also as witnesses who can testify that those tidings 1iro true." 'l'he apCIStle spoke and wrote freely of himself, but did not preach himself, i.e. did not set himself before the people as the leader or the Saviour. It was the fault of those factious teachers at Corinth, who tried to disparage the authority of St. l'nul, tho.t they commended themselves, taught their own speculations, eyed their own advancement, and drew away discifles after thew. 'l'his wns what tho npostlo disclaimed and abhorred, and what al preachers of the gospel must scrupulously, nn,l oven jealously, avoid. It is positively fatal to spiritual succoss to projoct one's self before the people instead of setting forth the all-sufficiency of Christ Jesus, !ho living Essence of the gospel. Some one complained to tbo excellent Willinm Ilomniuo of his constantly preaching Christ; and he answered, "We havo nothiug ciao to preach;" i.e. we preach nothing separate from him or disconnected with him. All sound doctrine converges towards, and all acceptable obedience i68ucs from, the oxccllency of tho knowledge of Christ. "Preach the Law," the Jews demanded of Paul; and l,o preached Christ, the end of the Law to evory believor. "Preach wisdom," cried tho Greeks; and hi, preached Christ as the Willdom of God. "Preach prnctic11l virtues nnd good cunduct,n cry many modern critics and monitors; and wo must 1,rcach Christ in onfor to make hearts new, and so mako li¥cs puro and upri~ht from tho roots. It is not enough to teach the existence of God, his attributes of bciug nnd character, his nilcontrolling providence, or even his universal fatherhood. ,vo preach Jesus, tho Teacher, the Healer, the Saviour, the Son of God. We preach h)m ns Christ, the Messiah announced in ancient prophecy, who should sufTer many thmgs nnd so ontcr into his glory. And we preach Jesus Christ as Lord. Ho is Lori! of nil. Ho is Lord both of the dead and of tbo living. He is Lord "to the glory of God tho Father." Do any think this impracticable? Do they p>int to the ignoranco that hns to be removea, 105 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [ea. 1v. 1.-18.

vice t-0 be restrained, selfishness to be corrected, and count it a mllre waste of time to 1,peak so much of a Personage who lived, and the things which he said and did in J udrea ever so long ago? Do they ask, " What good can this do?" We a.re bold to answer-If this will not do good, nothing will. Moral directions and monitions cannot lift men out of themselves or raise them above low levels of thought and conduct. There must be some new and near relation to God, some help from heaven; and this is gained only through faith in Jesus Christ the Lord. In no other way ban been produced powerful and permanent transmutations of human character. In no other way are men rescued from evil habits and made good, and kind, and just, and pcre. Therefore we will persist in preaching what Paul preached, 11. THE PLACE TAKEN BY THE APOSTOLIC PBEACHEB, We do not wish to lord it over the Church. "\Ve are your servants for Jesus' sake." 'rhe factious teachers at Corinth sought their own advancement, and, judging St. Paul by themselves, alleaed that he assumed more authority than he was entitled to, and wished to play dicta.to~ to the Churches. The sensitive and generous heart of the apostle acutely felt the imputation. He was, indeed, bound to assert his e.postolate, but, absorbed as he was with the thought of his Saviour's authority as Lord, he abhorred the idea of claiming lordship over God's Church, and was careful to describe himself as a servant, and to associate with himself by name such fellow-servants as Silas and Timothy. Much more al'C modem ministers of the Word, while maintaining the reality and dignity of their ministry, to beware of anything that savours of lordly assumption. They are servants of the saints for Jesus' sake. Not for the sake of men, or for any inducement or remuneration which men can offer. They are not employes of the people, engaged by them to do their religious work, and responsible to them for their conduct. ln fact, they are servants of the people, and yet the people are not their masters. One is their Master, even Christ; and they serve the Church under his orders and for his sake. So Jesus Christ himself became the Servant of all because he was God's elect Servant. Among his followers it is always better and nobler to serve than to be served. What an example Paul showed as a servant for Jesus' sake !-wearing out his frame in severe and dangerous travels and voyages, caring for all the Uhurches, praying for them, writing to them, visiting and revisiting them, running all risks, enduring all thingseven that which was hardest of all, the ingratitude and fickleness of those to whom he had ministered-that he might fulfil the service which had been assigned to him by the Lord Jesus. Others might spare themselves, but he never did. "I wiU most gladly spend and be spent for your souls." It is a high standard; but we do well t.o keep lofty models before us, and try to rise to them according to the necessity and opportunity of our own time, and the ability which is given to us of God.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 4:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Light of the knowledge of Divine glory. The Christianity of St. Pm1l was not a formula.ted religion, but the revelation or unveiling of God in his Son our 8aviour 1. '1'1m GLORY OF Goo IN THE FACE OF JESUS CHRIST. ln that face, turned 80 graciously on the sons of men, is not merely the glow of human sympathy aud pity, but the ineffable glory of the most high God. There is no thought here of the comparison sometimes made between the Divine glory in creation and that glory in redemption. The contrast still in the apostle's mind is between the Law and the gospel. He recalls the glory of God that once shone on the face of MoAes as he descended from the holy mount; and he sets above it the glory in the face of Jesus Christ. '!'ho lustre on the prophet's countenance was trnn~ient, and its effect on the people wns only to agitate them and make them desirous to have it softened by a veil. But Christ is the permanent aud gracious Image of God; and ho reveals it, not to drive men away in terror, but to save thorn and change them into the same imago. II. '1'1rn KNOWLEDGE OF THE GLODY OF Goo IN THE FACE OF JESUS CnnIST, Without this the salvation in the gospel profits us not. We can determine nothing about the benefit which may be derived from or through Christ by those who have had no opportunity to hear of him or know him. That will be as God sees meet. But to us who have the gospel, the blessing must come through spiritual knowledge. If knowledge of law and orrlinances could save, Paul would have been saved while he was a Pharisee; but he entered not on a. stnte of salvation till he gave up all for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ. Taught by his own experience, he commended ea. IV. 1-18.J 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 109

this knowledge to others. It was his daily care and effort to epread abroad that knowledge. And its prop11gation in the early ages of Christianity seemed like a fulfilment of the ancient prophecy that" the knowledge of the glory of the Lord shall cover the earth as the waters cover the sea." Ill. THE LIGHT OF THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE GLORY OP GOD IN '1HE FACE OP JESUS CHRIST. God was light. 'l'he nations, estranged from him, sat in darkness. In Judrea. there was a lamp for his Name, but it was dim. Pharisaic pride a.nd Sadducean scepticism threatened to put it out. Then the true Light came into the world. And now, as Christ becomes known in the Spirit to this man or that, he lights up both mind and heart. There is to every believer a revelation of the Lord. It is a light above all other lights-calm, pure, searching, gladdening. And the shedding abroad of the light of Christ and the love of God is always by the operation of the Holy Ghost. Thus "the excellency of the knowledge" of God in Christ is imparted by "the excellency of the power" of the Spirit.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 4:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The lamp in the pitcher. This verse is often quoted to express human insufficiency far the ministry of the gospel. It deserves to be quoted, for, if St. Paul felt so deeply bis powerlessness without Goel, how much more should this feeling influence ordinary ministers of the Word of life I I. Tm: TREASURE. Paul, working in the factory making tents, or passing through the street undistinguished by dress or retinue, may have been taken for a poor artisan. But he was conscious of possessing a treasure by the use and distribution of which he, while poor, made many rich. It was no store of silver or gold. It was not even the trea.t'ure of intellectual eminence, the wealth of a large and lofty mind ; for, though be had this, he could not impnrt it to others. It was the ministry of righteousness and liberty whereby he communicated to his fellow-men "the unseo.rchalilo riches of Christ." There is no need to draw a distinction here between the ministry which is the topic of the whole context and the light of knowledge which is the immediately preceding subject. In the apostle's thought these are intimately and necessarily combined and together constitute the treasure. It was as an illuminated man th11t ho showed the light to others. And so at this dny, only a man in whom tho true light &bines can boa minister of Christ. But who has the light may spre11d the knowledgo of the glory of God, and bas a treasure better than silver an<l more to be desired thau fi.ne gold. II. Tm: EABTBEN VESSELS. It was and is the custom of Orientnls to keep vnlunblos and money in jars which might be hid, and, in case of danger, might ho buried under- ground. A mc,re eartbon jar might thus contain an enormous tro,\sure. Alluding to this, St. Paui pointed to bis own body, har<l pressed by labours nncl nffiictions. HiH bodily prcsonoo was weak. He had no external advantages for making n.n impression on either Jews or Greeks. Yet in such an earthen vossol WI\S contained o. treasure beyond 111! computation, and not needing to have its worth enhanced by ndventitious surroundings. If we think of the treasure as ono of light-the light of the knowledgo of God's glory-there is a story in the Old 'l'este.ment which may illustrnte the phm~e. 'l'he followers or Gideon bad their lamps in pitchers, or earthen vessels, when they stole a march on the invaders from Midian, and, with sound of trwnpet aud loud wnr- shouts, fell upon their camp. So, by the light in earthen vessels, with the trumpet. notes of their tOlltimony, did the apostles and other early preachers 11Ssnil nnd defeat those opposing powers of the world that would have laughed nt their weakness. It is still the same. G011pel victories are gained, not by a gren.t array of humnn might, but by tho treasure of light in earthen vessels, and by tho shout of faith that makes appeal to Heaven. III. THE POWER. "'!'hat the excellency," etc. This corresponds to the previous expression,," excellency of the knowledge," and both illustro~ an Hebraic f?rm ?f the superlative. 'l'he excellency_ o_f the power was that surpassmg energy which, ~n St. Paul's time, attended the m1mstry of tho gospol, and bore down tho most form1daLlo opposition. 'l'he contrast betw_eon t~e )?OWCr of _the ministry aml the wcalme~s of tho ministers struck the apostle m thrnkmg of his own early labours at Cormth (seo 1 Cor. ii. 1-5). It is a remarkable, and in some respects a mortifying, fact that tho modem Christian ministry, with all its advantages of special training, public respect, 110 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [OH. 1v. 1-18,

and perfect prot.ection by law, shows less of conscience-convincing and heart-compelling power than the primitive ministry did when it was surrounded by difficulty and threatened with death. When it seemed weak, it WAS strong; and now that it seems strong, it is weak. As some explanation of this, it is only fair to admit that the modern ministry in Christendom bas no longer the charm which lies in novelty. It has to be exercised where the terms and facts of our religion are already known and the Holy Bible is the most widely circulated book. And when it goes to fresh fields as India, China, or Japan, it has this disadvantage as compared with the apostoli~ ministry, that in those countries there is no such preparation for the crospel as there was in the countries and cities which were visited by St. Paul. The "settlements of Jews, and the very considerable number of proselytes who knew the Old Testament in the Greek Version, and looked for a Messiah, gave an important facility to the Chris- tian preacher, who formed out of them an intelligent nucleus round which to gather, his converts from among the heathen; whereas now preachers must go to heathen communities that know not their language, and! are wedded to religious conceptions quite different from those in which the missionaries have been trained, and, if there be Christians living among the heathen, holding office or in pursuit of commerce, too often they impede rather than promote the success of the gospel. All this may be recognized, and still it is true that the ministry might and should exert much more spiritual power everywhere than it does. Let prayer be made for this, since the power belongs to God, and only he can enable the ministers ot his Word to overcome the dulness of religious routine as well as the hardness of anti-religious prejudice; to sober the frivolous; to abase the proud; to arrest minds that engross themselves with trifles, and recover those that have debased themselves with fleshly vice or avaricious deceit; to wound and to heal; to warn and to win ; to kill and to make alive. Oh for power to prevail, to search the breasts of men, to make conscience start and hearts quiver, to reprove sin, to shatter vain excuses, to kindle new resolves and hopes! We cannot do it; but be who supplied all-sufficiency to St. Paul can supply it to us. "Our sufficiency is of God."-F.

entries.title: 2CO 4:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" Cast down, but not destroyed." In ministering the Word, we need to play, if we may so speak, on various instruments of music. We take the silver trumpet when we would utter II the joyful sound.". We take the harp when we show forth God's praise. What shall we take for encouragement and comfort to the weary? As a great poetess has it- .. Experience, liko a po.le musician, holds A dulcimer of patience in hie hand." Let us play on the dulcimer. A good man struggling with adversity has been the subject of many moral reflections. We wo.nt to go further than the more.list, and show how the man of God is preserved in time of trouble. What heroism in the immortal Jew of Tarsus I All tbe sharp ordeal through which be pe.ssed-;his personal disadve.nte.gee, the disparagement by false apostles jealous of h_ie influe~ce, the col_dness of fo~er friends when he was in bonds at Rome, the hardship and m1sconstruct10n under which his great work had been done,-all served only to bring out more fully the BingleneBB of his aim and fortitude of his spirit- .. And give the world neeurance of o. man.• "Strock down, but not destroyed." Trouble threw him down, as one wrestler might throw another in the arena; but the ca.st was not mortal. Ho revived, for Christ lived in him. Nay; his sufferings increased his usefulness. No follower of Christ ever me.de such an impression on mankind, or did so much for the gospel, e.s this troubled, persecuted, perplexed, cast-down Paul of Tarsus. 'l'imes be.ve changed. Religious liberty prevails. Gross forms of persecution for confessing Christ are prevented by law and condemned by public sentiment. But it doe~ not_follow that the course of a faithful Christian ia made easy. It is often beset with difficulty, broken, and uneven. Good men are II cast down;" and it is painful to have the skin grazed, even when the bones are not broken. Under such disappointing experiences feeble souls are apt to become more timid and more querulous, while bolder natures grow selfish and cynical, These OJL IV. 1-18.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 111

!~et, if they h!l-ve been struck down when grsppling ':rith something to them impracticable or forbidden, resolve to knock others down, and, 1f need be for their own interest trample on them. But natures that are sweet and sound ·1earn wisdom consideratio~ for others, and knowledge of themselves through hard experience. A~d hearts that trust in God have this joy in the worst defeat, that they are not they cannot be destroyed. Life is not wrecked by every trouble or by a score of tro~bles. A mistak~ may be the very making of a man, if he knows how to correct it. If the way is blocked in one direction, other paths are open. And if helpers fail and friends forsake God still lives. We do not, _indeed, conceal from ourselves that some overthrows can;ot be quite remedied in this world; some losses are irreparable on earth, just as some diseases are incurable. But no Christian needs to be inconsolable. If he be stripped of ever so much that he valued, his best treasure remains, and is above the reach of worldly vicissitude. There is a good part which shall not be taken away. Thus life is always worth living. For a brave man it cannot be utterly wrecked by misfortune. For a devout man it cannot be shattered, though once and again struck down to the ground. The good Shepherd restores the soul. But many are the uses of adversity. Remember your faults and correct them ; your mistakes, and avoid them; but do not waste time in vain regrets or temper in weak complaints. What purpose docs it serve to brood over disappointment and " feed with sighs the passing wind "? How much better to gird up yonr purpose and make the best of what is left to you of time, strength, and opportunity I You mny yet stand all the more firmly because of that casting down. The ill you have suffered may lead to higher good. "Though the outward man porish, thti inward man is renewed dny by day." Gou knows how to give- .. Secret refroshings that repair your strength. And fainting spirits uphold."

entries.title: 2CO 4:16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Inward rmewal and outward decay. The contr:i.st hero is not that which the apostle draws elsewhero between the flesh and tho spirit, or tho old mnn nnd tho new. That is a moral distinction. But this is between the physicl\l nnd tho spirit.uni in man, the outward and palpable on the one hand, the inward and impalp1\ble on tho other. These are intimately connected. 'l'hey have e. constant syrnpo.thy. 1\.n nching body jades the mind; e.n aching mind jades the body. A healthy body iuvigorutm1 the mind; a cheerful mind sustains the body. Each affects and is affected by tho other. Yet there is sometimes witnessed a glorious mastery over outward di~ndvnntngcM by the force of the inward man. The heroic mind is firm, even when tho physical frame is shattered. And nothing is so productive of this heroism as faith. 'fhey who have "the snme spirit of faith" as was in Paul "faint not." I. OF mwABD RENEWAL. The case in view is th11t of II rogenerato ml\n, It is aaaumed that ~iritual life has been received. And now it is shown that "the washin~ of regeneration 'is followed by" the renewing of tbo Holy Ghost." Good men aro Jiablu to fits of inward fainting, languor, and emotional deadness, when they nre in grc11t danger of being overcome by temptation. 'l'herofore they need to pray often for ll stronger lifo. "Renew e. right spirit within me." 1. WhBrein is tho inuor man renewed? "In righteousness and holiness of truth" (Eph. iv. 24). And so in oil spiritual strength-tho power of resistance to sin, of self-donial, of patience, nnd of goneroue charitable action. 2. Whereby ie the inner man renewed? lly the power of God; by the energy of the Holy Ghost. It is he who, with the Word of truth, makes vivid demonstration of righteousness to the conscience, strengthens holy purposo in the will, and gives fervour to devout affections in the breast. 3. How often is the inner man renewed? "Day by day." Not that all days aro alike. As a nation has its special dates in history, days by which its future has beon monld_ed! on which its decisive battles were fought or its independence was won, so m~y a Chmtmn mn_n hav_e his dates more or less clearly marked, outstanding and prec!ous days by wluch l11s spiritual history has been determined, on which his fight of fa1_th was well f~ught, n~,l his liberty in Christ became established ond sure. But w~1le we rcc~gn1zo spcc111l days or eras of spiritual progress, we are disposed to say that m grace, as Ill ~o.turo, the, ordinary is, after all, more e1.pr~esive of Divine goodnes~ tlian the ext~a?rdrnary, and more euential to our welfare, 'Ihe daily revival and m111ntcnance of spmtua! hfe Is a 112 THE SECOND EPISTLE 'l'O THE CORIN'l'HIANS. LclI, 1v. 1-18,

better and greater thing than any occasional and exceptional blessina, "He holdeth our souls in life." The strength, moral a.swell as physicul, which i~ daily expended is also daily restored. John Bunyan makes the Christian pilgrim see a man secretly feeding with oil a fire on which another cast ,vater, and the fire burned "hotter and hotter." The Interpreter explained it of Christ's secret and constant renewal of the sacred fire in "the souls of his people." II. OF THE RELATION WHICH INWARD RENEWAL MAY DEAR TO OUTWABD DECAY. St. Paul was conscious of two changes-an outward descent to feebleness and earth, and an inward ascent to firmer strength and higher vitality. 1. The inward defies the outward. "Though our outward," etc. 'l'he constancy of the believing heart is all the more triumphant because of the feeble or decaying frame. What might of spirit has shown itself in tender women under acute suffering I What force of character and ~plendour of patience in men who scarcely had a day without bodily pain! 2. The inward renewal is cften helped forward by the outward decay. It pleases God to further the spiritual life of his children in ways that are hard to flesh and blood. Indeed, we seldom see a keen relish for the things of the Spirit of God, a weaned spirit, a holy fervour-while the outward man is quite at ease and commands every gratification. There is need of trouble in the outer sphere to exercise and quicken the inner life. Bengel, near the end of his course, said to a friend, "Illnesses serve to quicken and enlarge us in spirit after we have been dwindling. When our spiritual lamp burns dimly, it is often because its wick needs retrenching; and retrenchments are made from time to time upon the outward man by sickness and affliction." Thus it is not merely "though," but also sometimes "because," our outward man perishes that our inward man is renewed. What a sad case is theirs whose outward man decays while there is no spiritual life in them! Time passes, health fails, life ebbs away, and there is nothing to put against it. The outward man perishes and the inward man perishes too. But why will ye die? The Lord wishes not that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 4:18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Seeing the unseen. I. THE HABIT OF :MmD HERE DESCRIBED. The apostle i;peaks, not of an act or effort, but of a steady mental habit which he had formed-an intentness of regard in a particular direction. He describes it in a form that sounds 11aradoxical, but the thing meant is well known to all experimental Christians. Tho things seen and not seen in this passage are not the visible e.nd invisible by mortal eyes, as in Rom. i. 20, The things not seen in the verse before us are so, not because they cannot be seen, but because the time has not yet come for their manifestation. The things seen, from which St. Paul turned away his eyes, were the toils and afflictions endured by him as a servant of Christ, The things not seen were the rewards of faithful service at the coming of the Lord-the "weight of glory." And the habit here indicated is that of looking off from labours and sufferings to the glorious appearing of the Lord, and the bright "recompense of reward." It is the highest form of looking on the cheerful side of things. As this is a habit, it must be formed by degrees and by reiterated efforts. By be!lding the mind as much as we can towardH the futuro with Christ, we must train it to habitual expectation and desire. II. THE BEASON ASSIGNED FOR FORMING THIS HABIT. "l!'or the things which are seen are," etc. St. Paul reflected that "the st1fferings of the present time" were, after all, of short continuance. The affliction he endured was only for a moment as compared with the eternity before him. So he felt that he would outlive and triumph over all his trials. 'l'hey were temporal, and so could not reach into the life beyond or mar the hope laid up for him in heaven. Was not this the way with the Divine Master himself? For the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising the shame. And so should all who are his bear the cross and endure patiently, because tht1 time will not be long and the things not seen are eternal. III. TnE BENEl'ITS WHICH ACCOMPANY 0B FLOW FROM THIS HABIT WHEN FORMED, 1. Elevation of the tone of life. Life is as its motives are; and tho motives come from the convictions, fears, and hopes that arc strongest in tho mind. A superficial religion has not power enough to cleanse tho heart or ennoble the principles of conduct. But a formed habit of regarding the things eternal as those to which we hasten must raise and refine the character. " Every one who has this hope in him purifies himself, oven

as. he is pure." And ~hie is no selfish h?pe, no ~otistical am~ition. It is the hope of being cro~ed along with all wh_o love his appean_ng, ~nd of being rewarded along with all the fa1thf~ servants of the Kmg. 2. U<>nsola~wn in hardship a'Tld adversity. Even when a lamp 1s not near enough to cast a clear light on our path, it is cheering to see it in a murky nigh_t; and so are we comforted as we look for the glory with Christ. We move towards 1t over ever so rugged a path. We steer towards it over ever so restless a sea. If we look at the things which are seen, the waves and the threatenin"' rocks, we lose strength and courage; but with the eye fixed on the light of that blessed hope, we make straight for the harbour. 3. Preparation/or departure hence. It is appointed to men to die. To take no thought about this appointment, and to occupy the mind with only the things that are seen, forgetting their transience, is to play the part of a fool. The wise man is he who, while fulfilling the duties of the passing time, looks much and steadily into the future, and so, when he departs, goes not into regions unknown, but to the Saviour, whom he has loved and served, to wait with him and with all the saints for the resurrection and the glory.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 4:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-J,'ull CO'Tlji,dence in the power of the ti-uth. "By manifestation of tho truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God." The great work of the Christian ministry is to set forth before men the truth. But we are not to understand by that term all truth or any truth. Reference is precisely to that truth about God, and, his relations with men, which had been partially revealed before, and was fully disclosed in Jesus Christ the Saviour. That special truth had been committed to the trust of the apostles. 'l'hey were to proclaim it freely to men, as they had or could make opportunity. And they were to be sure that God would make that truth his power unto men's salvation. Referring to the work of the modem ministry, it hna been well said that we have not so much" to tell the truth as to make the truth tell." The apostle, in these verses, reminds us of some things that are necessary if we would efficiently set forth the gospel truth. I. PERSEVERANCE. "We faint not." There must be no shrinking back in face of difficulties, no losing heart because things will not go smoothly, no wearying in our well-doing. St. Paul himself gan the noble example of what he enjoined. He did not count his life dear to him so that he might finish his course with joy. Succeed or fail, in strength or in weakness, he was "instant in season and out of season." II. SillPLICITY. 'l'he faithful minister will absolutely refuse all morely sensational aide to his work. He will wholly separate himself from worldly and guileful schemes for accomplishing his ends. He will refuse in any way to "do evil that good mny come." lt had been made an accusation against the a~sUe that he bad shown cmftiness and guile in his dealings with the Churches. '!his charge he most vigorously rebutted, a:id was led to urge that guilelesMness is essential to the faithful minister, whose conduct and motives may be searched through and through. Illustration mny he taken from the ministry of the Lord Jesus. He resorted to no arts, or schemes, or tricks, either of speoch or of conduct. His work was simple. It wus the living of u life, the delivery of a message, a genuine effort to bless iind save men. Ill FAITH. In the witness which the truth ever makes, and the rosponso to it which is alwnys given by men's consciences. We may pronch with this confidenceconscience will surely acknowledge the claim of God, and the guilt of sin, a.nd the need of redemption. Men may indeed silence conscience and put away the truth, but we always have this assurance-the best and deepest in every man responds to our mesMge. IV. 'l'HE ooNSCI0UBNl!:BB or BEING UNDER Goo's EYE. "In the sight of God." 'l'lmt Divine presence the minister realizes as the fulfilment of Christ's words, " Lo, I nm with you alway, even unto the end of the world." There is a hardness and coldness about the idea that we should work "as ever in the great Taskmaster's eyo." '!'here is warmth, tender sympathy, and inspiration in the BBSurance that the spiritual "Man, Christ Jesus," is with us everywhere. In conclusion, such points as these need careful treatment. 1. Is this confidence in the power of the truth justified by experience? 2. Does Christ's truth over really stand in peril? 3. If so, from what sources or in what directions does the peril come? Agencies and organizations and human moulds imperil it, and in every a.ge men are raised up who can set Christ's truth free from our human limitations and bondages. IL CORINTHIANS, I 114 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. iv.1---:!S..

The true revival is the freeing of the truth to win its own good way. We can haRe no ground for glorying comparable to this-" the Word of God is not bound.'.'-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 4:4
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -(Jhrist as tM Image of God. "The glorious gospel of Christ, who is the Image of God..n From 1 Cor. xi. 7 we learn that there is a sense in which man is the "image_ an~. glory of God." . In Col. i. 15 the Son of GoJ. is spoken of as the "Image of the mvis1ble God, the F1rstborn of every creature." The word used in our text is exactly equivalent to our word "likeness.'' "An image, or likeness, is e. visible repre- sentation of an object. So Christ, in his humauity, is a visible representation of the unseen God. No revelation of the wisdom and power of God that man has received can compare with that made in the life, death, and resurrection of the incarnate Son." The point to which we ask attention is this-the gospel sets forth the glory of Christ. Bnt, when it is rightly viewed, this is found to be the setting forth of the glory of God. For God can only be known in image and symbol; and this is the perfect and wholly satisfact.ory image, precisely adapted to our human faculties and necessities. Jesus Christ is the "Brightness of the Father's glory, and the express Image of his person." His sonship is the earthly presentation of the Divine fatherhood. The Son is the very image of the Father. Philips Brooks well says, "This is the sum of the work of the Incarnation. A himdred other statements regarding it, regarding him who was incarnate, are true ; but all statements concerning him hold their truth within this truth-that Jesus came to restore the fact of God's fatherhood to man's knowledge, and t.o its central place of power over man's life. Jesus is mysteriously the Word of God made flesh. He is ths Worker of amazing miracles upon the bodies and the souls of men. He is the Convincer of sin. He is the Saviour by suffering. But, behind all these, as the purpose for which he is all these, he is the Redeemer of man in:to the fatherhood of God." Christ brings the light of God's fatherly love 1o shine on prodigal and sinful sons; that light wakens the old son-spirit in their hearts, and wins them home, iii penitence and faith, to their heavenly Father. And just this is the mission of Christ and his gospel-to shine God's light into men's sciuls.-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 4:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Light from God and light on God. The new Revised Version makes an important alteration in this verse, reading it thus : "Seeing it is God, that said, Light shall shine out of darkness, who shined in our hearts, to ,rive the light [or,• illumina- tion'] of the knowledge of the glory of God in ,the face of Jesus Christ." I. LIGHT FBOM GoD IS' CREATION. (Gen. i. 3.) 'l'he following points may be illus- trated. 1. All material light, as a warming, life-giving, beautifying agent, is from God. 2. All moral light, as the intimation of what is good and right in the relation- ships of men, is from God. :l. All revela.tional light, as the unfolding of -the mysteries belonging to God and his claim and mercy, must come directly from himself. On spiritual things man can have no knowledge, save as God is pleased freely to give it; and, on these higher themes, all light must be tempered to the capacity of thoee on whom it shines. II. LIGHT oN GoD m ClmlBT. Calvin says of this verse," A notablo place, whence we learn that God is not to be investigated in his unsearchable height, for ho inhabits the light unapproachable (1 Tim. vi. 16), but t.o be known as far as he rev_eals ~imeelf in Christ. . . . It is more useful for us to behold God as he appears ID hie only begotten Son than to investigate his secret eee.ince." The face of Christ is said to reveal the glory of God, as the shining of Moses' face told of the splendour about the mount where ho had been with God. But tho glory of God is his redemption-1vork. That showed (1) pity, (2) love, (3) wisdom, (4) holy purpose; and all these wo find in the face of Je8116 Christ. Illustrate the power of expression, and the power of revealing thou<>ht and heart, that are in the human face, and then show how the face of the Lord° Jesus reveals to us the " heart of God." Before Christ came God was a halfknown if not au unknown, God. And the incomplete conceptions of him involved, too of(en, imperfect and unworthy ~oncept!ons. We now know ~e "tr~e God and eternal life" in the face of Jesus, hlB manifested Son-or rather, his marufested j:ielf, -R.'l'. Ver. 7,-Heaventy_treaaure in earthen vessels, "It was the practice of Eastern kings, CB. rv. 1-18.] THE SECOND El'ISTLE TO THE CORINTIIIANS. 115

who stored up their treasures of gold and silver, to fill jars or earthenwnre wifo coin or bullion" _(see J_er. :uxii 14).. To t1?Js ~ns_tom allusi?n is !llade. St. Paul says that in these frail bodies of ours, with their limited faculties and powers, in these "earthen vessels " we have that priceless treasure, the knowledge of the glory of God as a. Redeemer. Cecil says, "The meanness of the earthen vessel which conveys to others the gospel treasure takes nothing from the value of the treasnre. A dyincr hand may sign a. deed of incalculable value; a shepherd's boy may point out the way to a. philosopher; a. beggar may be the bearer of a valuable present." Three points cla.im attention. I. THE TBEASUBK. This may be regarded as (1) a revelation, (2) as a gospel (3) as a life. In either respect, the personal Christ being the very Centre and Essenc~ of it , he is properly the Treasure. Christ himself is our most sacred Trust. We have the on; Saviour for men .committed to our care. Then how jealously we should guard the treasure! and how wisely we should.put it to use I II. Tai!: NEED FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF THIS TREASURE. For it is not to be stored up in hiding-places, but somehow made the treasnre of all· men. It is a spiritual treasure, and needs some kind of material conveyance. Christ himself must be ministered to men by his disciples. III. THE V.ESSELS FOUND FOR THE DUE CONVEYANCE OF THE TREASURE. Humbly spoken of as earthly, or as mere earthenware. Enlarging upon, them beyond St. Paul's immediate thought in the use of the term, we may show (1) their frailty; (2) their fitness, especially in that they do not take away the honour that is due to the treasure by Jirecting attention to themselves; (3) their safety, since God, who guanls tho treasure, will guard the vessel that holds it; (4) their usefulness, as the human agency commends the heannly truth; and (5) their reward, for God will surely commend those who, in such a trust, are found faithful.-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 4:10
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Suffering 1h'111rin9 forlh character. It has been said that "affliction n is the one predominant word in the Second Epistle to the-Oorinthians. And perhaps no other Epistle is so charged with wounded personal feeling and reminiscences of varied suffering. This may be explained by the ciroumstances under which this letter WHS written. Perhaps we do not sufficiently realize how much personal suffering, from diBease and bodily infirmity, the apostle ho.d to endure; and yet this is evidently the key to many of his intense expressions. Either from constitutional weakness, or in con.sequence of his many exposures, he had upon him some pl\inful and humiliuting form of disease, whioh was incurable; and this.his _enemies made tho occasion of scorn and insult, until they wounded him to the very quick, l\nd drove him to tho throne of gra~,.seeking, with threefold importunity, to have the" thorn in the flesh" removed. When we apprehend this, we begin to feel the meaning of our text; he wns "always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus:" pain, diseaso, suffering-like a dail;y dying-brought on hi.m in the fulfilment of his ministry for the Lord Jesu.s. But St. Paul never dwelt long on the merely sad side of things, anJ so ho goes on to say- Even if our life on earth be like the dying of the Lord Jesu.s, this also is true, through our very su[eri.ng and dying, the life of Jesus is made manifest in our mortal flesh aud earthly epher88.. "St. Paul felt that every true human soul must repeat Christ's existence. He conld bear to look on his decay; it was but the passing of the human; and, meantime, there was ever going on witbiu him the strcngtheniug of tho Divino. Pa.in was sacred, since Christ also had suffered. And life•bccamo gro.ml whcu viewed as a repetition of the lifo of Christ." L ST. PAUL'S CONCEl'TJON OF 0011. Loan's LIFE. It had been a daily dying which ncverthBl~ showed up himself, in the glory of hill character and spirit. '!'ho dying manifested to men the life that was in him. St. Paul had, probably, never seen Christ in the flesh, but it was given to him, by his fellowship of sulforing, to understand, better than all. the, rest what a suffering Saviour Jesus was. It is St. Paul who writes &0 much about the cross of the Lord Jlll!Us. lie dwells oftener than any other early, teacher upon our Lord's death, but when you apprehend his meaning, you find that he looked upon Christ's whole life as a dying. Ho saw that Jesus w~ every day dying to self, dying with shame, pain, exhaustion, conflict, ond agony. And you do not read Christ's life aright unless you can see in it what St. Poul saw, even humilintionp limitation, suffcriug, burdening it every day. Dut that_ was not all St. Paul's conceptiuu 116 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [en. 1v. 1-18.

of Christ. In that, standing alone, he could have found no nst, no inspiration. He saw also this, that our Lord's sufferings were just the dark background that threw out so perfectly,_ wilh such well-defined lines and graceful forms, his noble spirit, his Divine charact<ir, his sublime sonship, his blessed life. And so he could speak calmly oven -triumphantly, of the suffering Saviour, and glory in the dying of the Lord Jesus through which the life of Jesus found its highest and best manifestations. How much a picture depends upon its background! Fill the front with the most exquisite figures or Jan~sca.pe, still all the tone and cha;llcter and impression of the figure will depend upon its background. You may so pa10t as to leave the forms and figures indistinct and uncertain. You may throw out into prominence the special thought or truth which you seek to embody in form; your picture may be calm morning, hot noonday, flushed evening, tender twilight, or gathering night, according to your background. St. Paul felt what shadows of suffering and woe lay all behind that life of his Lord• but they helped him to see the glory of Christ himself; they seemed to bring out s~ clearly the Divine and blessed life that was in him. Illustrate by the language ot Isa.. liii. and Phil. ii. 5-11. Also from the scenes of Gethsemane and Calvary. The Captain of our salvation was made perfect, to our view, through suffering. n. ST. p AUL's CONCEPTION OF HIS OWN LIFE. He could wish nothing better for himself than that what was true of Christ might be true of him, and that his sufferings, too, might show up bis character and help to make him a blessing and a power for good. St. Paul never could glory in mere suffering. Suffering is grievance and loss. But if they could be like Christ's sufferings, not merely borne for him, and in the doing of bis work, but actually like his, and ordained by God to be the same to him, and to others through him, as Jesus' sufferings did! The apostle felt be could glory in that. And this is the view of suffering that we also need to gain. Our troubles and sorrows are as the dying of the Lord Jesus. Once laying hold of this, we find that we havo one thing tt1 be supremely anxious about-it is that our dying shall show up Christ's life in us, shall make the Christly virtues and graces manifest in our mortal flesh. We have our sorrows. Does our character shine out clearly on the darkness of them? Do men see and feel our "whiteness" by the contrast of them? Are we beautiful with a Divine patience, and fragrant with a Divine sweetness, in the very darkness? On the background of our pain do men see our submission? In the hour of our disappointment do we show up to men our trust in God? When heart and flesh fail does the sanctifying Spirit of Christ make our very faces glow with the heavenly light? Is it true of us that the "life of Jesus is manifested in our mortal flesh" ?-H. 'l'.

entries.title: 2CO 4:16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The outward and the inward man. For the word" perish" in this verse, the Revised Version reads "is decaying." "Outward man" is the body, "inward man" is the soul, so far as the terms may be understood by anybody. "Outward man" is the whole sphere of the senses and the flesh; "inward man" is the whole sphere of the moral, the spiritual, the Divine, the eternal, so far as the terms may be apprehended by the quickened and regenerate of mankind. 'l'he "outward man " is man related to the "seen and temporal ; " the "inward man" is man related to the " unseen and eternal." And what the apostle so plainly says in our text is this-the "outward man," the material framework of the body, and the whole. circle of purely human and earthly relations, are yielding to a gradual process of decay, and soon they must all pass away. But the" inward man," the spiritual life, the very man himself, is day by day rising, through successive stages or renewal, to yet higher life. And the very decayings of the body and of the earthly surroundings bear directly nr,on the nourishment and growth of the soul's life, and so upon the soul's future. 'lhis is the thought which is set before us for our consideration, and we begin with that familiar truth on which the statement of the text rests. L BODY-LIFE AND SOUL-LIFE BOTH DEPEND ON NOURIBHJIIENT, ON FOOD. This is the law of all created life. Angels live on angels' food. Souls live on appropriate souls' food. And bodies live by meat and drink and air. Science tells us that bodily life, health, fatness, and vigour directly depend on the character and quantity and appropriateness of the food supplied. Given vitality and freedom from active disease, and any bodily result that is desired can be obtained by giving flesh-forming, or boneforming, or brain-making foods. And the health, the vigonr, nnd the work of our on. 1v, 1-18.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 117

soul's life just as directly depend upon the food with which it is no11rished. Would you get more good work out of your souls? '£hen you must feed them better. Do you expose your souls to much peril? 'l'hen you must improve and increase their food. We may speak of the soul's life as beingfaith and love, and as havina for its natural expression worship and work. Then the soul's food which we provide must bear, in the most direct and efficient way, on these four things. Here is a most practical problem for each one of us to solve in our daily life-What will nourish into the fullest health and strength my soul's faith and my soul's love? What will strenathen the soul's brain and heart for holy worship, for prayer and praise, and the soul's mbuscle and nerve for holy work? As life unfolds there come to us a.II times of special stress and strain. Business has its unusual anxieties. Home has its unusual cares. Decisions of grave importance have to be made, and we too easily forget at such times that we need better soul-food; we must be oftener at the secret sources of spiritual nourishment; we must find out how strong they can become who eat of the tree of life, who partake of that Bread of life which satisfies, and that "flesh and blood" which a.re "meat indeed and drink indeed." ll Notra!SH THE BODY-LIFE HOW WE HAY, rr IS WEARING DOWN TO DECAY AND DEATH. "The outward man yerishes." "The fashion of this world passeth away." All the feeding, all the nourishing, all the fresh air, cannot keep the bodily powers working over-long; for soon the sight grows dim, and the bearing fails, and the taste palls, and the hands tremble, and the breath goes hard, and the limbs totter, and then the golden bowl is broken at the fountain, and man goeth to his long home, aud the mourners go about the streets. There is a fixed limit beyond which the body cannot go. None of us can with impunity exert ourselves beyond the limits of our physioal strength, for gradually, as the years pass on, our vital force is lowered, our recuperative power fo.ils, the body ie really decaying and wasting down to helplessness and death. But why shoultl we trouble because we cannot feed these bodies of ours into a strength that sb11ll resist disease u.nd old age, and make our years last through all the genero.tions? 'l'bey are not ua. They are but the machinery, the agency, the sphere, of our sublime moral trial. They may last no longer than is needed for the perfecting of the trial. I sh11ll not want this frail body, with its limited sensos and relations, nor shall I want this "ower sin-burdened earth," when God sees that my moro.l trial is over; when he ho.s found out, by this practical experiment, what I really am. I can see thorn both po.ss away, and euter God's spiritual and incorruptible body-tho glorified counterpart of this body I now ho.ve--which is fashioned akin to the "new heavens o.nd new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness." III. NOURISH THE SOUL-LIFE, AND rr WILL GROW ON FOR EVER. For there 11re no forces that can touch the regenerate soul to destroy it. "I give unto thorn etemnl life," He said who brought life and immortality to light hy His gospel, "11ud they sbnll never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
