entries.title: 2CO 5:1–7
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0hdstian knowledge concerning the future 1,o,Zy of tn.e goorl. "For we 1':now·that if our earthly hollile," etc. Two things are to be noticed at the outset. I. Metaphorical representations of the body. 'l'he body is here spoken of under the figure of a "tabernacle" or a tent, and of a vestment or clothing. These two tbings would not be so distinct in the mind of the apostle as they are in ours, for both had the same qualities of movableness and protection. . The "house" to which the apostle refers was not a building of bricks or stone, a superstructure that would be stationary, but a mere tent to be carried about. 2. The implied necessity of the body. Paul's langu:i.ge implies that the body is a clothing or protection. As a clothin~, or protection, for the soul it is necessary, both hero ·and in the other world. The soul must have an organ whereever it ia. Now what does the Christian know concerning the future body? I. He knows it will be BETTER THAN THE PRESENT, 1. It will be directly Divine. "A building of God." The.present body is from God, but it comes from him through secondary instrumentalities. 'l'he future body will come direct, it will not be transmitted from sire to son. 2. It will be fitted for a higher sphere. "In the heavens." 'l'he present body is fitted for the earthly sphere, it is of the" earth, earthy." 'l'he future will be fitted for the more ethereal; and celestial. 3. It will be more enduring. " Eternal." This body is like the tent, temporary; it has no firm foundation; it is shaken by every gust. We "perish before the moth." The future body will be eternal, free from the elements of decay. 4. It will be more enjoyable. "For in tbis we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven," etc. In this body we "groan, being burdened." To what pains and diseases is the present body subject I By implication the apostle states the future body will be free from all this, for all that is mortal will be "swallowed up of life." In that body there will be no groaning, no sighs or sorrows, no burden, no weight to depress the energies or to impede progress. The future body will be more fitted to receive the high things of God, and IUore fitted to communicate them also. II. He knows he is now DEING DIVINELY FITTED FOR THE BETTER BODY OF THE FUTURE. "Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Bpirit." Every seed has its own body; it is the seed that makes the body ; the organization does not produce the life, but the life the organiz:ition. And this spirituol life in man God is now preparing to pass into a higher body. Just oe the chrysnlis is being fitted to struggle into on orgnnization with higher appe-- THE SECOND EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [cn. v, 1~21,

tencles, more exquisite in form, and with faculties the.t shall bear it into mid-heaven, When will you he. ve this body? When your soul has the life-energy to produce it. Vel'B. 8-10.-The phi7osopliy ef courage. "We are confident, I 81\Y," etc. Paul says wee.re courageous, or of good courage. Courage is often confounded with recklessnesa of life, a bnita.l insensibility to de.nger. True courage always implies two thing~. 1. The existenc.e of unavoidable dangers. He who rushes into danger is not couracrcous, but reckless. Paul had unavoidable dangers: "Wo are troubled on every side".'" 2. True convictwn., of being. Ignorance of existence may make men reckless, but never courageous. What was Paul's view of life? (1) Ho regl\l'ded the body as the organ or himself. He speaks of it as a "house," a " tabernacle," etc. (2) The soul he regards as the personality of his being. "We that are in this tabernacle," etc. Tb.e soul, not the body, is the "I," or self. (3) He regarded death as a mere change in the mode of his being. Death changes the house and the garment; it is not the extinction of the tenant or the wearer. (4) He regarded heaven as the perfection of his being. "The house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." The courage of which the apostle here speaks seems to have been based on three things. I. A consciousness that his death would not ENDANGER THE INTERESTS of his being. Notice: 1. His view of the interests of being. It was being" present with the Lord.'' 2. His view of the bearing of death upon the interests of being. He regarded it e.s the flight of the spirit int.o the presence of the Lord. "Absent from the body, present with the Lord." A view of death this antagonistic to the ideas of purgatory, annihilation, soul-deep. 3. His state of mind under the inflnence of these thoughts. "Willing rather to be absent from the body." II. A consciousness that death wonld not DESTROY THE GREAT PURPOSES of being. It is tLe characteristic of a rational being that he has some purpose in life--the pnrpose is that in which he lives, it makes life valuable to him. To a man who has no purpose in life or has lost his purpose, life is deemed of little worth. What was Paul's purpose in life? "Wherefore we labonr, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him." Is not this purpose sublimely reasonable? If there be a God, does not reason teach that to please him should be the supreme purpose of all intelligent creatures? Now, Paul felt that death would not destroy this purpose. It destroys the purpose of the voluptuous, avaricious, etc.; and hence to them it is terrible.. But it does not destroy the chief purpose of the Christian. In all worlds and times his cLief purpose will be t.o be "accepted of him." Ill. A consciousness that death would not PREVENT THE BEWARDB of being. "We must all appear [ or, 'be ma.de manifest'] before the judgment-seat of Christ." Success, while it should never be regarded either as a rule of conduct or a test of character, must ever have an influence on the mind of man in every department of labour. Nonsuccess discourages. Paul felt that his labour here would appear and be recognized hereafter. "We must all appear," etc. 1. Every one shall receive the recompense of labour after death. "Must all appear." None absent. 2. Every one shall receive a reward for every deed. "That every one may receive the things done in his body.• No lost la.hour. With this consciousness we may well be courageous amidst all the dangers here and in view of the great hereafter. Dread of death is a disgrace to the Cl.iristian. "If," says Cicero, " I were now disengaged from my cumbrous body, and on ruy way to Elysium ; and some: superior being should meet me in my flight and make mt the offer of returning and remaining in my body, I should, without hesitation, reject the offer; so mnch should I prefer going into Elysium to be with Socrates and Plato and all the ancient worthies, and to spend my time in converse with them.'' How much more should the Christian desire to be" absent from the body, and present with the Lord" I

entries.title: 2CO 5:11–18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Man in Christ a mw man. "For whether we be beside ourselves," etc. To be "iu Christ" is to be in hie Spirit, in his charact.er, to live in his ideas, pcirici1,lts, etc. Such u man is "a Dew creature." I. The wan in Christ has a new JllP£BIAL IMPULSE. "The love of Christ constraiueth us." Whether tht " love of Christ" here means aie love to us or our love for him is of no practical import. The latter impliea the former; his love is the flame· that on. v. 1-21.] 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE C:ORINTHIANS. 125

kimllos ours. Now, this love was Paul's dominant passion; it" constrained" him• it co.rri?d him 011 like a. reRist_les~ torrent; it was ~h~ regnant im~ulse. Two thought; in relation to this new 1mpcno.l impulse. 1. It is incomprehen.,ible to those who posse.,., it not, " Whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God," etc. Probably Paul appeared as mnd to his contemporaries. They saw him brave the greatcRt perils, oppose the greatest' powors, mako the greatest sacrifices. What was the principle that moved him to all? This they could not understand. Had it been ambition or avarice, they could h~ve understood it. But" tho love of Christ" they knew nothing of; it was a new thinn- in the world. Only the man who has it can understand it; love alone can interpr~'t love. 2. It arises from reflection on the death of Christ. It is not an inbred passion, not a blind impulse, not something divinely transferred into the heart. No; it comes "because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead." Paul as~nmes as an undoubted fact that Christ died for all. Because of this fact be concludes: (l) That the whole world were in a ruined condition: "Then were all dead." (2) That this fact should inspire all to act with the same sacrificing spirit as dhrist. " He die.d for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him." II. 'l'he man in Christ has a new BOOIAL STANDARD. "Henceforth we know no man after the flesh." The world has numerous standards by which it judges men, birth, wealth, office, etc. To a man filled and fired with love to Christ these are nothin:!, He estimates man by his rectitude, not by his rank; by bis spirit, not by his station; by his principles, not by his property. Paul might have said-I once knew men after the flesh, Jew or Gentile, rich or poor, learned or ignorant; but now I know them so no more; I see them now in the light of the cross, sinners dead in trespasses and sins ; " Yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh," etc., I think no more of his body, but of bis mind, not of his station, but of his Spirit. The fact that this is the true standard serves: 1. As a test by which to try our own religion. 2. As a guide for us in the promotion of Christianity. 3. As a principle on which to form our friendships with men. 4. As a rnle to regulate our social conduct. III. The man in Christ has a new BPIBITtJAL HISTORY. "Therefore if any man be iu Christ, he is a new creature." In what sense can this change be called a creation? 1. It is the production of a new thing. This passion for Christ is a new thing in the universe. 2. It is the production of a new thing by the ag,mcy of God. Creation is the work of God. 3. It is the production of a new thing according to a Divine plan. The almighty Maker works by plan in all. IV. 'l'he man in Christ has a NEW STANDING. "All things are of God, who bath reconciled us," etc. That is, all things pertaining to this new creation. The great want of man is reconciliation to God. Man's alienation or apostasy from bis Maker is the sin of all his sins, and the source of all his miseries. His reconciliation is not the means to his salvation; it is his salvation. Friendship with him is heaven. On the other hand, alienation is hell. A river cut from the fountain dries up; a branch cut from the tree withers and dies ; a planet cut from the sun rushes into ruiu. Separate a soul from God its Fountain, its Root, its Centre, and it diesdies to all that makes existence tolerable. Such, then, is what Chri~tianity does for us.

•Vers. 19, 20.-God's work in Olirist. • To wit, that God was in Christ," etc. God is a great Worker. He is the eternal Fonntain of life in unremitting flow. He is essentially active, the mainspring of all activity in the universe but that of sin. There are at least four organs through which he works-material laws, animal instincts, moral mind, and Jesus Christ. By the first he leads on the great revolutions of inanimate natnre in all its departments; by the second he preserves, guides, and controls all the seritient tribes that populate the earth, the air, and the sea; by the third, through the laws of reason and the dictates of conscience, he governs the vast empire of mind; and by the fourth, viz. Christ, he works out the redemption of sinners in our world. There is no more difficulty in regarding him in the one Person, Christ, for a certain work thnn there is in regarding him as being in material nature, animal instinct, or moral mind. The words lead us to make three remarks concerning God'l! work in Christ. I. It is e. work of RECONCILING HUMANITY TO Goo. "God was in Christ recon• ciling the wol'ld unto himself." 'l'he work of niconciling implies two things-o-nmity 128 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [on. v. 1-21.

on the side of one of the p&rtiea, and a change of mind in one of the .parties. Tho enmity here is not on God's part-he is love; but on man's. 'l'he "carnal mind is enmity with God.'' Nor is the change on God's part. He ronnot change, he tteed not change. He could never become more loving and merciful. The change needed is on man's part and on man's e.ulus,:vely. Paul speaks of the world being reconciled to God, not of G~d to thr world. The " world;" not a seotion of the race, but all mankind. II. It is a work involving the REMISSION OF SINS. "Not imputing [reckoning] their trespas..'1011 unto them." The reconciled man is no longer reckoned guilty. Thr<.>e facts will throw light on this. The state of enmity towards God is : 1. A sUJ.te of sin. 'fhere is a virtue in disliking some characters, but it is evermore .11, siu to dislike Gou, for he is the All-good. 2. A state of sin liable to punishment. Indeed, sin is its own punishment. 3. In reconciliation, the enmity beino- removed the punishment i8 oln-iated. What is pardon? A separating of man fro~ his si~ and their consequences. This God does in Obrist. ,, IIL It is a work in which GENUINE MINISTERS ABE ENGAGED.· " He bath committed unt-0 us the word of reconciliation. Now then we are a.mbassadors for Christ, as though God <lid beseech yon by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye recon- ciled to God." Observe: L The position of the true minister. He acts on behalf of Christ, and sta.uds in" Christ's stead." 2. The earnestness of the truo minister. "We pmy you." .; From the whole we observe concerning this work : 1. '11hat it is a work of vnbounde.d mercy. Whoever heard the offended party seeking the friendship of the offender? 2. It is a work essffltial to human happiness. In the nature of the case there is no happiness without this reconciliation. 3. It is a work exclusively of moral -influence. No coercion on the one hand, no angry denunciations on the other, can do it ; it ce.n only be effected by the logic of love. 4. It is a work that must be grad'll,(J;l, :Mind cannot be forced; there must be reflection, repentance, resolution. ,

entries.content:
-<Jhrist made sin. "For he h&th made him to be sin for us, who knew no ein; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." " Him who knew n'd sin he made to be sin on our behalf; that we might become the righteousness of God iii him " (Revised Version). From this passage we gather three wonderfut truths. L That Christ w.as .A.BSOLUTELY sn.'LESS. "Who knew no sin." Intellectually, of courae, he knew a.II the sin in the world; but he never experienced it, he was absolutely free from it. 1. He was "with.out sin," although he lived in a sinfuZ. world. Of all the millions who have been here he alone moved amongst the world and received no taint of moral contamination. 2. He was " without sin," although he was powerfully tempted. Had he been untempte.ble there would have been no virtue• in his freedom from sin, e.nd had there been no tempter there would have been nothing praiseworthy in his sinlessness. "He wast.empted like as we a.re, yet without sin!' 1 :

IL That, though sinless, Christ was in some sense MADE SIN BY GoD, " He hatb. ma.de him to be sin for us." What mee.neth this? 1. It cannot mean that God made the sinless One a sinner. This would be impossible. No one can create a moral character for another. 2. It cannot mean that God imputed to him the sin of the world, and punished him for the world's ·sin. The idea of literal substitution ie repugnant to reason anu:unsustained by any honest interpretation of God's ,Holy Word. '.l'he atonement of Christ consists, not ii:. what he said, did, or suffered, but in what he was. He himself is the .Atonement, the R«nr1,cil,er. What, then, does it mean? 'l'wo facts may throw some light. (1) '!'hat God sent Christ into a world of sinners to become closely identified with them. He wu related to llj,l:mers, mingled with them, ate and drank with them, IIDd was in theoommUDity, counted as one of them.· "He was numbered with the transgressors." (2) That God permitt.ed this world of sinners .to treat 01,ritJt as a Binner. He was calnmniated, persecuted, ineulted1 murdered •. God permitted all this, and what he p,nnits is, in Scripture language, often ascribed to him.' Ill. That the sinless One was thus made sin in order. that men HIGHT PARTICIPATE IN, Goo's lllGHTEOUSNESS. "That we might be made the righteousness of God in him.'' Never did Divine moral excellence or the righteousness of God shine out with such glory to man as in the sufferings which Christ endured in consequence of this connection with sinnem. As the 1tar11 can only ahow the!Il8elvea at. night, and as e.romatic plants ea, v. 1-21.J TUE SECOND EPIS'fLE TO TUE CORINTHIANS. 127 ----------------- ----------- can only emit their preclot1s odour by pressure, so the highest moral virtues crm only cotne out by suffering and battling with the wrong. What self-sacrificing love, what unconquerable attachment to truth, what loyalty to the infinite Father, what sublime heroism of love, was here exhibited in the incarnation, the beneficent deeds, and overwholming sufl'orings of Jesus I

entries.title: 2CO 5:1–10
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-.Assurance of eternal life; faith and its effectB. Death Intervenes between the present state of affliction and the glory of heaven, but death is only the destruction of the body now existing. It is not an end to bodfiy form and life. This is no speculation of the apostle's ; it is an assn ranee, "for we know" that if this eartply tent be destroyed, it will be followed by an enduring habitation-a mansion not a tabernacle. In the earthly body he groans, not because it is a body, but because'it is fle~h and blood suffering under the effects of sin, and hence he longs for the " house which is from heaven." It is a heaven for body as well as soul that he so ardently desires. 'l'o be bodiless even in glory is repulsive to his nature, since it would be nakedness. Death is repugnant. '!'he separation of soul and body, however, is only temporary; H is not for unclothing, but for a better clothing, one suited to the capacities of spirit. If the fourth verse repeats the second verse, it enlarges the idea and qualifies it by statint the reason why he would be "clothed upon," viz. "that mortality might be swallowed up of life." And this longing is no mere instinct or natural desire, bnt a feeling inspired of God, who "bath wrought ns for the selfsame thing." A Divine preparation was going on in this provisional tabernacle-a training ·or the spirit for the vision of Obrist and a training of the body for the immortal companionship of the spirit. An " eatp.est" or pledge of this was already in possession. The sufferings sanctified by the Spirit, the longing, the animation of hope, were so many proofs and tokens of awaiting blessedness. • How could he. be otherwise than confident? Yea;. he is "always confident." '!'hough now confined to' the body, yet it is a liome that admits of affections and loving fellowships; and though it necessitates absence from the Lord and the house of " many mansions," nevertheless it is a home illumined by faith. "For we walk by faith, not by sight." The borne is in the midst of visible objects that exercise our sense of sight,·but our Christian walk, or movement from one world to another, is not directed by the eye, but by faith, the sense of the invisible. We know what are the functions of the 'eye. I'f we did not, the antithesis would convey no meaning. The eye receives impressions from external things, communicates them to the son!, is a main organ in dev~loping thought and feeling, acts on the imagination and the will, and is continually adding something to ,the contents of the inward nature. Faith is like it as a medium of reception, unlike it in all else. Faith is not conversant with appearances. We do not 5ee Clirist in his glory; we. see him (using the term figuratively) in his Word by means of the Spirit; and this seeing is faith. How do we know when we have faith? It attests itself in our capacity to see:the path leading to eternal glory, and it enables us to walk therein. The path is from one home to another-from the home on the footstool to the home by the throne of Christ, and faith has the reality and vigour of a home sentiment. So strong and assuring is St. Paul's confidence that he prefers to depart and be with Christ. " At home in the body;" yes, but it is a sad home at best, and trial and affliction bad begun to make it dreary to him. To die is to be with the Lord, and be was "willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." Whether absent or present, at home or away from home, we labour that we "may be accepted of him." To make himself and his life acceptable to Christ was paramount to every other desire; to labour was his absorbing thought. Such an energetic soul as his must have felt that its energies were immortal. There was no selfishness in his hope of heaven, no longing to be freed from work, no yearning for the luxury of mere rest. It was to be with Christ, for Christ was his heaven. If this was his confidence, if he was labouring untiringly to be acceptable to the Lord Jesus, was he understood and appreciated as Christ's apostle and servant among men? The burden of life was not the work he did, but the obstacles thrown in his way-the slanders he ha.d to bear, the persecutions open and secret that followed him everywhere. He thinks of the "judgment-seat of Obrist." It will be a judicial inquiry into works done and "every 128 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIAXS. [cu.,,. 1-21.

one" shall '' !'('Ceh•e [receive back] the things done in hie body." Measure for measure wh11tsoever hRs boon done here sh11ll retnrn to every one. The individuality of th~ judgment, t.he complc>te unveiling of personal character, the correspondence between the rew11rd and the i;i:nod done on Mtth and between the retribution and the evil done here he hrings out distinct.ly. This was with him a fixed habit of t.hono-ht. "\Vhatsoove; a nrnn 8oweth that, shall he also rCRp." How near the two world~ are-the growing field hero, the hanrest in another existence hereafter ! llut observe another idea.. " w0 must all appear," we must be made manifest, every one shown in his true character. Not ouly will there be recompense as a judicial procedure, bnt a revelation "in the day when God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ." St. Paul had vindicated himself again and agRin from the charges made against him; but the battle was now going on, nor was there any sign of its speedy abatement. It was natural that he should have the idea of manifestation prominent in his mind, since we all think of the future world very much according to some peculiarity in our experience on earth. How engrossed, heart and soul, in his apostleship is beaut:fully indicated by the fact that heaven itself was the heaven of St. Paul as the apostle of Christ. The sufferings of the man are never ~entioned. First and last, we have the autobiography of an a.11ostle, and hence, lookmg forward to the glory to be revealed, the supreme felicity is that he will appear in his true character as the Lord's servant.-L.

entries.title: 2CO 5:11–21
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Person and ministry of the aposlle further considered ; his work as a; ambassador. How was he coaducting this ministry, -0f which he had spoken so much an<l had yet more to say? It was in full view of account.ability to the day of judgment. "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men," adding motives to affect them, and not remaining content with arguments to convince their understandings. And in this work he now felt God's approval; before he had declared, "we are confi- dent," and he reaffirms it in the words, "we are made manifest unto God." Every hour he stood at the bar of his conscience an acquitted man, and this conscience was a manirestation of God. Honestly was he striving to plea.qe God, as hon·estly labourin" to save them, and in this spirit he was ever seeking to manifest himself to their con~ sciences. If he were a temporizer, a man-pleaser, he might adopt worldly arts and captivate them. No; he would address their consciences; the best in them should come to his side or he must lose them. " Savour of life unto life" or "savour of death unto death;" no other alternative. Bnt do not misunderstand us. Commendation is not our object. If we have, as we trust, manifested ourselves to your consciences, then let your consciences speak in our behalf, and let their voices boast in this-that we are truthful in the sight of God and man. This is the way to answer our enemies w:ho "glory in appearance and not in heart." Suffer he would rather than be wrongly vindicated. Do it in the highest way or not at all "Your cause "is the great interest. No doubt we seem" beside ourselves," or we may appear" sober," but you may boast of this-" it is for your cause." And in this devotion to your well-being what motive presses with weight enongh to make us endure all things for your sakes? " The love of Christ constraineth us." And wherein is this fove so signally demonstrated as to embody and set forth all else that he did? It is love in death. Look~ng at this Divine death, we form this jndgment or reach this conclusion, that he " died for all" because "all were dead-" dead under the Law of God, dead in trespasses and.sins, dead legally, morally, spiritually. Nothin& less than su_ch a°: atoning ~e.ath for all men-so it seems to us the apostle meant--couJd exert on him this constrammg mfluence. And how should this influence operate? "They which live should not henceforth live unto themselves." The very self had been redeemed by Christ's vicarious death; body, soul, and spirit had been bought with a price, and the price was Christ's blood; anJ with such a constraining motive, the most potent that the Holy Ghost could J..ring to bear on the human mind, how could men live unto themselves? If, indeed, the constraining power ha.d itl! legitimate eJfect, only one life could result, a life consecrated to "him which died for them and rose again.' If, therefore, all being dead, one died for all, that all might live in freedom from selfishness and be the servants of him who had redeemed them from sin and death, we can know henceforth no man after the flesh. The very purpose of Christ's death was that the fleshly life of sin might pass out of ,-jew (might be covered over ~d thus disappear from siyht), aud another life be entered uH, v.1-21.] THE SECOND EPIS'J!'LE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 129

on, o. life in the redeeming Christ. Admitting that this passage presents the moral aspects of Ohrist's death and the obligations consequent thereupon as they act on moral sentiment, yet the fundamental idea. of the apostle is that Christ stood in thP, stead of sinners, took their guilt upon himself, and made an offering of his life for their rescue. 'l'o strengthen this doctrine, he says that, though he once knew Christ after the flesh (119 a mere man), he knew him now in e. very different wa.y. We are not to suppose t.hat he had seen him in his earthly life, but merely that he knew of him. St. Paul, after his conversion, had an experimental knowledge of Christ as hie Redeemer through the sacrificial death of the cross; nor was there any room in his heart for moral sentiment, nor any spiritual force in Christ's teaching and example, nor ground for any trust or hope, till he as "chief of sinners" had realized the righteousness of God in the atoning blood of Calvary, Such a change was a creation. He was "a new creature," and whoever experienced this power of the Lord's death was a new creature. Old things had passed away-the old self in taste and habit, the old unbelief rooted in the fleshly mind, the old worldliness-and all things had become new. No wonder that "all things'' had become "new;" for" all things" pertaining to this change in its cause, agency, instrumentalities, "are of God." Strong language this, which sounds even yet to many as the rhetoric of excited fancy; but not stronger than the blessed reality it represents. Nay; words cannot equal the fact. A man may overstate his own experience of Divine grace; never can he exaggerate the grace itself. "AU things are of God;" and how is this fact manifested? In the method of reconciliation which is God's e.ct through Christ. "Who bath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ." To understand what is implied in reconciliation, we must remember that much more is involved in it than the moral state of a sinner's mind toward God. entries.title: 2CO 5:14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The love of Christ. Every quality met in the Lord Jesus which could adapt him to accomplish the work which he undertook on behalf of our human race. But if one attribute must he selected as peculiarly and pre-eminently characteristic of him, if one word rather than another rises to our lips when we speak of him, that attribute, that word, is love. I. THE 011.IBOTS OF CHRIST'S LOVE. Look at his earthly life and ministry, and the comprehensive range within which the love of Jesus operates becomes at once and gloriously obvious. 1. His friends. Of this fact-Christ's love to his friends-we have abundant proof: "Greater love bath no man than this, that a man lay down his life fur his friends." .2. His enemies. . This is more wonderful, yet the truth of what tho apostle says 'is undeniable: "While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." And we cannot forget his prayer offered for his enemies as they nailed him to the cross:" Father, forgive them." 3. All mankind. During his ministry the Lord Jesus was gracious to all with, whom he came into contact. His aim was by the bands of love to draw all men unto himself, that they might rest and live in his Divina and mighty heart. II. TJiE PROOFS OF CHRIST'S LOVE. The great facts of his ministry and mediation are evidences of his benevolence. 1. His advent. "Nothing brought him from above- Nothing but redeeming love." 2. His ministry. He went about doing good, animated by the mighty principle of love to man. Every sickness he healed, every demon he expelled, every sinner he pardoned, wa11 a witness to the love of Christ. 3. His death. His was the love "stronger than death;" for not only could not death destroy it, death gave it a new life and power in the world and over men. 4. His prevailing intercession and brotherly care. III. THE CHARACTERISTICS OF CHRIST'S LOVE. 1. It is sympathizing and tender, "passing the love of women." 2. It is thoughtful and wise, ever providing for t!ie true welfare of those to whom it is revealed. 3. It is forbearing and patient, otherwise it mi"ht often have been checked and repressed. 4. It is self-sacrificing, counting nothi~cr too "feat to be given up in order to secure its ends. 5. It is faithful: "Having loved his ow':i he loved them even unto the end." 6. It is unquenchable and ever- lasting : "Who can separate us from the love of Christ? "-T.

I. Tm,; NATURE OF THIB OONBTRAINT, Men are lnftucnced. by many and varloua motives, some lower a.nd some higher. Physical power is of two kinds-it is either energy or resistance; e.g. the ocean and the dyke, the powder and the cannon, the st~am and the boiler. As with physical, so with moral power. 1. Christ's love acts by way of restraint. entries.content: -" Ambassadors/or Ohrist." Even among the members of the Corinthian Church there were those who had offended the Lord by their inconsistency and who needed to be reconciled. Probably the language is most justly applicable to the apostles only, inasmuch ae their commission and credentials were altogether special. An ambassador owes his importance, not to himself, but to the power he represents, the message he bears. The preachers of Christ are all heralds, if they cannot be designated ambassadors. They may leam hence the dignity of their office and their personal unworthiness and insufficiency, and they may be admonished as to the imperative duty of fidelity. II. BY WHAT COURT ARE THESE AIIIBABSAD0BS OOllfMISBIONED? They are the ministers of the King of heaven, and their authority is that of the King's Son. To WHOM THESE AMBASSADOBB ABE BENT. Properly speaking, au ambaSBador is one accredited to a power sovereign and equal to that from whom he comes. But in this case the resemblance fails in this respect, inasmuch as the ministers of the gospel address themselves to offenders, to rebels, to those who cannot treat with Heaven upon equal terms, or any terms of right. entries.title: 2CO 5:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The tent and the house. I. TIil!: CONTB.A.ST EXPLAINED. The foundation of this passage is to be found in eh. iv. 18, where a contrast is clrawn between "the things seen," viz. the toils and afflictions endured in t.he service of Christ, and " the things not yet seen," viz. the joys of resting in Christ from present labours and of receiving from him approval and reward. Pursuing this train of thought, St. Paul writes, "We are here in a tent upon the earth, surrounded, affected, and limited by the things which are seen. But this tent will be struck, to be set up no more. The things which are seen are temporal. The present conditions of our life of toil and suffering will cease, and we shall enter a house of everlasting habitation." 'l'he apostle mixes together the figures of a dwelling in which we reside and that of a garment with which we are clothed. It was not an unnatural combination of metaphors; for the haircloth tents with which Pe.ul was familiar, and which his own hands had made, suggested almost equally the idea of a dwelling and that of a vesture. The tent is to be taken down, the clothing to be removed. The present condition of labour and trial · will come to an end. What then ? Things not yet seen ; a building from God ; a new condition of life and order of things which will be permanent. Hancls of men have not provided it and cannot destroy it. It is a house where nothing fades, nothing falls to ruin, nothing decays or dies-ii. house eternal in the heavens. IL THE CHRISTIAN PERSPECTIVE OF THE FUTURE. It was St. Paul's habit to regard the state after death and the state after resurrection as from one angle of visiou, and to describe them together. Probably he had no idea of the long interval which was to extend through all the Christian centuries. In his first Jetter to the Coriuthians he had said, " We shall not all sleep," as thongh some of that generation might not sec death. But now the feebleness of his body was as "a sentence of death" in himself. He expected and even wished to clie; and yet his thoughts never paused on death or even on the rest of the departed, but rushed past death to the coming of Christ and the glory to be revealed. There is a real and obvious distinction between the postdecease and the post-resurrection state; but let us not overdo distinctions between conditions of blessedness which to an apostle's eye were so intimately blended. If some of the thincrs which belong to the ultimate state are supposed by any to belong to the proximate, n~ irreat harm is done. The future is not mapped out with the precision of a chart. It is not for definite knowledge, but for hope. St. Paul, as we have said, neve1 paused on death, took no pleasure in the thought of being " unclothed." At the resurrection be would be clothed w',th a hotly of incorruption and immortality. Nay; before that great day of triumph over death, he knew that he would be well clothed or guarJed. He would be in Go 1 l' building, "clothed upon" with the house which is from heaven. ou. v. 1-21.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE C.:ORINTHI ANS. 137

III. THE MOOD OF HIND THAT WISHES FOB DEATH, St. Paul wrote this in dejection of spirit. To his sickness, which had much enfeebled him was added at that time much anxiety about the condition of the Churches in Gre~e and their feelings toward himself. So hie heart, as tender and sensitive as it wae ardent and brave was bruised and weary ; and he fell a-thinking of death as welcome. Let the outward man perish ; let the earthen vessel break ; let the weary spirit escape and be at rest. A mood this into which, at one time or other, many Christians fall; but it should not be elevated into a pattern or rule, as though it were the duty of every Christian to Jong and sigh for death. Our holy faith requires nothing so unnatural. They who are in health and well omployeu ought to make the most of life-to value and not despise it. Enough that they do not forget death ; and they need not fear it if they Jive well. We must do Paul the justice to acknowledge that there was nothing peevish or impatient in bis mood. So long as there was service for him to render to the Church on earth, he was willing to abide in the flesh and to endure any toil or suffering in order to finish his course. But the mood that was on him led him to long for the finish, when he might leave the little horsehair tent on earth and be at home in God's building in the heavens.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 5:14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The secret of devotedness. No one now flings a charge of madness at the sublime enthusiasm of St. Paul. He is looked on as a paragon of Christians. But, while he lived, ho had no such general appreciation to encourage and sustain him. What he had above other men were not praises, but labours and reproaches. He endured all because he had in himself the mainspring of faith and the holy energy of love. Throughout this Epistle he shows his feeliags and motives with the utmost candour, and in this passage tells how he came to be so enthusiastic toward God and so thoughtful aud self-controlled toward his fellow-Christians. I. THE :r,rnvmo PRmCIPLE OF CHRISTIAN DEVOTEDNESS. It is the strong unchanging love of Christ to his people, assured to them by his Spirit and his Word. Paul had a fear of God, a reverence for the Law, and walked in all good conscience; but when the love of Christ was revealed to him and sufl'nsed his spirit it made a new man of him-thrilled, stirred, animated, constrained him to love and serve Chlist and the Church. And as the apostle grew old and experienced, this motive lost nothing of its power. The love of Christ became to him, as it does to all experienced Christians, more aud more wonderful-a Shepherd's love, that led him to die for us, and that now secures that we "shall not want;" a Brother's love, and "love beyond a brother's; " a Blidegroom's love, who gave himself for the Church and will present the Church to himself. II. '1.'HE WAY IN wmcu THE MOTIVE ACTS. It is through DO mere gush of feeling, but through consideration of the purpose and efficacy of Christ's death and resurrection. I. He died for all to tbis intent and with this result, that all of them died. Virtually and in the estimate of God this crucifixion of the whole Church took place when Christ was crucified. In the actual realization of it it becomes true to each man as and when he looks to Christ crucified and is united to him by faith. And with effects both legal and moral. He who was married to the Law dies to the Law, and is freed from its claims, so as to be married to the risen Christ. He who lived in sin dies to sin, and may not any longer live therein. He who loved the world is crucified to it, that he may love and live to God. 2. He rose again; and all the crucified ones live by him. So they have justification, ns represented by the accepted One, who has gone to the Father; and sanctification too, as separated to God in holy living and guided by the indwelling Spirit. The former manner of life is marked by self-regard. The new manner of life exchanges this for the habit of regarding Christ. So his con- straining love induces his followers "to live unto him." III. USES OF THIS DOCTnINE. I. Let it instruct us. Many are very ill informed on the relation of our Lord's death and resurrection to the Divine will and to human salvation; and for this reason they are much less constrai_ned br his love than t~ey ought to be. Study these things. Brina thouaht and cons1derat10n as well as emotion to the theme. 'l'ho love constrains "bc~ause ;e judge." 2. Let it humble us. Has the Son of the living God so loved us, and where is our love to him? "Lord, it is my chief complaint That my love is oold and faint," 139 'l'I-IE SECOND .h.PISTLE TO TH~ CORINTHIANS. Lon. v. 1-21,

3. Let ,,:t impel us. What we need to ovcrcotl'le out mt>ral Indolence and hl\\.iite of self-pleasing is the pressure of strong convictions and motives; and we can best get these in contemplating the love, the death, and the resnrrection of Christ. This, too, is a great security against departure from the Lord. When we know and feel little of Christ's love we a.re easily temptlld; but when this is in our thoughts and affections we abhor and repel whe.tevor might separate us from him. 4. Let it comfort us. ,ve are delivered from the wrath to come. Christ loves us. Then the Father also loves us. Duties a.re pleas&nt, afflictions a.re light; to live is Christ, to die is gain.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 5:18–21
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Reconciliation. Great troths hang together. When the Lord Jesus had told Nicodemus of regeneration, he immediately proceeded to teach him salvation through e. Redeemer. So when the Apostle Paul has spoken of new creation in Christ (ver. 17), he instantly follows it with the doctrine of reconciliation through Christ. • I. THE lIEED OF RECONCILIATION. The world is not in harmony or at peace with God. Sin has done it. On the one hand, God's displeasure is declared against the workers of iniquity; on the other, those workers are afraid of God and alienated from. him. .'A great gulf yawns between God and man; and the need of reconciliation is· the need of a bridge across that chasm. Or, a great mountain is cast up between God and man ; and the need of reconciliation is the need of that mountain becoming a plain, so that God and man may not merely approach, but unite and be at 1ieace. " What can be the difficulty," some exclaim, "if God desires it? Is he not omnipotent, and can he not accomplish whatever he pleases?" But we speak of a moral obstacle, not a physical .And, while God can certainly do what he pleases, he cannot please to do anything but what is perfectly righteous. So there is a difficulty. It is twofold: there is a sentence of condelllDILtion in heaven against the transgressors of the law of righteousness; and there is an enmity to God or a cowering dread of him in the hearts of those transgressors on earth. II. 'l'HE AUTHOR OF RECONCILIATION. "All things [i.e. all the things or the new creation] are of God, who has reconciled us to himself." Man, the_creature and the sinner, should have been the first to seek the healing of the ,breach, by suing for pardon and imploriug mercy from God. But it has not been so. The initiative has been taken by God, who is rich in mercy, and, loving the world, has provided for its reconciliation by Jesus Christ. IIL THE METHOD OF RECONCILIATION. Messages sent from a distant heaven or throne of God could not suffice. There was need of an authorized Messenger. So G;od sent his only begotten Son. For so great a work was constituted a unique ~d wonderful personality. 'l'he Son of God became man and yet continued Divine. So, in the very constitution of his person, he brought the Divine and the human together. And thus his relation to both parties was such as perfectly fitted him to be the Reconciler. He loved God, and therefore was faithful to all Divine claims and prerogatives; while at the same time he loved man and was intent on securing his salyation. l. He dealt with the difficulty on the side of eternal righteousness. He d~d sc;> by faking the room and the responsibility of. the transgressors and making atonement for them. And the hand of God was in this. "He hath made him," etc. (ver. 21). "Made . . . sin," though he never was a sinner, and laden with it as a bqrden, enveloped in it as a mantle of shame. "Jehovah laid upon him the iniquity of us all." The issue is that we "become the righteousness of God in him." And in this is nothing illusive or :fictitious. There was a real laying of our sins on the Lamb of God, that there may be a real laying or conferring of Divine righteousness on us whp believe in liis Name. 2. He deals with the difficulty of alienated feeling. No change is needed in the mind or disposition of God. He does not need to be persuaded to love the world. All the salvation in Christ proceeds from his Jove. But the enmity of men to God must be removed, and this is effected by the revelation of God as grncious and propitious to sinners in Christ Jesus. When this is known and believed, the hearL turns to God and actual I econciliation is made. IV. THE WORD OF RECONCILIATION. (Vers. 19, 20.) When St. Paul preached the gospel it was as though God entreated or exhl)rted the people through bis servant's lips. He was an ambassador, not a plenipotentuiry with powers to discuss and nego- tiate terms of peace, but a. King's messenger sent to proclaim terwij of free gracb and on. v. 1-21.J THE SECOND F:PISTLE TO THE COnINTHIAKS. 1.19

to press the nccoplance of them on the enemies of the King. This embassy continnes. Do not ·meet it with excuses a~d delays.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 5:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0ur'permanent building. 'l'aking the aposUe's worcls in a general way, a1:,, not confining them to the precise topic which he has under consideration, we are taught by' them that,'regarding all our present things as bnt shadows and symbols, we neeJ. not trouble ourselves overmuch about their changing forms, or even about their passin" away. All our heart and all our efforts should go out in the endeavour to brin~ nearer, and make clearer and fuller, the sense of our dwelling in, breathing in, workin~ in, the unseen, the spiritual, the eternal. Our sphere is God. "In him we live, and move, and have our being." The real is the unseen. The stable and lasting is the eternal. And this view of things alone can put us in right relations with the body nod set us upon the right use of things seen and temporal. Whenever we are brough{ face to face witl;i any passing, dissolving, removing, earthly thing, then God seems to call us, saying, "Hemember the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." 'l'e.ke for illustration- !. 'l'HE TENT AND THE HOUSE. No figure could be more appropriate than this for the apostle, who gained his living as a tentmaker, and was familiar with its material, its construction; aµd its US\l, We can well imagine how, as he wrought, either at weaving the rough Cilician cloth, or at sewing together the various lengths, and the holes for the poles and ropes, he would meditate on the frailty of the tent which he was thu~ making, contrasting it with the stable marble and stone mansions found in such cities as Corinth. In his day tents were chiefly made for travellers; for those who journeyed from _place to place, either for business or for pleasure, in districts where accommodation at inns could not be found. They had their settled homes in the great cities, anci. tµey went forth on their travels with quiet hearts, because of the cherished feeling that they had a home. They used the tent awhile, camping out in the open country ; but if the wild storm did com~, and even lift and carry away the tent; if the midnight robber did overthrow it, and, seize the epoil,-the traveller might bear the hardship and the loss, in pleasant confidence that he had a home. If the worst came, it could be but the shadow of his home passing away; in yonder city stood his secure dwelling. II. THE DOCTRINE AND THE TRUTH. For doctrine is _like the frail tent, and truth is like the granite mansion that outlasts the passing ages. We cannot be too thankful for the_ forms in which sacred truth is conveyed to us, unfolded before ns, or impressed upon lis. We bless God for all holy and helpful words, full of tender and dear associations ; words of simple catechism for our· childhood's weakness ; words of formal doctrine fashioned to help us when, in our youth-time, we tried to get personal hold of mysteriou~ and many-sided truth. Let no man despise the doctrines whicb, like tents, have often given us their shelter and their help. And yet they are only like "earthly houses of this tabernacle." Truth i~ the " building of God, the house not made with hands," wherein alone human souls may find quietness from controversy or from.fears. Doctrines are only symbols and shadows, the human representations of the Divine and eternal things, the unspeakable realities which yet our souls may apprehend. Within, behind, above, around, the doctrine ever dwells the truth; and, at first, we are very dependent on the/orms which it gains for mortal eyes and ears and minds; but, as the soul grows, and gains its vision, its hearing, and its touch, we get loosened from our dependence on the forms, we can calmly see them change and pass. Resting in the stable house of truth, we calmly look on all transitory forms, even of doctrine, and say, "We have a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." Ill NATURE AND GoD. Nature, the world of things seen-the firmament, golden- glowing, cloud-shaded, and star-sprinkled; earth, with its vales, and hills, and flowera, and trees; the great and wide sea-is in a very serious sense God. It is God manifest to our senses. Behind what is called pantheism there is a deeply poetical and spiritual truth. Nature is God seen; God in toned picture for mortal eyes to see ; God, if we may so say, in photograph. Enrth is the plate which has caught all that human eyes may see of the figure of God. Nature is the tent-symbol of the eternal house. 'l'he Jew called his mountains "the hills of God," because they brought to him the sense of the hi"'hness and almightiness of God. He called the spleudid trees " the cedars of Jehov:h," because they brought to him a sense of the stately beauty of God. HO THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORIN'l'HIAWS. [en, v. 1-21,

Yet nature is not r<'ally God himseH, only God in expression for our npprehendino, only the veil that he shines through. Therefore we turn from the eho.aow to the substance which throws it; from the form to the reality which it does but exhibit. And if all nature passed away, we should lose nothing. It would be but dropping the veil that we might see the/are. IV. Oun EARTHLY AND OUR HEAVENLY BODIES. St. Paul was plainly thinking of hie body, the ,;-ehicle by means of which our souls come into contact with the world of created things. But he cherished the idea of a spiritual body, which could be the clothing and vehicle of bis soul through the long, the eternal a"es. Thinkincr of it he could say, " What matter if my tent-body be destroyed? I bve a building of God, a house not made with haods."-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 5:5
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" The earnest of the Spirit." The apostle has been referring to the great hope set before us in the gosRel, which, as he regards it, is this, that" mortality might be swa~lowed up ~f li!e." 1hat is_ the object of the Divine working in the believer, and of its final realization he has this" earnest," or pledge of assurance, God has given us already the " earnest of the Spirit," who is the power that alone can work out such a sublime result as our final triumph over the flesh and sin, and meetness to take our place and part in a spiritual and heavenly state. "It is because the Spirit dwells in us by faith while we are here that we are to be raised hereafter. The body th119 possessing a principle of life is as a seed planted in the ground to be raised again in God's good time'' (comp. the sentence in eh. i. 22 and Rom. viii. 1-11). Observe that the Holy Spirit is presented to us under many aspects and figures; no one representation of his Di ,;-ine mission can exba.nst his relations to us. We must see his work on one side after another, and be willing to learn from all the figures under which it is presented. L WHAT IS MEANT BY AN "EABNEST "? It is something offered as a pledge aud assurance that what is promised shall surely be given. But it has been well pointed out that an "earnest" me.terially differs from a "pledge." A pledge is something different in kind. given as assurance for something else, as may be illustrated by the, 1111Craments; but an earnest is a part of the thing to be given, as when a purchase is made and a. portion of the money is paid down at once. The idea of the I' earnest " may be seen in the "firstfruits," which are a beginning of, and assure the character ot, the coming harvest. II. WHAT IS THE SPIBIT .AS "EARNEST" TO us Now? St. Paul's one point here is that it is an assurance of the final victory of the higher life over the lower. We have indeed that higher life now, in its initial and rudimentary stages, in having the Spirit dwelling in us. m w HAT FUTURE IS PLEDGED IN OUR H.A VING THE SPmIT NOW? Precisely a future in which the spiritual life shall be victorious and supreme, and our vehicle of a body simply within the use of the Spirit. That is full redemption, glory, and heaven.-R. T. Vm.7.-Walkingbyfaith. "We walk by faith,not by sight." "Walking" is a familiar Scripture term for a. man's life on the earth. It seems to have been aesociated with the figure of life 1111 a "pilgrimage" in the Old Testament, and as a. "racecow-se" in the N L'W Testament. It is joined to another word sometimes, and our "walk and conversation" are spoken of, our "going forward " a.ad " turning about." L w ALK .AS DESCRIPTIVE OF HUMAN LIFE. Its suitability will he seen if we notice: L That it is a moving on. The days of our life go by as do the scenes in a. panorama. 2. It is a slow moving on, steady and regular as the clock; time moves on, bearing all i~ aons away. 3. It is a moving on through ever-changing scenes, as is the path of the traveller, now up the hillside, now along the dusty highway, and now through the shaded valleys, with ever-varying sights and sounds a.round us. 4. It is a moving on somewhere; for he who walks has some end before him or some home in view. So our human life has its goa.L We pass on into the eternal, where we may find our home. II. WALK BY SIGHT .AB DESCRIPTIVE OF THE WORLDr,Y LIFE, " Walk by sight" does not mean "in the power of our vision,'' but" under the influence and persuasion of thingB ,reen and temporaL" It is the one essential characteristic of the worldly man that his oe, v.1-21.] THE SECOND EPIS'fLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 141

judgments and decisions are made, bis affections are ruled, and his conrluct is ordered by what may be gathered under the term "the fashion of this world." Sense-conr\itions determine his place. Sense-requirements command his allegiance. Sense-principle~ inspire .his doings and decide his relations. lie "walks'' with a. horizon no further off than yonder ridge of hills, and with no thought really bigger in his soul than "What shall we eat'? what shall we drink? and what shall we enjoy?" Saying this is the saddest revelation of man's essential wrongness before the God who "made him for himself." III. WALK BY FAITH AS DESCRIPTIVE OF TEE CHRISTIAN LIFE. We are not yet face to face with the eternal realities, but faith as the "substance of things hoped for" gives us a present actual possession of those eternal things, and makes them exert their power on our "walk." Faith in the unseen and eternal can (1) cheer; (2) raise the tone; (3) bring steadfastness into our walk and conversation. The realities are revealed. to faith; human sight can only see passing shadows of things.-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 5:10
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" The judgment-seat of Ghrist." It is needlessly forcing language to regard this expression as referring to the general judgment of mankind. This letter is addressed to the saints, the Church at Corinth, and it may be specially instructive to keep within the limits of St. Paul's thought when he said, "For we "-that is, we Christians_-" must all appear before the judgment-seat of Christ." Such a judgment, or appraisementi of our conduct is involved in the very idea of our mastership to Christ. He will be sure one day to take account of his servants, and this Jesus himself taught ·11s in his parableli of the talents and pounds. Christians are as stewards, men entrusted for a time with their Master's goods. They are even to be thought of as " slaves," wholly the Master's possession; and he has full power to estimate their conduct, reward faithfulness, and punish neglect and disobedience. St. Paul even loves to think of himself as the bondslave of Jesus. And the apostles long to prove so faithful in all things that they may not be ashamed, or terrified, or loth to meet their Master a,t his coming. " The feeling of accountability may take two forms. In a free and generous spirit it may be simply a. sense of duty; in a slavish and cowardly spirit it will be a sense of· compulsion." To us it should be a joy and an inspiration that our own loved Master will appraise our lives; and that, if he is true to observe our faults, ne will be no less gracious to recognize what he may call our goodnesses and our obediences. The thought of his judgment can only be a terror to the rebellious, dis- obedient, ·and wilful among his servants. We notice three things. I. LOYALTY TO CHRIST IS OUR SPIBIT. "We call him Master and Lord, and we say well; for so he is.'' 'l'be rule of our life is the will of our glorified and ever-present Lord. We have voluntarily given ourselves to him. To him we owe our supreme allegiance. He is to us what his queen and country are to the general who leads forth his army. We must be ever true to him; and he, and he alone, is the Lord whose approval or condemnation of our work we should seek. Because I am loyal to Christ I will c:i.re about nobody's judgment of my life until I know his. II. SEBVIOE OF CHRIST IN RIGHTEOUSNESS IS OUR LIFE. '!'his is the very essence of .the matter. Christ is served by righteousness, and really by nothing else. Our place of service, our kind of service, our success in service, are quite the secondary things. The first thing is the rightness with which we do the service. Was the work good t-this it is that Christ asks. Herein Christ differs from all other masters. They can only judge the work; he judges the charactlfr which found expression through the work. It is that personal righteousness that Christ.will search for when he judges his servants. III. THE APPRAISEMENT OF CRRIST 18 OUR EXPECTATION AND OUR HOPE. .A day of finaljudgment is men's expectation, but not their hope. It is too often a terror to them, a thought put away in fear. Christ's judgment of his saints is our hope ; it is the first day of our glory. The thought of it may make us serious and watchful, but it never can make us sad. Christ will test and try our lives. Christ will weigh us in his balances. Christ will apportion our future place. Christ will chastise if there be found evil in us, and his chastiseWflnts shall be our joy; for we too want all the evil in us found out and put away. We even glory in'this coming appraisement by our Lord; for if, in subtle disauises, evil lurks in any of our secret places of heart a.nu life, Jesus will find it out, and will not leave ns until we stand in the likeness of his own spotle,s HZ THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, [mr, T. l-21,

purity. And upon onr Lord's jndgment of 118 onr foture, our eternal location and work, must depend. The life of an Intelligent being must be under the sway of some ohosen and cherished motive, High degrees of intelligence find their expression in the careful selection of the motive. Where the intel- ligenoo is low and untrained, we find men blindly obeying motives which the accid~ of the hour may have raised up, or to which the bodily passions may excite. We can look into the face of no fellow-man and say, " That man is living without a motive." The considera~ion of the motives that actually rule men's lives give us very sad thoughts of our humanity. They range all the dista.nce between the animal and th11 Divine, b.ut they belong for the most part to the lower levels, The entire aspect and character of a man's life may be changed by a change of his motives. A new and nobler motive will soon make a man a better man. No man ever did rise to do noble things while his motive concerned only self and self-interests. All noble lives have been spent in service to others. All the best lives in private spheres have been self-denying lives. .All the heroic lives in public spheres have been the lives of patriots, the lives of. the generous, the pitying, and the belpful. St. Paul was in every way a remarkable man, full of energy, consecration, self-denial, and the" enthusiasm of humanity~" and in the passage now before us he tells us what was the 6Upporting motive, ~e secrot strength, of it all " The love of Christ consLraineth us." But if you used that word in any bad sense he would iudignanUy deny such an accusation. It was indeed a life to which be was con~trained, )leld fast, impelled, coerced, and that by the intense love of bis soul for ancither-a. love passing the love of women. But St. Paul would most earnestly urge tha~ this love of hiB .was no mere passion, no mere impulse, no blind force taking sudden lllllStery of his heart, and crushing down and silencing thought and judgment and will.. • ~e dec1ar~s. it to be a love based on jud,,"lllent, and strengthened by maturer judgm~tit. That sober consideration took up: 1. The sadness of man's condition. " Then were :ill dead;" or, as otherwise read. " then all died." ~ St. Paul's jrid,,,ament decided that it was quite true about Je.rus Christ-he bad intervened to save Dien by his.own swierings and death. " He died for all" Paul-or ,Saul, as be was· then called-was nearing the fulness of manhood when he heard of the appearance of a new prophetteacher in the land of his fathers. But all bis prejudices arrayed themse.lves against the acceptance of him. and against belief in bis specW collimissfon •aiid autliority, It appeared from the reports that he was a poor man; that be came from the dospised Galilean Nazareth, about which Old Testament Scriptures prophesied no such great thing ; that he made him.self the "friend of publicans and sinners;" that be was a:n unsparing foe of Paul's own sect, the Pharisees; but that at last he bad been stopped in biB mischievous career, and made a public example of by an ignominious and sham.eful death. And then one day prejudice was overthrown, Prejudice waf! made tq see the living glory of him whom it had tried to believe was disgraced Sf-d dead, Prejudjee beard the authoritative voice of the supposed impostor speaking out of the heavenly place.s. Prejudice was conquered; the reason, the jud.gment, and the heart wete enthroned, and set to '.form a judgment concerning Christ. Die, did he, a. mournful shameful death? Judgmcnt says-There, amid the verv shame of the cross, thrown' up by the very darkness thot lies behind it, shine forth rays of transcendent glory. There, in those hours of agony, may be seen sublime self-sacrifice, mystery of spiritual sufferina, Divine sin-bearing, and the most persuasive manifestation of Gcxl's love to men. The~e is God "not sparing his own Son, but delivering him up for us all;" and there is God's Son "bearing our sins in his own body on the tree." On that sober judgment the apostle based his new life-motive. He set the love of that dying Saviour so high in his soul that it became from henceforth the master motive of all that he did. II. TBE WAY IN WHICH THE CHRISTIA.N MOTIVE WORKS. "They which live shoulrl not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them,and rose again." The motive works by establishing a new law for the ruling of our life and conduct. It is the not-unto-self law. We do not know ourselves as we really_ are in our carnal state if we think that is not a new law. Gratification of self is the great unnatural human law. The not-unto-self law is the chosen life-principle of all the good. It is the law of God, the life-rule of Jesus the Christ; and, learnt of him, it has made many a. human story since then beautiful and gracious. Could it be established. in all hearts, the golden age would have come, in which the unselfish King can rei,,.an for ever and ever. The only possible deliverance from the sway of the old self-law is found in the elevating of some new and inspiring love to the throne of the heart. And Jesus makes himself the Object of just such love. The new motive also works in another way. It gives an inner spiritual force to sustain us in the endeavour to obey the law. Love becomes to us what it is to the child. The love of the parent becomes the law of the child's life; but the love, as it dwells in the heart of the child, makes obedience easy. entries.title: 2CO 6:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Tlae !fMC6 of God received, in vai"- "We then, as workers together," etc. There are three topics here for meditation. . I. ~ Bul!L~R MISSION, " ~ork~rs together with him." What is the grand work in which God 1s engaged and ID which we can co-operate? He is engaged in numeroua works-works of creation, government, conservation, in which we can have no hand. The work here is evidcmtly the work spoken of in the preceding chapter-the work ot reconciling man to himself, the work which he does in Christ. Now, all genuine mfo.isters co-operate with him in this ; their grand endeavour is to bring alienated· souls into friendship with him. Blessed partnership this. IL A SOLEMN POSSIBILITY. "Receive not the grace of God in vain." The grace of God here evidently refers to the offer of this reconciliation. This may be looked upon objectively or subjectively. Objectively it is the gospel, which is called the" gospel of the grace of God;" snbjectively it is personal Christianity. It may be received "in vain" in two forms. Many have the offer of reconciliation and reject it, and to them the offer has been received "in vain." It is possible for those who have personally experienced it to lose it. The free agency of man, the exhortations of the Scriptures,' and the facts of apo~tasy-as in the case of David, Peter, etc.-show the possibility of losing this. No greater calamity can happen to a man than to receive this "grace in vain ; " hence the earnestness of the apostle. . ., III. A Sm'REME OPPORTUNITY. "For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of 68.lvatian have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of aalvation." 'l'o use the words of a modern .writer, "There is, so to speak, a' now' rnnning through the ages. For each Church and nation, for each individual sonl, there is a golden present that may never again recur, and in which lie boundless possibilities for the futnre. The words of the apostle are, as it were, the transfigured expression of the generalization of a wide experience, which tells us that ' there is a tide in the affairs of men.'., •
