entries.title: 2CO 11:7–12
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: ~Misinterpretation. I. OuB BEST AOTS MAY BE llllSINTEBPBETED. Acts of the greatest nobility and unselfishness have often been. The world's greatest benefactors have tasted the bitterness of being-misunderstood. 1. We should not judge of our acts by man's estimate of them. 2. We should not be surprised by any interpretation put on them, 3. We should not be dismayed by any interpretation. 4. We should rejoice that we have a higher, wiser, and more impartial tribunal than the human. Our Master said, " Woe unto you when all men shall speak well of you I " (Luke vi. 26)-a pregnant warning to those who live upon the approval of men! II. MISINTERPRETATION SHOULD NOT HINDER US FROM CONTINUING IN A RIGHT COURSE. 1. We have not to give account to men, but to God. 2. To change our conduct might not avoid misinterpretation, but rather give occasion for it (ver. 12). ill. MISINTERPRETATION MAY DE MET AT SUITABLE TIMES BY EXPLANATION AND JUSTIFICATION OF CONDUCT, 1. It is well to take away occasion for misinterpretation. Misinterpretation, like martyrdom, should not be courted. Both should be borne heroically when they meet us in the path of duty. 2. It is often well to show that misinterpretation is misinterpretation. We should not forget that misinterpretation may (1) injure our usefulness; (2) injure those who misinterpret us; (3) brin~ dishonour upon Christ. In this matter we have need to be wise 1111 stirpents 11.lld harmless as dove~.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 11:14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-.A very beautiful angel. I. A STARTLING FACT. We learn from Paul that the most sable of Ethiopians can change his skin and the fiercest beast of prey throw off his warning garb. The blackest devil can appear as the brightest angel. This is, indeed, a transfiguration, the most marvellous of transformation scenes. As an angel of wisdom Satan appeared to Eve; a~ an angel versed in theology, to Christ, glibly crying, "It is written." Satan was an angel of light. He thus knows well how to play the angel. Herein is he to be feared. It is not the ugly devil we need dread 110 much as the pretty devil. 'l'he old Scotchman's comment on the horned and hoofed Satan of a celebrated picture of "The Temptation" is full of point : " If that chiel cam' to me in sic ao qgly ~hape, I thivk hti wud bae" teuch job wi' me too." 286 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE COHIN'fHIANS. [ell, x1. 1--33,

II. AN EXPl,ANATION OF BOl[E MYSTERIES; l; The powet' of temptation, Men fre• quently fall before white temptations rather than black ones. Satan is an adept at whitewRshing the sepulchre, The voice that calls us to sin sounds often more like tho Yoicc of an angel than the voice of a deviL 'l'he great adversary traniforms his temp- tatiMl.s as well as himself. 2. That wron,g often seems 1nuch lik6 right. Satan is a clever editor. 3. That folly often Sflems wisdom. A most dexterous counsel is the de,·il ; BI" we listen to him, folly is evidently wisdom, a.nd wisdom certainly folly. His splendid intellect overmasters ours when we cope with him a.lone. III. AN IMPRESSIVE WARNING. 1. To ever be on oor gua,·d. We need have our wits about us whilst we have such an enemy about us. To be careless in such peril would be suicidal. Onr guard should be severe; none should be admitted within the gates but proved friends. 2. Not to judge by appeai·ances. Our tendency is to do so, and therefore the devil transforms himself. " 'l'here is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" (Prov. xiv. 12). We must get below the surface of things. We must take pains to e.scertain the right and the good. Every trap is baited, and the fool who concludes that there can be no difference between a bait and a meal, is soon caught. 3. To seek trw wisdom and discernment. Conceit in our own unaided powers is just what delights the devil, and he often preaches to us 1an angelic discourse upon the pleasing theme of our wonderful faculties, before demonstrat~ ing our unutterable folly and weakness. We need know that we are know~nothings. Self-distrust baulks Satan. When a man is on the pinnacle of pride,he can easily deal with him, but when he is in the valley of humility and self-abnegation the enemy gets sorely perplexed. Let us empty ourselves of the wind of conceit and selfsufficiency, that God may fill us with his own wisdom. 4. To ever abide with Ghrist. Thus alone can we be truly safe. Here alone shall we secure the victory. Christ overcame the devil when he spake least like a devil, a.nd, if we are truly with Ghrist, no disguise of Satan shall deceive us, and no might of his shall overthrow us. The cross of Christ is Ithuriel's spear, which, touching the tempter, reveals him in his true character.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 11:23–33
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-.Apostolic experieneei; on earth. I. THESE EXPERIENCES, AS NARRATED HEBE, ABStJldE A GLOOMY CIIARACTEB. 1. Painful. (1) Bodily sufferin,g. Excessive toil, prison privations, scourgings, stoning, shipwrecks, a night and day in the deep, sleeplessness, coldness, foodlessness, nakedness. (2) Mental suffering. (a) Persecution from Jews as well as Gentiles. His "own countrymen" hated him more fiercely than any. (b) Hostility of false brethren. Peculiarly painful to such a noble nature as Paul's. (c) Anxieties respecting the nu.merons Churches. (d) Acute sympathy with the weak and hindered ones (ver. 29). 2. Perilous. What a catalogue of perils in ver. 26 ! bow extreme the one instanced in vers. 32, 33 ! how pathetic and suggestive the expression, "in deaths oft" (ver. 23) ! Paul lived on the margin of the next world. Of him was it peculiarly true that he knew not what a day would bring forth. lL :MUCH OF THE PAINFUL AND PERILOUS EXPERIENCE OF THE APOSTLE A.BOBE FBOH HIS IIURVELLOUB ZEAL AND ENTERPRISE, He might have avoided not a little by: L Being only moderat,ely active. That delightful "mean " coveted by so manyit was too mean for Paul ! 2. Being more compUant. If he had been· a man of expediency, and not, as he was, a man of principle. If he had bent to the storm; but he intended that the storm should bend to him, or rather to those God-truths which he proclaimed. 3. Pl,acing G~s honour in tM second place. The. servant was persecuted so vindictively because he would talk so much of his Master. It wa.s not Pa,d that Jew and Gentile hated so much, but Christ; but where Paul was there men could hear of nothing but the contemned Nazarene. 4. Loving himself more than iJ perishing worl,d. It was a question which should suffer, Paul or tha world? Paul said, "I will" In Ms sphere he thus imitated his Lord, who, though he was rich, for our sake.s became poor. llI. No SU11'l"EBING OB PBBll, SUCCEEDED IN DAHPING THE .APOSTOLIC ARDOUR. How keen must have been his love for Christ and for his fellow-men I Ever before him be had. the future exaltation of Christ and the "saving some." We have here a marvellous triumph of mind over matter, and a still more marvellous one of spirituality over carnality, The life of the apostle was ao vigorous that he could bear ~ die daily, Oil, XI. 1-33.] 'fHE SECOND EPISTLE 'ro 'l'HE CORINTHfANS. 287

What little aohos and pains sto·p 118 I An avalanche of grief and trial failed to arrest Paul I IV. IT WAS ONLY WHEN SUBJECTED TO GREAT PRESSURE, AND THEN ONLY UNDER PROTEST, THAT THl!l APOSTLE ALLOWED HIMSELF TO DWELL UPON THIS PERPETUAL MARTYRDOM, He rejoiced in it; yet he did not like to speak about it. He almost calls himself n fool for doing so, The martyi- has sometimes sullied his crown by pride• but the apostolic affliction _seemed strangely sanctifi~d to him. Some are not great en°mgh to suffer much for Chnst, God does not allow 1t. It would make them so intolerable that prayer would ascend on all hand.q for their transference to a world where they would have a humble opinion of themselves. Paul went through all the privation anguish, peril, catalogued here, and came out fr()'TYI, it with the spirit of a liltk child.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 11:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-T/ie simplicity in Ohrist. "So your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ." Some manuscripts read," simplicity and chastity." By the term " simplicity" is first meant "singleness of affection," "single-minded devotion to Christ," and the word is used in connection with the marriage figure of vers. 1, 2. It should be remembered that, in the East, the time of espousal is regarded as sacred, and any infidelities.during the time of espousal are treated as adulteries are after marriage. In St. Paul's conception the Church is the espoused bride of Christ, and he had been the means of arranging the espousal in the case of the Church at Corinth. "What the apostle now urges is that it is as natural for him to be jealous for the purity of the Church which owes its birth to him, as it is for a father to be jealous for the chastity of the daughter whom he has betrothed as to a kingly bridegroom." The older theocratic :figure of idolatry as adultery, which so often appears in the books of the prophets, should be compared with this. The term "simplicity" may, however, be more full and suggestive to us, and mean singleness of devotion to Christ, entireness of service to him, unmixed love for him. F. W. Robertson says that the expression, "the simplicity of the gospel," is constantly mistaken. " People suppose simplicity means what a. child or a ploughman can understand. Now, if this be simplicity, evidently the simplicity of the gospel was corrupted by St. Paul himself; for he is not simple. Who understands his deep writings? Does one in a thousand? St. Peter says there a.re things hard to be understood in St. Paul's Epistles. We often hear it a.lleg~d as a. charge against a. book, a. lecture, or a sermon, that it is not simple. If we are told that what we a.re to preach must be on a level with the most inferior intellect, so that without attention or thought it may be plain to all, we are bound to disclaim any obligation to do this; if it is supposed that the mysteries of God, of which we a.re the stewards, can be ma.de as easy of comprehension as an article in a newspaper or a novel, we say that such simplicity can only be attained by shallowness. There must be earnestness, candour, patience, and a certain degree of intelligence, as well as a sort of sympathy between the minds of the preacher and his hearers, and there must be a. determination to believe that no man who endeavours to preach the gospel will deliberately and expressly say what he knows to be false or wrong. 'Simple' means, according to St. Paul, unmixed or unadulterated." I. THE PLACE OF CHRIST m THE CmraCH. It is as unique as that of the husband in relation to the wife. entries.title: 2CO 11:4
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0ne Jesus, one Spirit, one gospel,, Evidently St. Paul recoanized a vital <listinction between the Christ whom he preached and the Christ pr;ached by the teachers of the Judaic party. The Christ whom he preached was the" Friend and Brother of mankind, who had died for all men that he might reconcile them to God." The Christ whom they preached was the "head of a Jewish kingdom, requiring circumcision and all the ordmances of the Law as a condition of admission to it." St. Paul could see no gospel, no good news, in such a Christ as that. By "another Jesus" we may understR.nd Jesus otherwise presented; "another spirit" is something opposed to the spirit of liberty in (:hrist from Mo!'ll.ic ordinances; and by" another gospel" the apostle means something different from the good news of God reconciled to faith. "His gospel was one of pardon through faith working by love; theirs was based on the old Pharisaic lines of works, ritual, ceremonial and moral precepts, standing in their teaching on the same footing." Here St.. Paul makes distinct claim to be the authorized teacher of the truth, a.nd we consider this claim. I. THE SENSE IN WHICH .APOSTOLIO TEAOHING w AS FINAL. In relation to this modern opinion differs from the older opinion, a.nd therefore the subject needs. to be treated with extreme care and prudence. When the genera.Uy received doctrine of inspiration wa.s that known a.s the verbal theory, which affirmed the direct communi- cation from God of every word of Scripture, the apostles were regarded a.s inspired for every detail of Gospels and Epistles, a.nd appeal to their expressions was regarded as final. We now more clearly see that they were inspired to guide men's thoughts, but not to fetter them, or force them into precise moulds. The apostles do fix the lines along which Christian tbonght ma.y safely run, but they leave full room for the diversities and idiosyncrasies of men to find free expression. 'l'hey make a. firm stand, a.nd plainly show the boundaries of Christian thinking, bat within the lines they leave us free. We properly use our own cultured Christian judgment-in the lea.dings of the Holy Ghost -upon the va.lne of their arguments, a.nd the precise applications of their counsels. And this appears to us quite consistent with a. becoming reverence for these divinely endowed men, and necessary to that persona.I lea.ding of the Holy Ghost, which we are permitted to realize as well as they. God's truth for the race ca.n be set within nc, permanent bonds, even though men may call them apostolic. II. THE LIMITS WITHIN WHICH DIVERSITY ·OAN JIE PERMITTED. 1. There can be no dispute with regard to the great Christian/acts. 2. There ca.n be no attempt to alter the supreme position of Christ in his Church a.nd relation to his Church. There is nothing so essentially Christian a.s the truth of the direct relation of the soul to Christ, a relation that is independent of doctrine, creed, ceremonial, or priesthood, though these all have their place. 3. There a.re great foundation truths and principles which ma.y be stated in simple and comprehensive terms, but ontside of which, or contrary to which, Christian thought cannot safely run. None may take from us our" liberty in Christ," but we may wisely "hold fast the form of sound words." III. THE WAYS IN WRICH APOSTOLIO TEACHING MIGHT BE lllPEllILLED. Unfold a.nd illustra.t.e the following ways. 1. By overloading it with the old, 2. By overstraining it to fit the new. 3. By applying it in a spirit that is out of harmony with its principles. 4. By the pressure of the peculiarities of men who are strongly self-willed. 5. By translating the claims into the things we should like to do, rather the.n into the things which we ooght to do. 6. By permitting the common philosophy e.nd sociology of men to give tone to the Christian revelation, rather than to make Christianity tone them. IV. THE TEBTB BY WHIOB SUOB PEBVEBBIONB OF APOBTOLIO TEACHINGS MIGHT BE DIBCOVERED. The all-sufficing te,tB of a.ny teaching, under the influence of which we may com&-wbether it be teachings of the pulpit or of the press-are these. 1. le it ill ha.l'UlOIIY with the first truth of the Christian revelation-the fatherhood of Go<!? on, XI, 1-33,] THE SEOOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, 280

2, Doos it uphold the honour, and the supreme 11dministraUve rights in souls, of the Lor Jesus Christ? 3. And does it practically tend towards the things that are pure, an trne, o.nd holy, o.nd good? Everything godly is helpful to godliness. In conclusion, o.rgue this point-Can we still safely receive truth upon the authority of men? and if so, nro there any limitations under which such reception is properly placed? And are we still open and exposed to the persuasions of self-interested or selr-deluded teachers? Wo have to find out for these times in which we live what is the secret of "holdina 0 fast the faith once delivered to tho eaints."-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 11:10
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Apostolic boaRtings. This is a most reproachful passage, and the intensity of St. Paul's feeling can only be accounted for by some knowledge of the bitter o.nd shameful treatmont he was receiving from the antagonistic Jewish party at Corinth. Archdeacon Farrar, in a very vivid and forcible manner, presents the kind of things that were being freely said at Corinth about the apostle. "He had shown feebleness in bis change of _plan-; his personal appearance, feeble and infirm, did not match the authoritative tone of his letters; his speech had nothing in it to command admiration ; he threatened supernatural punishments, but he did not dare to put his threats to the proof. What right had he to claim the authority of an apostle, when he had never seen the Christ in the flesh? Was it certain that he was a Hebrew, a Jew of the pure blood of Palestine, or even,tbat he was of the seed of Abraham? Who was this Paul, who came without credentials, and expected to be received on the strength of his everlasting self-assertions.? Was there not a touch of madness in his visions and revelations? :could he claim more than the tolerance which men were ready to exteud to the insane?" "lJonceive all these barbed arrows of sarcasm falling on the ears, and through them piercing the very soul, of a man of singularly sensitive nature, passionately craving for affection, and propor.tionately feeling the bitterness of loving with no adequate rcfurn; and we may form some estimate of the whirl and storm of emotion in which l3t. Paul began to dictate the Epistle." As a rule, boastings are only evil both for him. ·who.boasts and for those who hear the boasting; but no rule is without exception, and there are times when a man is absolutely driven to boasting-it is the one thing that he.can do, and that he ought to do. It becomes the plain duty of the hour. A man may never boast until he is thus driven to it, and then his boastings will have their foun- dation in his humility. The apostle's boastings had direct reference to the accusations made against him. I. THERE WERE BOASTINGS OF HIS JEWISH BIRTH AND RIGHTS. These had been o.ssailed. He was a foreign~born Jew, and the Palestine Jews rather looked down upon all stich. 'It was easy to raise prejudice against the apostle on this ground. He therefore pleads the facts of his pure birth, his Pharisaic relationships, his Jerusalem training, and his manifest Jewish sympathies. He was proud of the fact that no Jew could plead superior Jewish birthrights to his. So far he did but boast of facts of his life that were beyond his own control. II. THERE WEI\E BOASTINGS OF SUFFERINGS BORNE IN MINISTERING FOR CHRIST. Seo vers. 21-3,0, the most amazing catalogue of woes ever written. One wonders how so frail a body could have.endured them all. But even this record we feel is holy boasting, for one can but feel that, under all the intensity of the utterance, there is a great sadness of heart in being thus compelled to speak of such things. He never would have said one word about them had it not been thatattacksupon his apostleship mee.nt dishonour to Christ, and mischievous hindrance to Christ's work. St. Paul never would have boasted if he had not thus been compelled to boast for Christ's sake. And this is the one law for us. Never put self in the front unless so putting self will e:lorify our Master. We may even boast if it ii; clear that our boasting will serve bim.-R. 'l'.

entries.title: 2CO 12:1–6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Supernatural communications as evidences of his apostleship. The old question as to his apostolic authority, which had recently been revived in a most exciting form, was not yet disposed of, and he must now discuss it in another aspect. So far as external circumstances were concerned, had not the prophetic declaration to Ananias been fulfilled?-" I will show him how great things he must suffer for my Name's sake." .And, furthermore, he had proved that ,his own state of mind, the in ward being of his soul, had corresponded with his call to suffer. The flesh had been subdued. Years of growth had brought him to a stage of experience that allowed him to speak of glorying in his infirmities, But he would now turn to another branch of experiences, viz. "visions and revelations of the Lord." Glorious as these exaltations were, they would see that, while they were exceptional in certain respects, yet they fell in with the providential discipline of his life, and opened the way for a keener sense of his infirmities 'by" a thorn in the flesh." All along St. Paul has been painfully aware that bis enemies were using these infirmities to his official disparagement. Painfully, we say, for it is obvious that he was sensitive to the disadvantages under which be appeared before the public. "Humble,"" fUdil in speech,"" bodily presence weak,"" speech contemptible," were things that had some fouudation in fact. Of course, his adversaries exaggerated them, but the apostle could riot escape instinctive feeling, and at times acute feeling, touching this matter. 'l'his, however, was only one source of depression. A fuller 206 Tl:IE SEOOND EPISTLE 'rO THE CORINTHIAN~. [tit. xn. 1-21.

account, of his BUl'furinga, physioal and mental, th&n he had ever given had Juet now been presented, and the oonolusion or it w1111 that his bodily disad\tantages as a 11peaker, his low repute as a public teacher, bis constant endurance of pain and: solicitude. be.cl. resulted in his realir;in~ the fact that this very weakness was his strength. Could •• visions and revelations ' be entrusted to him-such visions and revelations--snd be not be hu~blcd bY: Divine direc~ion? The more !tlorious tb~ revelation, the greater the necessity for him to be remmded, and most pamfully remmded, that the treasw·e was committed to an" earthen vessel." Witness the following: a man fourteen.years agothe memory of it still vividly present aa a reality of to-day-such a .man whether in the body or out of the body it was impossible to tell, elevated to ihe third heaven, and hearing" unspeakable words not lawful for a man to utter." 11 Fourteen years ago " the fact now first divulged, and yet the fact alone ; the secret disolosures still a secret and person&} to the man alone; and the sanctity such that it would be profanation to make the contents of the communication known. 11 Caught up to the third heaven, caught up into Paradise," face to face 'llith the Lord Jesus in his mediatorial glory ; and there, the senses laid to rest and the body forgotten and the spirit opened to receive instruction and inspiration, the man taught what he was to be . and what he was to do as the servant on earth of his Divine Master. Intellectual pride and vanity, spiritual pride and vanity, pride aIJd vanity as a Jew to whom the God of the fathers had manifested bimself.,..how could these be kept down except by mortifications of the flesh? If, nevertheless, ~e were to boast of these revelations, he should do it truthfully. Suppose, then, that J:i,e should , make this boast; who would be able to transfer himself into the proper a,Hitudii of a . listener? entries.title: 2CO 12:7–10
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Need of humuity and the means appointed to secure it. Uthe Lord Jesus passed from the baptism in the Jordan, and the dovelike \l..~sccnt of the Holy Ghost upon him, to the solitude of the wilderness and the assaults of the tempter;. if he came down from the mount of transfiguration to witness the failure of the disciples to heal the lunatic boy, and to give expression to his sorrow in the words, "O_faitbless and perverse generation! "et.c.-it is not surprising that an apostle should be sorely tried after his exaltation. New endowments must have new te8ts. New and larger grace wust be immediately put on probation, since there are many probations in this one probatio1dhat have eternal issues. "Lest I "-this man in Christ, who fourteen years ago was prepared by special revelation for the toil and trial. of his Gentile apostleship- •• lest I should be exalted above measure;" and what was the danger? "The abundance of the revelations." .Against that danger he must be fortified. If new endowments and new graces are instantly put on trial, and the conditions of !if.i's general 1•robation changed, then, indeed, a new check to guard against abuse of incr_eased gifts must not be lackiug. The man is not precisely the same man as before, nor is he in the same world that he previously occupied. Accessions of outward advant~ges, such as wealth and social position, are full of risks, but accessions of inward power are far more perilous. To preserve St. Paul from self-glorification, th~re was given him II a thorn in tb~. flesh." First of all, the revelations were as to the fact itself to be kept a secret, and this was a . means of humility, but the thorn in the flesh was added.. What it was we knml' not, but it we.s a bodily infirmity that caused him much suffering. "This is significant. It is of the very I1J1.ture of thorns to be felt rather than seen, and to appear triflirw evils to all but those directly stung by them " (Dr. Bellows). It was " a messe~aer of Satan," though this does not imply that it was not unq(;lr God's direction. The ide~ is that this "ar.gel of Satan " was an impaling stake that produced severe and continued pain, and the reason therefore is twice stated, 11 lest I should be exa~ted above measure." So, then, it was not as an apostle, but as the apostle to tho Gentiles, that he was specially afflicted. Pain is instinctively resisted as an enemy to the acti- vily, comfort, and pleasure of life. Naturally, therefore, St. Pa~l f~lt that it would interfer1: with bis energy and happineS1,, and, of course, the Satamc side of the torture on. ut. 1-21.l ·ftlE SECOND gpJS'l'LE 'l'O 'I'IIE CORIN'fHIANS. 20,

would be uppermost in hie thought. 'l'he evil in p&in Is what we Bee first. Ir this were not re&lized, it could not be nu affliction. Hence he prayed thrice to the Lord that It might dep11rt from him. But his prayer was demtid. At the aame time, the promise was given-a promise worth far more than the removal of the pain-" My grace Is sufficient for thee : for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn was to continue--a Hfelong suffering in addition to his other infirmities was to bo fastened upon him, a special and grievous suffering. Yet, while it had to remain a sad memorial, not of bis exaltation, but of human frailty in connection with great endowments, there was an assurance direct and specific of suataining grace. Along with that a most important truth wae taught him, namely, that the perfection of strength is attained through the consciousness of our utter weakness. First, then, the evil of pain ; next, the good of pain under the agency of God's grace ;-this is the rµetbod. of providence and grace, for the two are one in the Divine purpose. Alas! had the prayer of those sensitive nerves of his been litera11y answered, what a. loser would he and we have .been! How much of his power would have vani.~hed with the pain I How many thoughts and emotions that have cheered the afflicted and inspired tb.e .weak to be' heroic, would have been unknown! Such Epistles as the apostle wrote (to say nothing of bis other services to the world) could never have been written under the ordinary experience of the ills of life. All men ha.ve thorns in the flesh, for there is no perfect health, no human body free from ailments. But in St. Paul's Clllle the thorn was a supera<ldition to existing infirmities. Nor is it difficult for us to see how tliis 'particular infirmity, sanctified by the Spirit, was specially adapted to guard him at a µ:iost exposed point. Inasmuch as he was the object of a peculiar and violent opposition, be was singula.rly liable to the temptation of over-asserting himself and his merits, the more so as his enemies took delight in taunting him with bis personal defects as to manner and appearance. The safeguard was provided where it was most wanted. Such, in fact, was his own view of the matter: "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ ma.y rest upon me." " My infirmities," he argues, "instead of being tbe hindrance they would be if left to themselves, are helpers, since they are the occasions of grace, and this grace rests upon me, i.e. abides continually. '!'he thought is precious; it must be repeated. "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities," etc.; for the power of Christ had been imparted to him with such. fulness as to transform pain into pleasure so far a.s his spiritual nature was conc~med. The body continued to suffer, the humiliations were increased, but his soul wa's filled with Christ as .the Christ of his pains and sorrows, and thus he had the victory, not only over physical misery, but over all pride and vanity that might have sprung up " through the abundance of the revelations." Glorious words are these. "When I am weak, then am I strong." Notice the clear view St. Paul bas of the Divine h·and. in his thorn in the flesh. If he is perfectly assured of the abundance of the revelations, if he can locate the scene in P:l.l'adise, if he realizes the sanctity of these disclosures in the " unspeakable words," he is just as certain that the thorn " was given " him. He knew it was a. "thorn," and he 1':new whence it came. He acknowledged God in it, and, in this feeling, prayed thrice for its removal. Christians o[ten fail at this point. '!'hey doubt at times whether their afflictions come from God. Somi, Christians cannot be induced to believe that their sufferings are sent from above, and they see in them nothing more than evil casualties. But if they fail to recognize God in the sorrow, they will not find him in the joy of his blessed promise, " My grace is sufficient for thee." It was not merely the " thorn" that St. Paul had to endure. This was a. source of pain, and it aggravated, doubtless, his other physical infirmities, nnd, in turn, was augmented by them. But we must not forget the state of mind such an affliction naturally produced-the surprise that it should follow such wonderful signs of God's favour as had been vouchsafed in the "abundance o~ the revelations," tho temptation to a rebellious spirit and the occas!o.n for unbelief it would furnish. A literal answer to his prayer was refused; a spmtual answer w:is granted. The "grace" bestowed was "sufficient," not only to bear the pain as a pecu- liar addition to his "infirmities" already existing, but to enable him to "glory " in it; 11nd the providence of it was specially manifested in the power it had given him to be po.tiout, forbearing, humble, in the late trouble with the Corinthians. 0 Christi,in~, who are cnlled to a lifelong <liscip!ine in the ~chool of suffering, think of the measure' 298 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. implied in the Sfl,fficient gro~ I Sufficient for wha\ P Sufficient, n<.>t only to ..glory in pnin and infirmity, but to glory" most gladly.''-L. .

Vcrs. 11-15.-Recummce to theformer a,-gwmmt. The intense feeling of St. Pau1 indicates itself by not oontinuing on <:me uu~ryiug l~vel. From the climax just' reached he reverts to what had been previously discussed in oh. x. ancL~.i. These rever- ~rations are very cha.r~risti~ of ~he man as a thinker, and they show how closely; i_n him, temperament was allied with mtellect. If aroused, he never became artificial or unnatural, but WIIS then most true to his organization. In the verses before us he resumes his ironical vein: "I am become a fool in glorying ; " but not of his own accord, for " ye have compelled me." The disaffected party at Corinth had not respected his jw;t claims, had not "commended" him, and they had failed in, this matter whian he ltad demonstrated that he was "in nothing behind the very chiefest ·of the apostles"-:- the same idea expressed in eh. xi. 6, adding in this insta~ " though I be notbin~.'; Was he thinking of the abundant revelations with which .he. could not. have b;en entrusted save on the condition of a thorn in t4e flll5h_? Only a prief utter~ce, yet very sincere-" though I be nothing." It was safe for such a nian in his impaled situation to dramatize the "fool," but he hastens to serious work and mentions that "the signs of an apostle" had been wrought among them. ,His language is full and earnest; "truly," "in all patience," "signs and wonders and mighty deeds;" no. lack no irritn.ting haste, no deception, number and variety and extraordinary power .all. provi<le.i for. Despite. of the accumulation, the magnitude, the unimpeachable quali(~'i • of these Divine evidences, God among you of a truth, Christ honouring his servant arid his servant's work, ye Corinthians, or some of you, have _not" commended" Ille I 'In what respect were ye inferior to other Churches? Look at Macedonia, look at Asia; wherein were you less favoured than they? They commemled me; what have you done to exemplify your sense of my apostleship? I remember but one thing in which ye were" inferior"-and the irony is ·keen now-I remember that I preached ~he:gospel gratuitously, so as not to be "burdensome to you;" and this is yow- acknowledgment, £his· your commendation of my coUISe ! What a mistake my disinterestedness wa.s ! What a "fool " in my goodness ! "For.give me this wrong I " Despite of it all, I am not weaned from Corinth. "The third time I am ready to. come• to yo1L" Though my . self-denying conduct has been used to bring me into contempt, I sliall repeat it without any abatement, for" I will not be burdensome to you." And now his heart swells as he says, "I seek not yours, but you "-words that he bequeathed .to the adqiiratfon of ages; for was he not their spiritual father? If, at the bidding cif natura.). instinct, children were not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children, then it became him to provide for his spiritual children. But was this all that his love had to promise? :Kay; what means he had or might have should not only be freely used in, their behalf, but he would give his faculties,his heart, his whole self, to'advance their well-being. "Signs of an apostle" had been wrought at Corinth, "wonders and mighty deeds," but the signs of a mbliwe moral manhood rise before us when he declares, " I will very gladly spend and be spent for you." Will this avail? "If I love you more abundantly, am.I loved the less? "-L.

-Forestallingfalse criticism. Assurances of fatherly regard, assurances of a willinp;neSll, ar, of a. gladness, in giYing all he had and all he was, even life itself, to their service and interest; would they pass for nought? And were there both history and prop,hecy in the melancholy words " The more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved ' ? ').'he fervent appeal, the p;otracted argument, the action and reaction, the irony and the profound sincerity, the grieved tenderness, the .sad ingratitude, the memory of noble self-sacrifice, gather iuto the climax," We 11peak before God in Uhrist," There, at that bar of judgment, Olf, XII, 1-21.J 'l'HE BEOOND EPIS'fLE ·ro THE CORINTHIANS. 299

J,w ma){es the solemn avowal, "We do all things, dearly beloved, for yoor edifying." Once more he would conciliate, nor should this long and impassioned outburst oome to a close without calling God in Christ to witness hie deep-felt e.ffection for these nngrateful {Joriuthians.-L. . Vere .• 20, 21.-E:i;pression, of his fears. Wby had he jnet spoken with so much earnestness? Why had St. Paul brought facts to their notice which he had never used iu addressing his Churches? Why had he referred to that extraordinary event in his career, .when he had ~een ushered inta the secret chambers of Paradise and permitted to hear things which were.not to be told? Why a, revelation to be umevea.led? It was to teach the rebellious and evil-disposed among the Corinthians that he was Christ's 11,postle .to them, and, as such, charged with maintaining the order, peace, and purity of' the Church.ea entrusted to hie oversight. Very tenderly had he appealed to the Corinthiaw, and now, having called God, even God in Christ, to witness the depth and sinc.erity of hie ,love for them, he would entreat them not to drive him to extreme measures, 'l'o exercise stern authority gave him no pleasure. The greatest thing in an apostle was love, and he wished to restore harmony and prosperity to the Chorch by means of forbearance and affectionate counsel. Therefore. he had pleaded so fervently; therefore he had condescended to boasting;. therefore he had told them more of bis infirmities than his enemies knew: ; .therefore he had gloried in those things which these very men used to alienate hie own spiritual children by putting contempt on him and his offi~e. ·, .Fears he had, lest :when he should come to Corinth, he should not find them such as he wished, and fears too that he would have to act in an apostolic way not agreeable to them, so that on .their meeting together. each party would be disappointed in the other., Hope .he had, and so he.11pe,1ks doubtingly. But the fatherly heart is overloaded with apprehensions and ".le11~ !' is thrice employed, for he would not conceal these a,pprehensions. What a dark ·llst .of vices and sins is spread out in the last two verses I If he should have to confront these evils, he will not find them such as he wciuld and they will find him such as they would not. First comes the catalogne of moral evils such as originated in the factious spirit so rife in Corinth, viz. strife, jealousy, wraths, (actions, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults. These things would reqiµre discipline; But, moreover, he feared the sensual wickedness which had su~h a holdon,Corintl;i. For he might have to deal with gross offenders, men who had commi,tted sins, of "uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness," and had not repented. Such a state of things would grieve him. Disappointed and afflicted by a blight like. this falling on his labours in the ministry of the gospel, he tells them, "My God will humble me among you." . To avoid these distressing results, to restore peace arid epiritual prosperity to a Church rent by faction and disgraced by immorality, be had written and laboured and prayed.. If all failed, "my God will humble me among you."-L. • Ver'. 2.- ".A man in <Jhrist." . When we consider what man is, and who Christ is, the conjunction seems wonderful indeed. Yet, when apprehended, this union appears one fraught with richest blessings for him who is the inferior and dependent member. The thought was one familiar to the apostle ; himself " a man in Christ," he spoke of others who were "in Christ before" himself, and he designated Christian societies, "Churches in Obrist Jesus." I., THE NATURE OF TIIE UNION THUS DESCRlllED, 1. The Christian is grafted "in Christ" as a graft in a tree, joined to 'him as a branch to a vine. The union is thus a vital union, and is to the Christian the means and the occasion of spiritual life. 2. 'l'he Christian is accepted "in Christ," i.e. in the Beloved. For Christ's sake the Christian is received into Divine favour. 'l'he Saviour is in this capacity a Representative, a Mediator, an Advocate. 3. The Christian is incorporated "in Christ" as the member in the body, and has a new function to discharge in consequence of this relationship. 4. 'l'he Christian is hidden "in Christ" as the traveller in the cleft of the rock, as the voyager in the ark, when u the Lord shut him in." 5. The Christian dwells "in Christ" as in a house, a home appointed for him by Divine wisdom !lnd goodness. IT. THE IMPORTANCE AND ADVANTAGES OF THIS U:!.'lON. 1. As is apparent from conijidcring t4e positiou of those who are out of Christ. For such, wh~re is safety, 300 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE OORIN'l.1llIANR. [ott. xn. 1-21,

where is II law of life, where is a prospect for immortality? For to be out of Obrist la to be without God, and so without hope. 2. From considering what in this life they possess who have Christ and are in him. Whilst; so far &s the bodily life ie concerned, they are in the world, they are in spirit in the Lord, and thus partake a hiaher nature nud existence than belong to earth and to time. 3. From considering the i~1perishable character of this union. To be "in Christ" now is to be " with Christ " for ever. To those who are in him there is no condemnation now, and from him there· shall be no separation hereafter. The visions which Paul beheld, and the declarations he heard when be was caught up into the third heaven, were to him, ancl. may be to us, an earnest and promise of inunort.-il union. Therefore "Abide in him."-T.

entries.content: -Glnryi111J in weaknesses. It is not to be wondered 11.t that Paul boasted; th.e wonder is that, instead of boasting of the extraordinary visions he had experienced, the extraordinary co=ission be had received, the extraordinary success which bad followed' his labours, he boasted of what other men would ha.ve concealed or have·lamented-""-1:ils' own infirmities, disadvantages, and troubles. I. THE WEA!i:NESSES IN WBl<JH THE APOSTLE GLORIED. 1. Hie own bodily infirmity was especially present to bis thoughts, when using this language. • Whatever this was,: whether general ill health or .some special malady, as of the eyes, it was· naturally distressing to himself, as it prevented him from• doing his work with the ease and 'pleasure which be might have experienced had he possessed health and vigour of body. 2.' The contempt he met with from some amongst whom he laboured was to Paul no cause ·or mortification, but cause of rejoicing. Let men despise him ; if he was able to. serve and please his Master, tbat w~ enough. 3. The hardships and privations and persecutions be endured in the fulfilment of his ministry were matter of glorying. In these he took· pleasure, contrary as such a fact was to ordinary human experience. • II. THE GROUND OF THE APOSTLE'S GLORTING IN BIS WEAKNESSES. 1. There~'n be no doubt that the deepest ground lay in Paul's sympathy with his· Divine Lord.' 'i'he humiliation and obedience unto death of the Lord Jesus in order to secure man's· salvation became a. new source of inspiration, in the direction both of human ac'tion a.nd of human suffering, and Paul was crucified with Christ unto the world. He bore a.bout with him in the body the marks of the Lord Jesus, and of this he justly boasted.·. 2. Personal weakness was t1e occasion of the reception of new and spiritual strength. For Christ made his own grace sufficient when his servant's strength was gone. And by a sublime paradox the apostle learned that, when he was weak, then was he strong. And tlms the very infirmities which seemed to disqualify for service became the occasion of tLe communication of such spiritual power and aid as rendered the apostle more efficient aud successful in the service of the Lord.-T. entries.title: 2CO 12:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Sufficient grace. Perhaps there is no verse in Scripture which has brought wore strength and corufort to the hearts of Christ's people than this. The expl,anation of its preciousness and its power is to be sought first in the spiritual, the revealed truth which it communicates, and secondly in the fact that it is the record of personal experience. There iH an instinctive persuasion in the human mind that the experience which bas been realized by one is possible to another. The grace which was actuall:r bestowed upon Paul does not seem inaccessible to the feeble, the tempted, the overbu1 • dened Christian who cries to Heaven for help. L THE NEED FOB THIS SUFFICIENCY. I. The manifold duties, the severe temptations, the varied sorrows and troubles, incidental to the Christian life. There are difficulties and trials common to the Christian with all men, but there are others peculiar to him, urising from the higher view he takes of life, both as a personal discipline and as an opportunity for serving and glorifying God. 2. '!'he conscious insufficiency of human re~ources. Tb,s, indeed. accounts for the universal practice of prayer, frequent. or occasional, deliberate or spontaneous. Men feel their utter helplessness in the presence' of the demands of life, a.ud therefore they call upon God. Ji'Iuch more keenly does the follower of foe Lord Jesus realize his need of a higher than human aid. Conscious that only Di.vine grace has reconciled him to God, he daily acknowledges his dependence ' uµm the sarue grace for the maintenance of l1iij 6piritual life ind usefuniwss. 11. 'l'W! lill()U!-1, o, THU; SUFFICIENCY. l. 'l'he divinity of the Saviour. Caii w11 oe, xu. 1-21,] THE SEOOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 301

Imagine any other th1m Christ ueing this language, "My grace ill Ruflicient"? It i~ becoming, it is possible, only to him who possesses Divine resources, who is spiritually present with all his yeople. 2. Christ's mediatorial position. This involves the posRession "nd the disposa of whatsoever is necessary for the spiritual welfare of those whom tbo Lord.Jesus saves. Accepted as our Representative, be has received gifts for men; nnd it is in the fulfilment of hie mediatorial office that he imparts to each individual disciple and friend the specially needed grace. 3. The spiritual dispensation over which the Lord Jesus presides. He is Head over all things unto his Church. He distributes to every man severally as he will. His Spirit is the Spirit of truth, of holiness, of power. III. THE EVIDENOE OF THIS BUFll'ICIENCY. 1. 'l'he personal experience of Paul as recorded in this passage. He tells 11e here, not only what Christ promised, but what he performed. He was perfectly satisfied with the course be had taken. He did not find his own personal weakness and insufficiency a barrier to bis efficiency and usefulness. What he lacked, his Lord supplied. 2. The recorded experience of all who have trusted to the same Divine Source of all-sufficiency.
