And every Christian has reason to acknowledge- , "'And when my all of strength shall fail, I ahall with the God-Man prevail." T

entries.title: 2CO 12:12
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Signs of apostleship. The evidences of deep feeling, which are manifest throughout this Epistle, are very promi.nent in this passage. There were special reasons why a sensitive man like Paul should lay to heart the treatment with which he met from the Corinthians. Considering what he had done among them and for them, he felt it bard that empty pretenders should be preferred to himself. And he was convinced that, in disregarding his authority, these members of the Corinthian congregation whom he had in view were doing injustice to bis ministry among them. For all the proofs of a Divine commission had been exhibited in his ministry in their city. He appeals to-- I. MIRACULOUS .EVIDENCES OF .APOSTLESHIP. Upon due occasion the apostle did not hesitate to bring forward and adduce as proofs of his commission the supernatural gifts which had been bestowed upon him. How could he have publicly made such a claim as this in an authentic letter, unless the Corinthians, friendly and inimical, were ready, to witness to the truth of his language? It would not be fanciful to discriminate among the terms which Paul in this passage applies to these miraculous evidences. Observe that they· are designated: 1. Powers, as pointing to the heavenly and Divine source to which they must needs be traced. Whether exercised in controlling nature, in healing disease, or in inflicting punishment, they bore upon their very presence the evidences that they were of superhuman origin. 2. Wonders, as fitted and indeed intended to awaken the interest, the inquiry, the amazement, of all beholders. Wonder may be useful in leading to such reflection, such emotion, as may surpass itself in value. 3. Signs, as indicating the authority of those at whose prayer or command these marvels were wrought " among" 'the Corinthians. IL THE HORAL EVIDENCE OF APOSTLESmP, Nowhere in the New Testament is the po1+.ent placed above the spiritual. Christ's mighty works answered their purpose when they prompted the exclamation and inquiry," What manner of man is this!" And in Paul's character there was seen an evidence of apostleship far more convincing and far more instructive than the most marvellous deeds which be performed. He justly claims to h11ve exhibited patience, both in his continuing to work for the Corinthians and to interest himself in them notwithetanding their ingratitude, and in his tender and brotherly ireatment of them with a view to their restoration to entire sympathy with himself.-T. Vor. 15.-Ministerial devotion. Paul rejoices and boasts that, however the Corinthians may misunderstand him, he cannot be accused of having acted towards them in a mercenary spirit. Disinterestedness at all events he must claim, and they must concede. They are the debtors, not he, He is the parent who lays up for the children. '!'his he does cheerfully, and is resolved that ho will do in the future as in the past, His determination is to spend and to be spent for their souls. 302 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [oH. x11. 1-91.

I. A t1INCEl!E PROFESSION. Had Paul ·been a stra.nger to his correspondents he ooultl not have used such langu&,..<YEI as this. But he was well known to them, having lived and laboured in Corinth, working with bis own hands for bis maintenance, and putting forth every effort for the spiritual enlightenment and salvation of the oitii:ene. 1. The minister of Christ~ for the enrichment of his people's souls. He bas "·treeeure" though in earthen vessels. H.e has "the true riches" committed to his keeping. His aim is to bestow the choicest and most precious blessings npon the spiritually necessitous. All be bas he loni,i to part with. 2. The minister of Christ is willing to be spent for bis people's souls, Labour often involves suffering. Bodily powers ma.y be exhausted • even the mind itself may give way under the strain of a toilsome, emotional, prolonged ministry. The missionary may sink beneath the burden of climate, of unrequited toil, of persecution. Every faithful minister must la.y his account, not only with effort ·but with self-denial and self-sacrifice. ' Il. AN ARDENT APPEAL. The Revisers adopt a rendering of the latter part of this verse which harmonizes with what we may well believe to have been the sentiment; of the apostle. I. Paul has proved the abundance of his love; and every true minister, animated by the love of Christ and by pity for souls, has shown himself to be a true lover and friend of ·his fellow-men. 2. Shall it, then, be the case that those whom the Christian minister loves, and whose welfare he seeks, shall be indifferent and ungrateful? It is sometimes so; the very faithfulness and earnestness of the minister may occasion the aversion of those who desire that he should "prophesy smooth things," and leave them to their sinful pursuits and pleasures uninterrupted. Yet the affection and devotion of spiritual workers deserve a very different return.-T.

entries.title: 2CO 12:19
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Edijication. The strain in which this portion of the Epistle is written may, the writer is conscious, mislead some readers. It displays a good deal of personal feeling; it reproaches those who have not shown themselves amenable to rightful influence and authority; it reveals a wounded hea.l't, Some readers may misinterpret these signs and infer that the apostle regards himself as on his defence, as excusing and vindicating himself, as asking that the best construction possible may be forbearingly put upon his condnct. .But all this is. erroneous.· Paul's one great aim is, not his own vindication, but, on the contrary, the edification of those to whom his Epistle ie addressed.. I. 1N WHAT DOES EDIFICATION CONSIST? 1. It he.e respect to -those .who are already built upon the one Foundation-Christ. The minister of .Christ, like other workmen, must begin at the beginning. When men receive the gospel, then, and only then; a.re they in a position to be "edified." 2. It consists in the building up of ·the Christian character in the case of individuals. The resemblance to Christ is what is mainly to be sought. 3. And in the formation of solid and serviceable Christian societies, all of which are parts of the holy temple which is being reared to the glory of God. • IL BY WHAT ldEAl!IB IS EDIFICATION P.BOHOTED? 1.. The means divinely appointed and approved are moral and spiritu~l. All employment of mechanical or political a"ency to secure such an end is to be condemned, as both inappropriate and us.eless. 2~ Personal agency is that which the New Testament exemplifies and which experience approves. Living spirits, full of love and sympathy, are divinely1qualifted to engage in such a work as this. 3. The presentation, .of truth, the addressing of language of encoumo-ement and promise, of admonition and rebuke,-thes11 are emphatically the scriptur;l methods-0f edification. Of all these abundant and very instructive examples may be found in this very Epistle. . • •• • fil WHAT PURPOSES I>OEB EDIFICATION BU11BEBVE? 1. The welfare, the highest spiritual development and happiness, of those who are edified. 2. Th11 impression thus made upon the world by the presence in. the midst of it of e. Divine temple reared with, human souls. 3. The honour and glory of the heavenly Architect himself.-T.

entries.title: 2CO 12:1–4
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Apostolic ezperiencea in heaven. I. TllE APOSTLE BAD A HEAVENLY EXPERIENCE DUBING ms EABTBLY LIFE. His earthly experience was, very largely,dark and sorrowful; but a01iiJst th& darkness appearij this brilliant flash of heavenly light. l. Be gives UB thiB ezperience a, an act11,1J,l /act, and as a'IJ,Ch Wt$ 'fMJBt receive it. It W&ll a reality to him. He records it that it !llay come before us aa a. reality, not as a mere ea. x11. 1-21.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 300

fancy or illusion, 2. Ie furniBhed him with U1T1, opportwnity of eontrastinq man's trer1tment and God's, In the closing verses of the preceding chapter we have a catalogne of Paul's tribulations, many of these occasioned by huma.n perversity and enmity. Men treated Paul evilly; God gave him this special and me:rvellous heavenly experience! II. TBE CHARACTER 011' Tms EXPERIENCE, 1. A real, entrance into the heavenly world. Paul has no doubt about this. His only doubt is whether he was in the body at the time. He most distinctly conveys that there was a removal of his spirit into another sphere; be ie not sure whether hls body accompanied his spirit. There could not have been a doubt as to whether be was "in the body" if bis ex!)Brience had been a mere trance or any special influence brought to bear upon bis mind. There wae a removal, but whether of body and spirit, or of spirit alone, the apostle cannot declare. We may note the apostolic belief that consoicus life is possi'ble to 'U8 when we are "out of the body." 'l'be apostle did not know whether his experience was of this order, but he evidently recognizes this order of experience as possibl,e. We may note further that the apostle regarded heaven or paradise as a place ae well as a state. "Third heaven•• and.'.' paradise " seem to be used. synonymously-" _third heaven " indicating the realm in which God's glory is pre-eminently manifested. The rabbins taught the existence of seven· heavens, but it is not probable that Paul refers to their notions. 2. An entrance effected by God_. It was not by the apostle's merit or power; it was by a Divine act-he was "caught up." Admittance to the heavenly world is in the hands of God; if we enter, then God must effect the entrance for ns. Christ, the Way, is given to us by God: •3. .Astonishing'visions. Paul saw much (ver. 1). 4. Wonderful revelations. He •heard much. "Unspeakable words," understood by him, but not to be repeated on earth. Possibly they would not have been intelligible to any who had not participated in the heavenly experience. Our curiosity craves to know what Paul saw and heard, but our needs do no.t demand it. We have the speakable words of the gospel, which, rightly received, will prepare us to hear by-and-by the" unspeakable words " of heaven and to behold the heavenly glories. III. THE OBJEOT 1 ·OF THIS EXl'ERIENCE. 1. To encourage the apostle in his many labours and sufferings. Christ took his disciples up into the mountain and was transfigured before them; then he brought them down into the world of men to toil and to endure, 2. To quicken his faith in the wnseen. Great natures doing great works have often great trials of faith. A big devil always comes against a big Christian. 3. To speed him onward to the· final rest qf God's peopl,e. He was a much-loved child; the Father·showed him special favour. 4. That others to whom the experience should be recowhl!!d might participate in the benefit. The experience was for us as well as for the at>Ostle. ·From wi its special features are largely hidden ; but it is revealed to us, and this knowledge may well encourage us in the earthly service, quicken our faith, and hasten our footsteps towards 'the glories beyond the veil. A general _lesson may be learnt from the event that those who have special trials and sorrows experience also special comforts and helps.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 12:7
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
:.._The thorn in the flesh. I. WHAT WAS IT? 1. In itself. '!'here have been almost infinite conjectures. As to· the figure: some prefer a " goad for the flesh," a sharpened stake; others, a: rankling thorn; others, a stake ·on which offenders were impal.ed or the cross to which they wi:re fastened. As to the reality: evil suggestions ; fiery aarts of Satan; some prominent adversary; some painful bodily affection, weak eyesight, defective speech, carnal cravings; whilst a bold imaginationist has had the temerity to suggest a termagant wife! Pos~ibly the precise nature of the affliction is concealed that no one may say, "Ah, that is not my trouble.'' It was very grievous to the apostle whatever its precise nature. 2. As Satan was concerned in it. Paul recognized Satan's hand (see Job ii. 7; Luke xiii.16). It was used of Satan to annoy, pain, depress, and harass Paul, and with the };ope that it would hinder his great work. Satanic malice rejoiced in the anticipation tha.t it might prove the last straw upon the camel's back. Paul interfered much with the devil's kingdom; it is no wonder that the devil s9ught to interfere with him. Satan can afford to leave some people alone; but if we faithfully attack his kingdom and his rule we may expect reprisals. Yet Satan is but a t'ool after all, and constantly overreaches himself. One has well said, " The devil drives but a poor t111,de by the persecution of the saints-he tears the r,est, but. 304 THE SECOND ErISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [on. xu. 1-21,.

U1e bird e~capes ; he cracks the shell, but lost>s the kernel," 3. As allowed by God. God's hRnd was in it as well as Satan's. This is so with all our tribulationR • in ono aspect they e.re messengers of Sat&n, in the other messengers of God. All' depends upon which 'l'TUJssage we listen to. •Paul's thorn in the flesh was God's teacher of h~mility. Th~re was danger that _th_e extraordinary i:evelation~ made to the apostle might ~oster pride. Huma.n nature 1s mtensely susceptible to ·this temptation. 'l.'hose who enJoy remarkable favours often experience remarkable affliction, 'l.'he ship in the high wind needs plenty of ballast. When we build high we must also build low-tho lofty building requires a deep foundation. It is well for us that God is not merely indulgent. God will not allow us to become spoilt children, II. TnE APOSTLE'S RESTLESSNESS UNDER TllE AFFLIOTION. Paul was very human. ' He would not have been so could he have borne this additional trouble with indifference, Remember his other troubles. If this special aftliction seemed likely to hinder his Jifo. work, how keenly would be feel it I 'Tis hard to dance in chains. Heavy labour tries the heal thy ; how exceedingly burdensome to the sick I • Yet he did not grumble or . make himself a nuisance, or find fault with God, or sit down in despair, It was s'aid , of him once, "Behold, he prayeth ; " it may be said of him again. Ill. HIS PRAYER. 1. In his distress he betook lii=elf, to the mel"cy-seat, Like . Hezekiah, be spread the matter before the Lord, Affliction should drive us to, not , from, God. And we should come to pray, not to complain. 'I'.he- t)lrone of arac.e is sometimes turned into a bar of judgment, at which men• arraign G.od. Wh~n some. strange experience comes upon us we should ask concerning it in the.~udience-chamber. 2. He prayed to the Lord Jesus. This seems evident from ver. 9, ." that, the strenath of Christ may rest upon me." The servant's difficulties may :well be submitted to tho :Master. Christ had directly appointed the apostle; to Christ, ther!lfore, Paul brings his seeming hindrance. Whilst usually we pray to the Father in the.,Name of Christ, . we may at other times pray to Christ himself. 3. He prayed with importunity, There was no mistaking his earnestness. As Christ in Gethsemane pr11,yed " the third time,'' so thrice did this Christ-like apostle knock at heaven's gate. He wei;it on knocking until he got a response. Many in prayer want nothiug, ask nothing, get npthing. Some are so polite that they dread lest they should disturb God, and knock so lightly and daintily that it would require a microphone to make the sound audible. Others ring . and run away. The apostle stood at the gate till he was answered. Such holy boldness delight.; God instead of affronting him. 4. He prayed definitely. (1) For" this thing." . Some pray for everything in general, and therefore get nothing in particular. (2) That it might depart. Here, perhaps, he woot too far. If our troubles were sent ,away, . our best friends might be sent away. The counterpart of "a thorn in the fleph" may . be "grace in the spirit." His a good thing that it does not rest with us to send awil,y , or to retain; we should often send away the good and draw to ourselves the iiijurious, and evil IV. THE ANSWER. L A true amwer,yet not what was loolced/or. (Ver. 9.) Such a prayer, offered in such a manner, was certain of a response, but not of the response anticipated. God often answers our prayers by not answering them. We get what we want, not what we wish. We dictate our prayer; God dictates the ans"1'er. Generally . we do not ask enough-the apostle did not; to take away the thorn was small compared . with sanctifying its presence. To eject the devil's messenger was poor compared with transforming it into a ministerini spirit. 2. A lesson of faith. Paul's faith must transcend his feeling. He must lay hold of Christ with more tenacious grasp; he must . believe that Christ can use this trouble for high purposes. Perhap,s as he l~ol!:ed to. Christ with stronger faith he could realize that, as great purposes wer~ accomphsherl by the manv thorns in the flesh of Christ (he was crowned with thorns), so the one thorn in his fl~h should not prove unfruitful. Grapes might be gathered froµi this tho~n. 3. A definite a6S?J;rance. There was a basis for the faith demanded, as there always is. " My grace is sufficient for thee" (ver. 9). Christ engage11 to bear him through; can he believe this? The Lord's resources are boundless; they are our resources when strong faith binds us to their possessor. My "gr~e" may mean my.". love,•: whi~h secures all things needful for my servants; or the aid of the Holy Spmt, which will prove sufficient for every exigency. 4. An intimation of purpose. 'l'here was no muta,lre in sending or allowing the " thorn in the flesh." Prayer becomes bla.sphemou~ ou. xu.1-21.] 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORIN"'l'HL\NS. 305

when it proceods upon the assumption that God has made a blunder! The thorn in the flesh was the stem upon which theflower of the Divine glory was to blossom. 'fhe "messenger or Satan" would be made a herald proclaiming the power of Christ. Th1J apostle's flesh was to be a battle-field on which Christ would triumph. V. THE ISSUE. A new thought hae been given to Paul-Christ's c,lory will be enhanced. At once he begins to glory in this infirmity, "Most gladly°'' (ver. 9) or most sweetly; it became a delight of the highest kind. What he wanted to lose he ~ow wants to keep. With the thorn in the flesh he can become, as he could not without it, the dwelling-place of the power of Christ. It is enough if through his humiliation Christ may be exalted, if through his suffering Christ may be glorified. Many are more than content with being resigned under suffering; to submit they think is a mark of highest grace. J,3ut the apostle is far beyond this. He can "take .plea.sure" ( ver. 10) in troub)es, b~ause .through his troubles the power of Christ is more strikingly and impressively exhibited.-H.

entries.title: 2CO 12:11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Much, yet nothing. I. THE APOSTLE'S CLAIM. A large claim, put strongly. Paul. clai.med to be on a perfect equality with the leading apostles. Unwillingly he referred to this matter, which might look like self-glorification ; but when the occasion ea.me, his utterance was full and unmistakable. There is nothing derogatory in magni[ying our office, the evil lies in magnifying ourselves in it. It is not conceitednesR but righteousness to assert for ourselves what God has already asserted for ns. Paul felt that he must not lightly esteem, or allow others to lightly esteem, a high office conferred upon him by God, and an office in which God had signally witnessed to his efforts. Paul speaks about "the signs" of an apostle; the interesting question arises- What were these signs? We may note the following :-1. Knowledge of the gospel derived by immediate revelation from Christ (Gal. i. 12). 2. Being specially under the influence and teaching of the Divine Spirit, so as to be able to announce truth with authority (1 Cor. ii. 10-13; xii. 8, 29; xiv. 37), 3. External manifestations of Divine favour sanctioning claim to the apostleship. 4. Continued faithfulness to the gospel (Gal. i. !:l, 9). , 5.. Success, in preaching the gospel (1 Cor. ix. 2). 6. Power of communicating. the Holy Ghost by imposition of bands (Acts viii. 18). 7. Power of working miracles (ver, 12; Ro.m. :xv. 18, 19). 8. Holiness of life (eh. vi. 4). Such of these as ,could be ex.hibited to the Corinthians, had been, and there was one rtl8pect in which .his readers would scarcely contest Paul's claim, and to this with bis accustomed dexterity the apostle refers. If founding great Churches .was a mark of great apostleship, what an apostle Paul must have been to found such a Church as the Corinthian (ver. 13) ! 'l'his was a perfectly sound argument, but it was an argumentum ad hominem of a singularly .happy character. There was only one thing lacking, and .here the apostle blends irony with pathos-" I myself was not a burden to you: forgive me this wrong" (ver.13). For reasons given elsewhere in the Epistle, he had resolved not to derive any part of his temporal support from them. They might esteem this a slight. Had they lived in later <lays they would have counted i& a virtue! IL 'l'BE APOSTLE'S AOKNOWLEDGMENT. Paul's humility is marvellous. Yet it was not one whit greater then it ought to have been. The "thorn in the flesh" (ver. 7) has accomplished a gracious work. Paul has at the same time the clearest view of the Divine power and glory, and of his own insignificance and impotence. He does not take to himself for a moment what was not of himself. Note in ver. 12 he says, not "I wrought," but "were wrought "-he distinguishes between God and Paul! We ·have a beautiful insight into th'l apostle's mind. He has risen too high to deck himself in plumes stolen from his Lord. Though divinely endowed, strikingly witnessed to in his labours, beyond question the pre-eminent apostle, he says, "I am nothing." We wonder not that God used such a man. We magnify God's grace in him. Truly the promise had been amply fulfilled, "My grace is sufficient for thee" (ver. 9). Our pride is our folly-it drives God out and lets the devil in. We cannot be great because we will be so great. 'l'he bag is full of wind, so that it cannot be filled. III. LEARN: 1. Humility becomes 'US, It became Paul. If he had so lowly an estimate of himself, how little should we think of ourselves! J:,;ven if we are "great men," WCI are very small men compared with h4m. ~- Ilumilit'!I is rea~onable. It is 11ot :P,, CORlNTlllANli, Ji: 308 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTIIIANS. [cu. xn, 1..... 21.,

ficticin, but fact, to MY that we are 11othing. Pride is based on a lie, 3. Humility is generally associated with large mefulness,-H. • ' •

entries.title: 2CO 12:15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Self·111tpenditure. I. A Sl'LENDID ILLUSTRATION 61!' 0HBT8TIAN BERVICll!:, The apostle is carried beyond the thought of givin~ some time, or strength or propertv, for his beloved Corinthians; he expresses his perfect willingness to give himself. Ii:e· will not count it & grief, but &gladness, to expend himself for thetn. Whilst many find great difficulty in giving a little for others, the apostle seems to find none in giving ell. Here we have: 1. Wl,ole-souled devotion. Nothing can transcend the apostle's offer. And the voluntariness and the joy of the devotion place it in the first rank of ex.cellence. 2. .Earnest desire for welfare. The love of Paul for the Corinthians could not have been more forcibly expressed. Men gauge our love for them by what we &re willing to give up for them ; when we are willing to give up ourselves for them, they ce.nnot but be convinced of our sincerity. 3. Indication of the importance of Christian work~ For nothing else in the world would Paul have. willingly spent himself. But Christian servioe more than justified the self-sacrifice. In his judgment nothfog could compare with it for a moment. We may remember that in all departments of life we can render Christian service; spheres of labour become insignificant and mean only when Christian service is excluded from them. 4. .A striking imitation of ·Oh'rist.' Paul has caught his Master's spirit. His Lord laid down his life for him ; he wiU now lRy down his life for his Lord. Christ "gave himself." The Lord's servant is most fitted to do his Lord's work when he is most like his Lord. 5. .A secret of success. When we labour for Christ in such a spirt as this we are CeI'tain to prosper. • Failure is the child of half-heartedness and selfishness. Christ honours an entire consecration' to his service. IL SELF-EXPENDING CHRISTIAN SERVICE J'ROMPTED BY A mGH MOTIVE. The apostle· was willing to spend himself for fhe souls of the Corinthians-'-" and be spent for your souls" (New Version). In this labour he was seeking at the same time the highest glory of God and Christ, and the truest welfare of men. These objects unite in Christian service, which aims pre-eminently to do good to· the souls· of men.· The saving and perfecting of souls redounds supremely to the glory of 'the Divirie Being, whilst it secures the highest good for humanity. So dominated_ was the apostle by the desire to do good to the souls of men, that what is usually a very strong motive for action, viz. the love of others for us, was quite r.wept away. ·He declares that he will ex.pend himself for the Corinthia=, though this strongest indication of his love to them should produce a decreasing love for him on their part. The disinterested character ''of ttui, Christian service is here very strikingly displayed. It was by such self-expenditure as that of Paul's that early Christianity won its triumphs; it is for such self-expenditure that later Christianity pathetically calls. God is al ways thoroughly in earnest, but men are not. When men become so then "the arm of the Lord is revealed."-H.

entries.title: 2CO 12:2
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-".A man in Christ." St. Paul spoke of himself. Once he had been. out of Christ, though in a legal fashion very religious. But he gave up his legality when. he found Christ. He looked to him for help, fled to him for defence, and thenceforward lived in him as a new creature. It is the best short description of every believer. ·' • I. CHoSEN IN CHRIST. (Epb. i. 4.) We put this first, because this must come first in the Divine order and in the very nature of things. But man does not begin with any k:nowledcre of this as affecting himself. He grounds his faith, not on the·secretpurpose, but on the revealed good will of God to all in the gospel. It is after he has believed that he learns gratefully to trace bill own calling and salvation, in common with that of ell his fellow-believers, to the graciolll! choice and purpose of God. Then, as the seventeenth Article of the Church of England expresses it, "The godly consideration of preJdestinaLion and our election in Christ is full of sweet, pleasant, and unspeakable comfort to godly persons and such as feel in themselves the working of the Spirit of Christ;'' II. FnEELY GRACED IN THE BELOVED. (Eph. i. 6.) The man in Christ is embraced in the favour with which God regards his beloved Son. He has redemption an\i reconciliation to God, unsearchable riches, spiritual blessings in heavenly places, e.nd contin'\1a.l freedom of acce&8 to the Father in heaven. III. CREATED ..uraw DT CBBIST JEB'US, (Eph. ii. 10.) God begins thi~ work, as of old. 011, xn. 1-21.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 307

by causing light to shine out of darkness; then he introduces a new order, peai.:e and fertile life, and this is wrought on and in every genuine Christian. "If any matt be in Christ, he is a new creation." And therefore he does what is right, not by a. continna\ strain 1md effort against nature, but spontaneously and naturally, because he bas a clean heart and a right spirit. IV. ESTABLISHED IN CHRIST. (Ch. i. 21.) He who comes to Christ under the drawino- grace of the Spirit of God abides in him by the same Spirit, eo as to imbibe bis wisdom"' experience his support, and learn what consolation there is in him, and what comfort of love. So God confirms and establishes bis people in Christ, making good to them bis promises, anointing them, sealing them, and giving "the earnest of the Spirit" in their hearts. Thie is much more than being settled in one's religions opinions and habits. It is the staying of the mind on Christ. And usually it is reached through conflicts and sufferings thnt compel the soul to grapple more firmly the reality of Christ and the security of Divine promises in bim,just as trees rocked by the winds strike their roots the more widely and deeply into the ground (see 1 Pet. v. 10). V. :AI'PBOVED IN CHRIST. (Rom. xvi. 10.) Establishment relates to faith, knowledge, and comfort; approval refers to service. La.hour for the Lord ought to be rendered in the Lord, i.e. in virtue of union with him, and by the power derived from such union. But as there are gradations of faith and love among true Christians, so also there are degrees of diligence and thoroughness in service; and some servants are more approved than others, and shall have a more full reward. Oh to serve so as to have our Master's smile unon us now, and to be openly accepted of him at bill con::.ing as good and faithful servants I VL PEBFEOT IN CHRIST JEBUB: COMPLETE IN BIM. (Col. i. 28; ii.10.) There is allperfect resource in our Lord. But all have not attained. There are babes in Christ, not perfect or mature; let them go on to fuller statme and strength. It is an object to be desired and worked for, that every believing man may be presented perfect in Christ Jesus, i.e. ripe and mature, not crude or ill-developed in the Christian character. VIL ABLEEP IN J EBUS. (1 Cor. xv. 18; 1 Thess. iv. 14, 18.) If we are Christ's, death is ours. It cannot do us hurt or·separate us from the love of God. For a man who is in Christ, the whole state of death-is brightened by the love and faithfulness of the Lord. Blessed-are the dead who die in him. Sweetly sleep the labourers who, when their day's work for Jesus is ended, fall asleep in him. • " Oh, never doleful dream age.in • Shall break the happy slumber when ' He giveth his beloved sleep.'" F. Vcrs. 7-9.-.Ar,; instructive experience. Like all true saints, Paul was modest about his own experience. He did not write down his heavenly rapture and what followed it, till fourteen years bad passed, and then he wrote it only because he felt compelled to prove to the Uorinthians that even " in visions and revelations of the Lord" be surpassed the false apostles as much as in labours and sufferings far Christ. Never did Christian tell an experience more .useful and strengthening to the Church. I. AFFLICTION THE ANTIDOTE TO PRIDE. we do not speak so much of the naturu pride of men over personal advantages of body or mind, over rank or riches, as of that subtle pride which ls apt to creep into the heart after a great influx of spiritual light and joy. One InaY be exalted overmuch on account of the clearer vision of heavenly things or the near access to the Lord which he has enjoyed. But there comes a timely affliction or rebuke, not merely to correct pride if it is indulged, but to anticipate and prevent its rising. "Lest I should be exal'ted." The wise man accepts this as a kindness from God. "There was given to me a thorn in the flesh." II. PRAYER THE ANTIDOTE TO DEBPOND]qi!CY. "I besought the Lord thrice." When one is ce.st down, worldly-wise friends can only bid him cheer up, cast off dull care, etc. But the resource of the Christian is to pray to the God of his life. And prayer must be repeated. The Saviour prayed thrice before the angel from heaven appeared to strengthen him.. Paul prayed thrice before the answer of grace and peace fell upon his fain ting soul. 30~ THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [en. xn. 1-21,

III. Grmrn's GRACE THAT BWEETENB At,L. Re knows well the piercing of thorn&i the fi<'ry <lart.s, nnd the "blRSt of the torrible ones," and he cn.n have compassion. Re did not, indeC'<l, ~oo fit to relieve his servant Paul at onoo of his distress, but assured him of compensative gl'BOO and sustaining strength; and so the apparent ovil was turned into a blessing, the pain and sorrow into joy. Be of good comfort, 0 believers I Ago.inst your own felt weakness set Christ's strength; and against all malice or Satan and his messengers l!et Christ's sufficient graoe.-F.

entries.title: 2CO 12:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Visiotls and revelatioM. "I will come to viAiona and revelations of tho Lord." The apostle bad been dwelling on his personal experiences. He had· been compelled by the evil things that were said or him to refer to his 01vn life condnot and sufferings for Christ's S1Lke, in self-vindication. He would, however, not' have spoken one word about these things if the honour of Christ had not been bound up with his claim to apostleship. He had now said everything that needed to be said about himself· and it was every way pleasanter and heaJ.thier to turn away from his own doings and 11ufferings, and to fix his heart and his thoughts upon what God had done for him. Upon the Divine visions and revelations given to him he in great part rested hie apostolic claim. To him an apostle was, just what a prophet of the olden time had been, a man who had direct and personal commnnications with the Lord Jesus, and received instruc- tions immediately from him. For such instances in St. Paul's career, see Acts ix. 4-6; xvi. 9 ; xviii. 9; xxii. 18; xxiii. 11 ; xxvii. 28 ; Gal iL 2; and the scenes recorded in the chapter now before us. This claim to direct revelation the enemies of St. Paul denied, and laughed to scorn his pretensions as the indications of insanity. Dean Plumptre te1ls us that" in the Clementine Homilies-a kind of controversial romance representing the later views of the Ebionite or Juda.izing party, in which most recent critics have recognized a thinly veiled attempt to present the characteristic features of St. Paul under the pretence of an attack on Simon Magus, just as the writer of a political novel in modern t.imes m~ht draw the portraits of his rivals under fictitious names- we find strt>ss laid on the alleged claims of Simon to have bad communications from the Lord through visions and dreams and outward revelations; and this claim is contrasted '\\•ith that of Peter, who ·had personally followed Ohrist during his ministry on earth. What was said then, in the form of this elaborate attack, may well have been said before by the more malignant advocates of the same party. The charge of insanity was one easy to make, and of all charges, perhaps, the most difficult to refute by one who gloried in the facts which were alleged as its foundation-who did see visions and did • speak with tongues' in the ecstasy of adoring rapture." Compare the expression, "whether we be beside ourselves," in eh. v. 13. When the particular visions c11me to which reference is made in the passage before us cannot certainly be known. St. Paul only aids us by referring to the time as "about fourteen years ago." The suggestion we prefer is that they were grpted during the time of his fainting.afrer the stoning at Lystra, and were the Divine comfortings of that hour of sorest peril and distress (Acts xiv. 19). L VISIONS AND REVELATIOli'S ARB AGBNOIBS WHICH GoD HAS ALWAYS USED. They do not belong to any one age. We have no right to say that they are limited to ancfent times. There have always been the true and the counterfeit ; but the true shonlci !lot be miSBed or denied because the false ha'l"e been found out. There are good gold coins, or men would not trouble to make spurious sovereigns. Fanaticism deludes its victims into imaginary visions, but souls that are kin with God, and open to him, can receive communications from him. Illustrate from all ages, e.g. Noah, Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Samuel, David. Isaiah, Joseph (the husband of, Mary), aged Simeon, Zacharias, ete. So in the Christian age we fµid visions granted to Cornelius, Philip, Peter, and John, as well as Paul, and traces of pro.phets, such as. Agabns, and even of prophetesses. St. Paul's visions were probably of ttie nature of a trance; the mind being absorbed in contemplation may be prepared to receive Divine revealings. It is right to subject all claims to visions to careful scrutiny, and the• things communicated to men at such times must bo tested by their harmony with the written revelation ; but we need not refuse to recognize the truth that God has direct relations to souls now as certainly as in past ages. Both truth and duty may still b1 directly revealed.

II. THEY COME TO OERTAIN PREPARED INDIVIDUALS. Not to masses, not to ChnrcheR, not to meetings. 'l'he vision is for individuals, who are thns made agents in the com- munication t~ men of the Divine thought and will. F. W. Robertson says, "To comprehend the visions we must comprehend the man. For God gives vi8ions at his own will, and according to cortnin and fixed laws. He does not inspire every one. He does not reveal his mysteries to men of ~elfish, or hard, or phlegmatic temperaments. He gives preternatural communications to those whom he prepares beforehanrl by a peen liar spiritual sensitiveness. There are, physically, certain sensitivenesscs to sound an,] colour tho.t qualify men to become gifted musicians and painters; so, spiritually,1 there are certain strong original susceptibilities (I say original, as derived from God, the origin of all), and on these God bestows strange gifts and sights, deep feelings not to be uttered in ~ume.n language, and immeasurable by the ordinary standard. Such a man was St. Paul-a very wondrous nature, the Jewish nature in all its strength. We know that the Jewish temperament fitted men to be the organs of a revelation. Its fervour, it8 rrioq1l sense, its veneration, its indomitable will, all adapted the highest sons of the nation for receiving hidden truths and communicating them to others." III. THEY COME ON PARTICULAR OCCASIONS. By the law of Divine economy, only when they a.re the precise thing demanded, the only agency that will efficiently meet the case. IV. THEY'C01'4E IN GRACIOUSLY ADAPTED FORMS. Heard voices sometimes, a.t other times dreams, ocular visions, symbols, trances, and mental panoramas. Close by showing that; because the modem mode is direct to souls, immediate to the sha.ping of men's thoughts, and not through symbols, or dreams, or visions, we need not lose the conviction that, upon due occasions still, God gives to some amongst us insight and revelation of his truth.-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 12:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Satan's messenger; or, the thorn in the flesh. It would be e. grave mistake to make this description of St. Paul's affliction the basis of any argument for the personality or agency of Satan. He does but use the familiar Jewish figure of speech, wh_ich may or may not embody for him auy doctrine concerning Satan. The figure is'most strikinglyused in the introduction to the Book of Job; but the following other passages illustrate how familiar it was to the Jewish mind : Luke xiii. 1ti; Acts v. x. 38.; 1 Cor; 5 ; 1 Thess. ii. 18 ; 1 Tim;. i. 20. "These are enough to prove that, while men referred special forms of suffering of mind and body, chiefly the former, to the agency of demons, they were prepared to recognize the agency of Satan in almost every form of botlily calamity." No single d~cription of Satan can cover the entire Scripture representation of him, but one aspect presented by it has not been dnly considered. He is sometimes regarded as the agent, or executor, of the Divine purpose in physical calamity, and even in moral testings through temptation. We may think of an angel of temptation as well as of an angel of death. We may not even think of Satan 33 in any sense actirig 'independently. He, too, comes fully within the Divine rulings and overrulings, What the nature of the apostle's affliction or temptation W33 cannot be certainly known from _his descriptions of it. Many explanations have been suggested. Lightfoot summarizes them thus: (1) a bodily ailment of some kind: (2) some opposition encountered from his enemies, or suffering endured; (3) carnal longings; (4) spiritual trials, doubtings, etc. Archdeacon Farrar thinks the "thorn" must have been some physical malady, and suggests epilepsy, of which be says," It is painful; it is recurrent; it opposes an immense difficulty to all exertion; it may nt any time cause e. temporary- ~uspension of work; it is intensely humiliating to the person who suffers from 1t; 1t uercises 9. repellent effect on those who witness its distressing manifestations." But he ,adds that there can be no doubt that St. Paul also suffered from ophthalmia, and that this disease fulfils in every particular the conditions of the problem. Dean Plumptre favours the idea of corporeal rather than mental suffering, and says," Nor need we b6 surprised that this infirmity-neuralgia. of the head and face ?r inflammation of the eyes, perhaps in some measure the after-consequences of the blmdness at Damascus- should be dcscribqd as • a messencrer of Satan.'" Another suggest10n has been made whicl'l is fresh and interesting, a;d worthy of very patient consideration. Prufessor Lias 'writes "Our lust alternative must be some defect of character, calculated to interfere with St. Paul's success as a minister of Jesus Obrist. AnJ the defect which 310 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORIN'l'HIANS. [oa. xn. 1-21.

f~lls in best with what we know of St. Paul is an ~nfi~mity of temper. Thero ,seems little doubt that he gave way to an outbreak of this kmd when before the Sanhcdrim, though he set himself right at once by a prompt apology (Act.a xxiii. 2-6), A similar idea is suggested by St. Paul's unwillingness to go to Corinth until the points in dispute between him and a considerable portion of the Corinthian Church were in a fair way ot being settled. In fact, his conduct was precisely the reverse of that of a person who felt himself endowed with great ta.et, persuasiveness, and command of temper. Such a man would trust little to messages and letters, much to his own presenoe and personal influence. St. Paul, on the contrary, feared to visit Corinth until there was a reasonable prospect of avoiding all altercation. In fact, he could not trust himself there. He 'feared that God would humble him among them' (eh. xii. 21). He desired ,above all things to avoid the necessity of 'using sharpness,' very possibly because he feared that, when once compelled to assume a tone of severity, his language might exceed .the bounds of Christian love. The supposition falls in with what we know of'the apostle' before his conversion (Acts vii. 58; ix. 1). It is confirmed by his stern language to Elymas tbe sorcerer (Acts xiii. 10), with which we may compare the .much niilde1 language used by St. Peter on a far more awful occasion (Acts v. 3, 9). The quarrel between St. Paul and St. Barnabas makes the supposition infinitely more probable. The passage, Gal. iv. 13, 14, may be interpreted of the deep personal affection which the apostle felt he had inspired in spite of his occasional irritability of manner. The expr=ion (Gal. iv. 20), that he 'desired to be present with them, and to. change· his voice,' would seem to point in the same direction. And if we add to these con- siderations the fact, which the experience of God's saints in all ages ha.s •conclusively established, of the difficulty of subduing an infirmity of temper~, as· well a.s the pain, remorse, and humjliation such an infirmity is wont' to cause .to thos~ •who groan under it, we may be inclined to believe that not the lea.at probable hypothesis concerning the ' thorn,' or ' stake,' in the flesh is, that the loving heart of. the apostle bewailed as his sorest trial the misfortune· that by impatience. il!, word. h,e had ofter.. wounded those for wbom he would willingly .have given ,h,is life." What- ever the form of the trial may have been, we note- ••: L ST. PAUL's THOUGHTS ABOUT IT. These may be unfolded and illustrated gene~, rnlly, in relation (1) to Christian culture; "(2) to Christian w'ork, and especially (3) in rela.tion to peril of spiritual pride. St. Paul saw clearly that t~e humiliation came " through the abundance of the revelations ; " and "lest he should be puffed up beyond 1 1 measure." •• . • • .

II. ST. PAUL'S LESSON LEABNED FROM IT. It was mainly tbis-'.-tliat the mission of smfering may be continuous through life. It may be the point of God'.s dealing with us that he does not sanctify ua by sudden, occasional, and severe afflictions, but by calling us to bear a lifelong burden of disability or frailtyr Troubles of this kind cannot be removed in response to prayer, because to remove them :wrould be to check the sanctifying process. God, in sendin,g a temporary affliction, may have a temporary end in view, and so, when that end is duly reached, the affliction may be removed. But if the work of our sanctification is, in the Di vine wisdom;. to }:le wrought by a continuollll life-pressure, then the response to our pra,Yer can only be this: " My grace is sufficient for thee." Dean Stanley points out that " St. Paul~s sufferings were to him what the mysterious agony that used at times to seize on Alfr~d, in the. midst of feast and revel, had been to the saintly and heroic king, a disci.(>line, ~orking for his perfection."-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 12:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Sufficient grace. The following incident from John Builyan's experience may serve to introduce this subject. One evening, as Bunyan· was in a meeting of Christian people, full of sadness and terror, 1mddenly there "brake in." upon him with great power, and three times together, the words, "My grace is 1:1u,fiicient for thee; my grace is sufficient for thee; my grace is sufficient for thee." And "Oh, methought," says he, " that every word was a mighty word unto me; as 'my,' and 'grace,' and ' sufficient,' and ' for thee,' they were then, and sometimes are still,. far bigger ,than others be." The grea.t practical questipn for us, in our endoovour to live th~ godly lifo, is not-What have we to bear? but,-Wha.t strength have we for the bearing? God's help never comes first to a man in his circumsuvn,cea, but always first in him, The 011. xn, 1-21.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO '!HE CORINTHIANS. 311

gmce given is gre.ce helping him in the circumstances, So the Christian often knows that he is helped when those around him can see no signs of the helping. God's promise from the olden time Is this, "As thy day so shall thy strength be." In all our relations with human trouble, our attention is directed to the removal of the trouble itself or the change of the circumstances which occasioned the . trouble. We move the pain-wearied sufferer into a position of greater ease. We soften and smoothe the pillow for the &Ching head. We offer temporary help to the man distressed in business. But God does not pro,1IJ.ise any man that he. will alter his circumstances or altogether relieve him from his trouble. The economy of life is arranged, in the Divine wisdom, for the greatest good of the greaj;est number1, and consequently some of those circumstances which brio"' tl'Ouble to Christian hearts cannot be altered without involving injury to other: God. "strengthens with strength in the soul." To him body and circumstance are secondary tp.ings; souls are of the first importance, and bodies and circumstances gain their importance by their influence on souls. Inward strength to bear is a far higher provision than any mere mastery of the ills and troubles of the life. A man is never lost until he he.s lost hElart. But if God supplies inward strength we never shall lose heart, and sp-we never shall be lost. Outwardly a man may be tossed about, worn, wearied, lost, wounded, almost proken, and yet inwa~dly he may be kept in perfect peace ; his mind may be stayed on God;· he may be "strong in the Lord,and in the power of his might." We may say of this '' sufficient grace " that it is- ,.J, ADAPTED, We are to conceive of the grace of God, not e.s a. great mass, a qui,.ntity of which is duly measured out to meet our need. but rather as a treasnry of.various kinds and various colours, from which may be obtained just those threads that will match our circumstances and repair the disasters into which we have fallen.. II. TrnELY. Here we require to distinguish between what we think to be timely and what. God thinks to be . timely, remembering that God never delays, but is never hurried. He waits for the moment of extremity. "'When the tale of bricks is doubled, then comes Moses," And ,it· should also be shown that we may not look for some particular. grace and help to-day, which God knows will only be required to-morrow. The, .very_ charm of •• sufficient grace" is that it is precisely the thing for the occasion." .Those who are looking for kinds of grace for which they have no immediaf;e and pressing needs will be in danger of missing the gracious provisions which thei,ir Lord is ~ver JUaking for them. The way between earth and heaven is a ladder- Jacob 'saw it-and ·the angels ea.me up and down it. We cannot reach the top by lookitig up; only by putting our feet up one round afteranother. And God is willing to be ever close beside us, holding us with his hand and strengthening us for each uplifted step. . ·• ; . .· . III. ABUNDANT. That. is assured in the fact that it is the grace of God, who is.able to do exceedingly abundantly for us above all that we ask or think. The man with " sufficient grace" is efficient to all work, whether it be bearing or doing. He is nowhere alone; grace is with him.-R; T .

. Ver. 9.-Glorying in infirmities. In introduction should be given some high and noble instances of triumph over disease, pain, or disability, in doing philanthropic and Christ.ian work; e.g. Baxter, Robert Hall, H. Martyn, C. Pattison, F. W. Robertson, e.k\ Show that, while bodily strength may be consecrated to God's service, it is also tme that physical weakness may serve him, and a man's very frailty glorify his Lord, This may be further opened out by showing how- l. IT BEARS UPON .HUMILITY. The grace which is the necessary completion and final adornment of Christian character. The grace which puts on Christian fruitage all the bloom. Humility is won by the pressure of God's hand upon us. . II. IT NOURISHES DEPENDENCE ON Goo. "When I am weak, then am I strong." This is the Christian paradox. Such dependence is .not easy ; it is one of the things to which experience of failure and frailty alone can bring us. He is fitted for life and for heaven who from his deep heart. says, ".I cannot, but God can." III. IT CULTIVATES OII.ARAOTEB. We know that physical weakness bears directly and continuously upon temper, disposition, and virtue. Afflictions never test us, never bear upon the whole culture of character, as does continuous pain or frailty, "As the outward man perishes, the inward man is renewed day by day," Sl2 THE SECOND ltPIS'l'LE TO 'l'liE COlUN'l'liIANS. IV. IT KEEPS A MAN OPEN TO God. By its constant reminder of the need of God. 'fhe frail man proves the preciousness of prayer. F. W. Robertson most forcibly sRyt1 of prayer, "The true value of prayer is not this-to bend the eternal will to ours, but this-to bend our wills to it." Frail, ever-sufferin~ Paul laboured "more abundantly than they all," and astonishing still is the soul-work that can be gotten out of feeble men and women-with God's grace.-R. T.

entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -0aught with guik. "Nevertheless, being crafty, I oaughtyou with guile." This expression occasions serious difficulty to the exegete. It may be that St. Paul is . referring to the Mcusation made against him that, being a orafty man he had cauaht the_~rintbians wit~ gui_le. He repudiates altogether such a charge, ~nd pleads, a~ a sufficient proof of his guilelessness, that no man could say he had ever used his official position to make perso~al gains. Archdeacon Farrar says," Bein~ confessedly one who strove for p~e and umty, _who endeavoured to ~eet all men half-way, who was ready to be all thrngs to all men 1f by any means he might save some, he has more than once· to vindicate his character from those charges of insincerity, craftiness, dishonesty, guile, man-pleasing, and flattery which are, perhaps, summed up ih the general depreciation . which he so indignantly rebuts, that' he walked according to the flesh,' or in other words, that his motives were not spiritual, bntlow and selfish.-" He paraphrases the sentence taken as our text thus: " But stop I though I did not burden you, yet ' being· a cunning person, I caught you with guile.' Under the pretext• of a collection I got money out of you by my confederates I I ask you, is that a fact?" A possible insinuation of the Corinthians is hereby anticipated and refuted; and we need not treat the statement of the text as a.ny acknowledgment by St. Paul that he had adopted , any gnileful schemes. No man could have been m·ore thoroughly genuine, 'more honourably straightforward. The subject_ for our consideration ma.y be treated under three di visions. • I. 'l'HE IDEA OF "CAUGHT WITH GUil,E" THAT IS INADmssmLE IN CHRISTIAN' WORK; ' 1. Anything approaching to" doing evil that good may <!Ome" is inadmissible. 2. So is any altering or qualifying the fundamental truths, claims, and ·duties• of the gospel. 3. So is any kind ·of action that is immoral, or of ,which the morality is even doubtful. Illustrate by some of the guileful principles enunciated by the Jesuit fa.there, and so mercilessly exposed by Pa.seal in the • Provincial Letters.' Sincerity- and simplicity a.re first virtues in Christian workers; both the man and his labours must be such as can be searched through and through. Guile, as the world understands the term, must not be once known among. us, as becometh saints. II. THE IDEA OF" CAUGHT WITH GUILE" THAT IS ADMISSIBLE IN CHBISTLU{ WOBK. In the sense of adaptation to capacity it is an essential feature of Christian service. This may sometimes appear to. the onlooker as guile. In teaching children or uneducated people, truth has to be simplified, to be set in figure and parable, and broken up into parts and pieces, and such guilefulness St. Paul recognizes as valuable. He fed the people with "milk" when he knew that they were unftt to receive "strong meat" of truth. Our Lord himself was guileful in this good sense, for at the close of his Intercourse with his disciples he said, "I have many things to say unto you, but ye cannct bear them now." It may also be shown that there is a " quick-wittedness" and skilful seizing of opportunities, which are gifts -finding honourable spheres in the Christian Church. • Ill. 'fHE IDEA OF "CAUGHT WITH GUil,E" THAT NODLE-JIIINDED :MEN SHRINK FBOH Elli'LOYING. Such are the various sensational devices of modern -revivalism. 'rhe masses are to be caught with the guile of trumpet, and drum,.and dress, and excited weetings. We need not ·say that such things are inadmissible, because they are not morally wrong. But where there is a fuU sympathy with the Divine·Lord, who l<did not strive, nor cry, nor cause his voice to be heard in-the streets," all such gui-lefulnessee cannot but be painful. Anything approaching to an advertising• of the gospel or the vreachers of the gospel grieves the sensitive feeling of all who ~now that the gospel needs no such introductions, but is itself God's power unto salvation to every one that believes. Our "yea " had better be simple " yea;" with DO blast of trumpet or roU .ot drum let 1ll! tell men of the life there is for all in Christ our living Saviour; and let our only guile be arlaptation..--R. entries.content: -The hwmbling of God's ministers. "I fear . . . lest, when I come again, my God will humble rno among yon." "There is something almost plaintive in the tone in which the apostle speaks of the sin of his disciples as the only real 'humiliatioo, which he has to fear." 'fhe following points will be readily worked out and illustrated nccording to the experiences of the preacher:- I. Suon HUMDLINIJS OOME FROM SEEMING FAILUilES. Compare our Lord's distressful roproach of Capernaum and other towns on the shores of the lak.e of Galilee. See also St. Paul's trouble over the failure of the Galatians from their primitive faith: "O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you ? " etc. II. SuoH HUMDLINIJS COME FBOM STRIFE AND DIVISIONS. As illustrated in the Corinthian Church (see 1 Cor. ii.). Such strife may arise from (1) false teaching; (2) masterful individuals, who make parties; (3) misunderstandings; (4) exercise of necessary Church discipline. III. Suoa HUMDLINGS COME FBOH INDIVIDUAL BAOKBLIDINGB. There is no sadder phase of experi~nce for Christian ministers than the spiritual and moral failure of their converts, and of those whom they have most fully trusted in Christian life and work. So often men fall fo.to temptation and are overcome in their middle life. When ministers look for the ripest fruitage, then there is blight and death; wealth, pleasure, vice, smite and kill the soul, and the pastor weeps over the toil of life that seems to have been all in vain. St. Paul spoke of the Corinthians as "his glory and joy;" and the things which he goes on to mention in this verse put shame on his work, for the gospel call is "not unto uncleanness, but unto holiness." And ministers spend their strength for nought if thos_c who b~lieve a.re not" careful to maintain good works."-R. T.

entries.title: 2CO 13:1–13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Paul's epistolary farewell to the Corinthians. "This iii the third time I am coming to you," etc. This chapter concludes Paul'~ letters to the Corin_thians, There is no evidence that he wrote a word to them after this, The letters had evidently. been a task to him. To a man of his tender nature no duty could be more painful, than tm,,t of censure and reproach, Nothing hut a sense of loyalty to the holiness of Ohristianit7 coold have urged hiui W, it. No doubt he felt & burden rolled from hie on. xm.1-14,) THE SECOND EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COBINTHIANS. 815

heart, nnd a freer breath, when be dictated the laet sentence. He was now to visit them for the third time, determined to execute the disciplfoe tha.t miaht be require<l, earnestly hoping at the same time that, when he was once more a.m~ngst them, the necessity for such discipline would not appea.r. In this concluding chapter we .find words of warning, exhortation, prayer, comfort, e.nd benedictum. I. WORDS OF WARNING. He warns them of a. chastisement which he determined to inflict upon e.11 offenders, both in doctrine e.nd conduct, against the gospel of Christ. Four things e.re suggested here concerning the discipline he intended to prosecute. I. The discipline would be righteous. "In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established." llere is e. rule quoted and endorsed by Christ (1\fatt. xviii. 16), e.n e.xiom of the Jewish Law and e. n:i.tural dictate of judicial policy. What he probably means to say, is, "I will not chastise any without proper evidence. I will not trust. to rumours or surmises; I will test every case myself, so that justice shall be c'.one. Therefore the true need not fear, the false alone need apprehend." 2. The discipline would be rigorous. " I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were prescn t, the second time; and being absent now I write to •them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare." He had threatened this in his former letter (1 Cor. iv. 13-19), in which he had also indicated severity (1 Cor. v. 5), and spoken of 0 delivering them to Satan "-an expression which probably means not only excommunication, but the infliction of corporal suffering. The blindness of Elymas and the death of Ananiae and Sapphir~ are instances of the power of the apostles over the b_ody of men. 'l'his chastisement would be dealt, not only to the notorious incestuous perso~ often referred to, but to " all other;" he would "spare" none. "I will not spare." A more terrible chastisement know I not than entire excommunication from the fellowship 'of the g9od. • 3. The discip,line would demonstrate the existence of Christ in him. ,"Since.ye seek a proof of Christ !!peaking in me." "They had called in q•Jcstion his apostoHc· authority, they had demanded the evidence of his Divine commission .. He ~ays he_ would now furnish such evidence by inflicting just punishment on all offenders, ancl they .should have abundant proof that Christ spoke by him." _He .could hav_e given, this proof sooner, but he acted in this respect like Christ, an_d. was. c9ntent to aJ>pear "weak'' amongst them, in order that his power might be more cc;mspicuously displayed. "For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we shall live with hirµ_ by the .Power of G9d toward 1ou." "The thought," says Dean Plumptre, "that underlies the apparently hard sayrng is that the disciples of Christ share at once in their Lord's weakness and in his strength. We, too, are weak, says the apostle, we .have our. share in infirmities and sufferings, which are ennobled by the thought that they a.re ours because we a.re his,·but we know that we shall live in the highest sense in the activities of the spiritual life, which also we shall share with him, a.nd wp.ich comes to us by the power of God. • This life will be manifested in the exercise of our spiritual power towards you and for your good." In the case of the truly good, i11 ,all weakness there is strength, and the weakness one day will disappear and the strength be manifest. 11. WORDS OF EXHORTATION. "Examine yourselves." Self-scrutiny is at once 11 duty the most urgent and the most neglected. Hence the universal prevalence of self-ignorance. Even men who know a very great deal of the world without are ignorant of the world within, the world of worlds. 1. The momentous point to be tested in self-scrutiny. "Whether ye be in the faith." Not whether you have faith in you, for all men are more or less credulous, and have some kind of faith in them; but whether you are "in the faith." The faith here is the gospel, or rather the Christ of the gospel; whether you are in Christ, in the character of Christ. Intellectually and morally, all men a.re living in the characters of others. The grand thing is to be 111 the character of Christ, in his principles, sympathies, aims, etc. 2. The momentou,s conclusion to be reached by self-scrutiny. "Know ye not [emphatic] your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" If you are in the faith, you iire in his character, and he is in your life; nay, your lilii itself. Should you find yo11 are not in the faith, ye are "reprobates," counterfeits, spurious, not genuine; tares, not wheat; hypoc~ites, ~lere, then, is a wol'k ~or every man to do-:-" examine" himself, introspect, scrutinize, decide, and thus know h1a real moral cond1t10D, :rtfl '.l'B:E SEOOND EPlSTLE TO 'l'HE CORlNTlIIANS. [oit. xtu. 1-u.

m. Wonns OF PBA YER. "Now I pray to God," etc. For 'Whl\t does he pray? Not for his own reputation or himself. As ir he had said, "I am not anxious about roy own standing amongiit you." He prays for two things. 1. Tlla,t they should. be kept from the wrong. " Now I pray to God that ye do no evil." "Do no evil," nothing inconsistent with the character and te!lching of Christ. "Cease to do evil learn t,o do well." 2. Thri,t they should possess the right. "Not that we should appc~r approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates." "We pray not that we may gain a reputation as successful workers in your eyes or those or others, but that you may do that which is nobly good (may advance from a negative to a positive form of holiness), even though the result of that may be that we no longer J;>llt our apostolic supernatural powers int,o play, and so seem to fail in the trial to which you challenge us." IV. WoRDS OF COMFORT. "We can do nothing agninst the truth." There are two comfortin~ ideas here. 1. That truth is v.nin;'urable. "We can do nothing against the truth." Let the" truth" here stand for Jesus, who is the" Truth," the great moral Reality incarnated, all that is real in doctrine and duty embodied in him; who can injure such? Man can do much against theories of truth, conventional manifestations of truth, ecdesia.stical_ representations of truth, verbal revelations of truth. The more he docs against these, perhaps, the better; but he can do nothing against ICthe truth,n its essence. :Man may quench all the gas-lamps in the world, but he cannot dim one star. The great ethical a.nd doctrinal truths embodied in the lire and teaching of Christ are imperishable, they live in all religions. Men can destroy the forms of nature, level the mountains, dry up the rivers, bum the forests, but can do nothing against the imperishable elements of nature, and these elements will live, build up new mountains, open fresh rivers, and create new forests. You can do nothing against the truth. 2. That goodness is v.npwnishable. " For we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong: and this also we wish, even your perfection.n It is unpunishable: (1) Because it is goodness. The best of men are too "weak" in authority to punish those who are" strong" in goodness. And in truth there is no authority in the univer~e, even God himself, to punish goodness. The stronger a man is in goodness, the weak~t the power to chastise him. Hence Paul wishes to find theni "strong.,. in goodness when he comes amongst them. He wishes this because goodness is their " perfection," or restoration. The way to paralyze all penal forces is to promote the growth of goodness. (2) Because it is restorative. "Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord bath given me to edification, and not to destruction." Its destiny is "edification," not "destruction;" hnilding up, not pulling down. Moral goodness •is .the restorative power in the universe. • V. WoRDs OF BENEDICTION. "Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, he of good comfort, be of one mind, live in pea.ce; and the God of love and peac~ shall he with you." His benedictory words imp:ly: 1. Be happy. "Farewell," which means rejoice. To he happy they must be "perfect," " of good comfort," etc. 2. Be blest of God.. "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, he with you u.U." • •
